uni-ba-eco-development.title: Development Economics — theories, measurement, policy
uni-ba-eco-development.description: Concepts and measurement of development, classic development theories, poverty and inequality, population, human capital and institutions, and trade, aid and sustainable development. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA (Hons) Economics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Meaning and measurement of development
courses.summary: Growth versus development, Sen's capability approach, per capita income and PPP, the Human Development Index and its computation, and other composite indicators.
outcomes: Distinguish growth from development
Explain Sen's capabilities and functionings
Compare incomes using PPP
Compute an HDI value from raw data
Critically assess composite development indices

scenes.text: Two Indian states have similar per capita incomes.
One has far higher literacy and life expectancy. Which is more developed?

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Economic growth**: sustained rise in real output/income per capita.
- **Development**: broader improvement in well-being — health, education, freedom, reduced poverty and inequality, structural change.
- **Seers' questions**: what has happened to poverty, unemployment and inequality?
- **Sen's capability approach**: development as expansion of **capabilities** — real freedoms to achieve valued **functionings** (being healthy, educated, participating in society). Income is a means, not the end ('Development as Freedom', 1999).

steps.title: Kerala example
steps.body: Kerala achieved high literacy and life expectancy at moderate income levels through public action in health and education — often cited to show development need not wait for high growth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using growth and development as synonyms.
- Saying Sen rejects income — he treats it as instrumentally important.

statements.s: Development is broader than growth in per capita income.
statements.why: It includes health, education, freedom and equity.

statements.s: Sen defines development as expansion of capabilities.
statements.why: That is the capability approach.

statements.s: High growth automatically eliminates poverty.
statements.why: Distribution and public action matter.

statements.s: Functionings are the things a person achieves, such as being well nourished.
statements.why: Capabilities are the set of achievable functionings.

quiz.why: Sen's 1999 book set out the capability approach for a wide audience.
He argued development requires improvement on these three.
It is instrumentally valuable for achieving functionings.

story.title: A haircut in Delhi and New York

scenes.text: A haircut costs ₹150 in Delhi and $30 in New York.
Market exchange rates understate how far rupees go at home — PPP corrects this.

steps.title: PPP
steps.body:
- Market exchange rates reflect traded goods and capital flows; non-traded services are cheaper in poor countries.
- **PPP exchange rate**: rupees needed to buy the same basket that $1 buys in the US (International Comparison Program).
- Developing countries' incomes look much larger at PPP than at market rates.
- **Price level ratio** = PPP rate / market rate.

steps.title: Solved: PPP conversion
steps.body:
Per capita income ₹2,40,000. Market rate ₹80/$; PPP rate ₹20/$.

- Market: 2,40,000/80 = **$3,000**.
- PPP: 2,40,000/20 = **$12,000**.
- Price level ratio = 20/80 = 0.25: Indian prices about a quarter of US prices for the basket.

steps.title: When to use which
steps.body: Use PPP for living standards and poverty comparisons; market rates for trade, debt and financial flows.

statements.s: PPP-based incomes of poor countries are usually higher than market-rate incomes.
statements.why: Non-traded goods are cheaper there.

statements.s: Market exchange rates are best for comparing living standards.
statements.why: PPP is better for that purpose.

statements.s: The International Comparison Program estimates PPPs.
statements.why: It is coordinated by the World Bank.

statements.s: A price level ratio of 0.3 means local prices are 30% of US prices.
statements.why: PPP/market = 0.3.

quiz.q: PPP comparisons are most appropriate for:
quiz.why: They reflect what incomes can buy domestically.

scenes.text: Health: how long people live.
Knowledge and income complete the HDI — combined by a geometric mean.

steps.title: Method (UNDP)
steps.body:
Dimension index = (actual − min)/(max − min).

- **Health**: life expectancy, goalposts 20 and 85 years.
- **Education**: mean years of schooling (0–15) and expected years (0–18); education index = average of the two.
- **Income**: GNI per capita (2017 PPP $), goalposts 100 and 75,000, using natural logs.
- **HDI** = (I_health × I_education × I_income)^(1/3).

steps.title: Related indices
steps.body:
- **IHDI**: inequality-adjusted HDI.
- **Gender Development Index** and **Gender Inequality Index**.
- **MPI**: multidimensional poverty (health, education, living standards; Alkire–Foster).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using an arithmetic mean (pre-2010 method).
- Forgetting the log transformation for income.

bands.text: Health index below about 0.38 — typical of high-mortality settings.
Health index 0.38–0.77: many developing countries lie here.
Health index 0.77–1.0: high-income levels of longevity.

quiz.why: Since 2010 UNDP uses the geometric mean.

scenes.text: A country climbs the HDI table while its forests vanish.
Political freedom and environmental sustainability don't appear in the score.

steps.title: Critiques of HDI
steps.body:
- Omits political freedom, security, environment, inequality (partly addressed by IHDI).
- Arbitrary goalposts and equal weights.
- Substitutability between dimensions despite geometric mean.
- Data quality in poor countries.

steps.title: Other measures
steps.body:
- **Physical Quality of Life Index** (Morris, 1979): literacy, infant mortality, life expectancy at age one.
- **Basic needs approach** (ILO, 1970s).
- **Green accounting**, genuine savings, ecological footprint.
- **SDG India Index** (NITI Aayog) ranks states on SDG progress.

steps.title: Answer structure
steps.body: For 'critically evaluate HDI': (1) what it measures and how; (2) improvements over GDP; (3) limitations; (4) newer indices that address the gaps.

statements.s: HDI includes a direct measure of political freedom.
statements.why: It does not.

statements.s: PQLI was developed by Morris D. Morris.
statements.why: Published in 1979.

statements.s: IHDI adjusts HDI for inequality.
statements.why: It discounts each dimension by its inequality.

statements.s: NITI Aayog publishes an SDG India Index.
statements.why: It ranks states and UTs.

options: literacy, infant mortality, life expectancy at age one
quiz.why: These are its three components.
It has no environmental dimension.

quiz.q: The basic needs approach was promoted in the 1970s by:
quiz.why: The ILO's 1976 World Employment Conference.

questions.q: Development differs from growth because it includes:
options: well-being dimensions like health and education
questions.why: Development is multidimensional.

questions.q: Sen's capability approach focuses on:
questions.why: Capabilities are substantive freedoms.

Same income, PPP ₹22.5/$. PPP income:

MYS 6, EYS 9. Education index:

questions.why: UNDP uses $100 and $75,000 (PPP).

questions.q: PQLI was proposed in:
questions.why: Morris, 1979.

questions.q: Which index adjusts for gender disparities?
questions.why: Gender Development Index and Gender Inequality Index.

questions.q: Kerala is often cited for:
questions.why: Public action raised health and education outcomes.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Classic theories of development
courses.summary: Rostow's stages, Nurkse's vicious circle, Lewis's dual-economy model of surplus labour, the big push and balanced vs unbalanced growth, and the Harris–Todaro model of rural–urban migration.
outcomes: Describe Rostow's stages and their critique
Explain the Lewis model and the Lewis turning point
Contrast balanced (Nurkse, Rosenstein-Rodan) and unbalanced (Hirschman) growth
Use linkages to prioritise sectors
Solve Harris–Todaro migration equilibrium

lessons.title: Rostow and the vicious circle of poverty

scenes.text: Rostow compared development to an aeroplane — a long runway, then take-off into self-sustained growth.
Nurkse worried poor countries were stuck on the runway: poor because poor.

steps.title: Rostow (1960)
steps.body:
Five stages: (1) traditional society; (2) preconditions for take-off; (3) **take-off** — investment rises to over 10% of national income, leading sectors, political/institutional framework; (4) drive to maturity; (5) age of high mass consumption.

**Critiques**: linear and Eurocentric; stages overlap; ignores external constraints and colonial history; hard to test.

steps.title: Vicious circle (Nurkse)
steps.body:
- **Supply side**: low income → low saving → low investment → low productivity → low income.
- **Demand side**: low income → small market → weak inducement to invest → low productivity → low income.
- Breaking it needs a coordinated investment push.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

statements.s: In Rostow's take-off, the investment rate rises above about 10% of national income.
statements.why: That is one of his take-off conditions.

statements.s: Rostow's model is criticised for being linear.
statements.why: Countries need not follow identical stages.

statements.s: Nurkse's vicious circle operates on both supply and demand sides.
statements.why: Low saving and small markets both hold back investment.

statements.s: The age of high mass consumption is Rostow's first stage.
statements.why: It is the fifth stage.

quiz.why: Take-off follows the preconditions stage.
Low incomes mean small markets that discourage investment.

quiz.q: 'A country is poor because it is poor' is associated with:
quiz.why: Ragnar Nurkse popularised the vicious circle idea.

scenes.text: Villages have more hands than the land needs; removing some workers would barely cut output.
Factories can hire them at a wage slightly above subsistence — and profits fuel more factories.

steps.title: The model (1954)
steps.body:
- Two sectors: **traditional/subsistence** (agriculture, MPL ≈ 0 for surplus workers, wage = average product/subsistence) and **modern/capitalist** (industry, profit-maximising).
- Modern sector faces **perfectly elastic labour supply** at wage w = subsistence + premium (e.g. 30–50% above, for migration costs).
- Hires until MPL = w; profits are reinvested ⇒ labour demand curve shifts right ⇒ more workers absorbed.
- **Lewis turning point**: surplus exhausted, wages begin rising; dual economy becomes integrated.

steps.title: Solved: modern-sector hiring
steps.body:
Modern-sector MPL = 200 − 2L (₹ per day). Subsistence wage ₹60; urban premium 50% ⇒ w = ₹90.

1. 200 − 2L = 90 ⇒ **L = 55**.
2. Profit reinvestment shifts MPL to 240 − 2L ⇒ L = 75: 20 more workers drawn from agriculture at the same wage.

steps.title: Critiques
steps.body:
- Reinvestment may be labour-saving (capital-intensive) — jobless growth.
- Urban unemployment exists (Harris–Todaro).
- Ignores agricultural productivity: Fei–Ranis extension stresses agricultural surplus and food prices.
- Wages may rise before surplus is exhausted (unions, policy).

statements.s: In the Lewis model the modern sector faces a perfectly elastic labour supply until the turning point.
statements.why: Surplus labour is available at a constant wage.

statements.s: Lewis assumed profits are consumed by capitalists.
statements.why: Profits are reinvested, driving expansion.

statements.s: The Lewis turning point is when surplus labour is exhausted.
statements.why: Wages then begin to rise.

statements.s: Labour-saving reinvestment strengthens Lewis's employment mechanism.
statements.why: It weakens labour absorption.

quiz.why: Workers need an incentive to move.

quiz.q: Fei and Ranis extended Lewis by emphasising:
quiz.why: Food supply from agriculture must keep pace with industrial employment.

lessons.title: Big push, balanced and unbalanced growth

scenes.text: A lone shoe factory in a poor region cannot sell enough — its workers alone won't buy all the shoes.
If many factories open together, each one's workers buy the others' products.

steps.title: Balanced growth
steps.body:
- **Rosenstein-Rodan (1943)**: **big push** — indivisibilities in infrastructure, demand complementarity, savings; coordinated investment across many industries.
- **Nurkse**: simultaneous investment in many consumer-goods industries to widen the market.
- Critique: requires resources poor countries lack.

steps.title: Unbalanced growth (Hirschman, 1958)
steps.body:
- Deliberately create imbalances to induce investment.
- Invest in sectors with strong **linkages**: **backward** (demand for inputs, e.g. auto → steel, tyres) and **forward** (supplying inputs to others, e.g. steel → machinery).
- Choice between **social overhead capital** (infrastructure) first or **directly productive activities** first.

steps.title: Solved: ranking by linkages
steps.body:
Index scores (backward, forward): Automobiles (1.4, 0.8); Steel (1.1, 1.5); Retail (0.6, 0.5).

Sum: autos 2.2, steel **2.6**, retail 1.1 ⇒ Hirschman would prioritise steel (strong in both), then autos.

statements.s: Rosenstein-Rodan argued for a big push of coordinated investment.
statements.why: Indivisibilities and complementarities justify it.

statements.s: Hirschman favoured balanced growth.
statements.why: He argued for unbalanced growth via linkages.

statements.s: A car industry's demand for steel is a backward linkage.
statements.why: It pulls investment in input industries.

statements.s: Balanced growth is criticised for requiring scarce resources.
statements.why: Poor countries struggle to finance many sectors at once.

quiz.why: Its output becomes others' input.
Albert Hirschman, 'The Strategy of Economic Development'.

quiz.q: Demand complementarity is an argument for:
quiz.why: Many simultaneous investments create each other's markets.

scenes.text: A young man leaves his village for Mumbai even though many there are jobless.
He bets that the chance of a well-paid formal job is worth it.

steps.title: Model (1970)
steps.body:
- Migrants compare the **expected urban wage** with the rural wage: E(wu) = p·wu, p = probability of getting a formal job = formal jobs / urban labour force.
- Migration continues until **p·wu = wr**.
- Implication: creating urban jobs can raise urban unemployment by attracting more migrants (**Todaro paradox**).
- Policy: rural development, reduce urban–rural wage gaps, education aligned with jobs.

steps.title: Solved: equilibrium
steps.body:
Urban formal wage ₹600/day; rural wage ₹300/day; 6 lakh formal jobs.

1. Equilibrium p = wr/wu = 0.5.
2. Urban labour force = 6/0.5 = **12 lakh** ⇒ urban unemployment = **6 lakh** (50%).
3. If urban labour force were 10 lakh, p = 0.6 ⇒ E(wu) = 360 > 300 ⇒ more migration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing actual rather than expected urban wages.
- Assuming urban job creation always reduces urban unemployment.

activity.label: Probability p of an urban formal job (wu = ₹600, wr = ₹300)

bands.text: p·wu below ₹300: expected urban income is lower — net return migration.
p = 0.5: expected urban wage = rural wage — migration equilibrium.
p·wu above ₹300: migrants keep arriving, raising urban unemployment until p falls to 0.5.

quiz.q: With 4 lakh formal jobs and p = 0.4, urban labour force:
The Todaro paradox says urban job creation can:
quiz.why: Higher job chances attract more migrants than new jobs.

questions.why: From traditional society to high mass consumption.

questions.q: A criticism of Rostow:
questions.why: Not all countries follow the same path.

questions.q: In Lewis's subsistence sector, the MPL of surplus labour is:
questions.why: Removing surplus workers barely reduces output.

questions.q: MPL = 300 − 5L, w = 100. Modern employment:
If MPL shifts to 350 − 5L at w = 100, employment becomes:
The Lewis turning point is when:
options: wages start rising as surplus labour runs out
questions.why: Labour supply stops being perfectly elastic.

questions.q: Big push theory is due to:
questions.why: 1943 article on Eastern and South-Eastern Europe.

questions.q: Hirschman recommended investing in sectors with:
questions.why: Linkages induce further investment.

questions.q: Sector scores (B, F): A (1.2, 1.3), B (1.5, 0.6), C (0.9, 0.9). Highest total linkage:

courses.title: Unit 3 · Growth, inequality and poverty traps
courses.summary: The Kuznets hypothesis, growth elasticity of poverty, inequality axioms, nutrition-based poverty traps, rural credit markets and microfinance, and redistribution through transfers.
outcomes: Explain and evaluate the Kuznets inverted-U
Compute the growth elasticity of poverty
State the Pigou–Dalton transfer principle and other inequality axioms
Explain nutrition-based poverty traps
Analyse informal credit and microfinance (group lending)

scenes.text: Kuznets observed inequality rising in early industrialisation, then falling.
Later data showed many countries don't follow this path.

steps.title: Kuznets hypothesis (1955)
steps.body:
- Inequality first rises then falls as per capita income grows (**inverted U**), as workers move from a low-income, equal rural sector to a high-income, unequal urban sector.
- Evidence: cross-country data weak; East Asian economies grew with low inequality; inequality rose again in many rich countries after 1980.

steps.title: Growth and poverty
steps.body:
- **Growth elasticity of poverty** = %Δ poverty headcount / %Δ mean income.
- More negative when initial inequality is low.
- **Pro-poor growth**: incomes of the poor grow at least as fast as average (relative definition) or poverty falls (absolute).

steps.title: Solved: elasticity
steps.body:
Mean per capita consumption rises 4%; poverty headcount falls from 25% to 23%.

%Δ poverty = −2/25 = −8% ⇒ elasticity = −8/4 = **−2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using percentage-point instead of percentage change for poverty.
- Treating Kuznets as an iron law.

statements.s: The Kuznets curve is an inverted U.
statements.why: Inequality rises then falls with income.

statements.s: East Asian 'miracle' economies combined rapid growth with relatively low inequality.
statements.why: This is a major counter-example.

statements.s: Growth elasticity of poverty tends to be larger in absolute value where inequality is low.
statements.why: Growth reaches the poor more readily.

statements.s: Kuznets' hypothesis is strongly confirmed by modern data.
statements.why: Evidence is mixed.

options: sectoral shift from agriculture to industry
quiz.why: Workers moving to the more unequal urban sector widen overall inequality initially.

options: poor's income grows faster than average
quiz.why: Distribution shifts towards the poor.

scenes.text: If ₹100 moves from a rich person to a poor person, inequality should fall.
Good measures must respect such common-sense axioms.

steps.title: Axioms
steps.body:
- **Anonymity**: identities don't matter.
- **Population principle**: cloning the population doesn't change inequality.
- **Relative income (scale invariance)**: doubling all incomes leaves inequality unchanged.
- **Pigou–Dalton transfer principle**: a transfer from richer to poorer (not reversing ranks) reduces inequality.
- Gini, coefficient of variation and Theil satisfy all four; the range does not satisfy the transfer principle.

steps.title: Solved: coefficient of variation
steps.body:
Incomes: 2, 4, 6.

1. Mean = 4; variance (population) = (4 + 0 + 4)/3 = 2.667; SD = 1.633.
2. CV = 1.633/4 = **0.408**.
3. Transfer 1 from 6 to 2 ⇒ 3, 4, 5: SD = 0.816, CV = **0.204** — falls ✓ (transfer principle).

steps.title: Why the range fails
steps.body: Incomes 2, 4, 6, 8. Transfer 1 from the person with 6 to the person with 4 ⇒ 2, 5, 5, 8. Inequality has clearly fallen, but the range is still 8 − 2 = 6. The range looks only at the extremes and ignores the middle of the distribution.

statements.s: The Gini coefficient satisfies the Pigou–Dalton transfer principle.
statements.why: Progressive transfers lower the Gini.

statements.s: Doubling everyone's income doubles the Gini.
statements.why: Gini is scale invariant.

statements.s: The range can ignore transfers among middle incomes.
statements.why: It depends only on the extremes.

statements.s: The population principle says cloning the population leaves inequality unchanged.
statements.why: That is its definition.

quiz.q: Scale invariance means inequality is unchanged when:
options: all incomes multiply by the same factor
quiz.why: Proportional changes keep relative shares fixed.

quiz.q: Which measure can violate the transfer principle?
quiz.why: The range ignores transfers that don't touch the extremes.

scenes.text: A labourer who eats too little cannot do heavy work, so employers won't hire him at the going wage.
Without work, he cannot eat enough — a trap.

steps.title: Capacity curve
steps.body:
- Work capacity rises with nutrition (income), slowly at first (body maintenance), then rapidly, then levels off — an S-shape.
- If income is below a threshold, capacity is too low to earn enough ⇒ stuck at a low equilibrium; above it, capacity and income rise to a high equilibrium.
- Implies **multiple equilibria**; temporary help (food, transfers) can push people over the threshold.
- Related: efficiency-wage theory (Leibenstein) — employers may pay above market wage to raise productivity.

steps.title: Solved: threshold logic
steps.body:
Daily work capacity: 0 units below 1,600 kcal; then 1 unit per 200 kcal above 1,600, up to 10 units. The piece rate buys 300 kcal per unit.

- At 1,600 kcal: capacity 0 ⇒ earns 0 ⇒ trap.
- At 2,400 kcal: capacity 4 ⇒ earns 1,200 kcal — not self-sustaining.
- Self-sustaining needs 300c ≥ 1,600 + 200c ⇒ c ≥ 16, above the maximum of 10 ⇒ no high equilibrium at this piece rate. A higher rate (e.g. 400 kcal per unit gives c ≥ 8) creates one.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding all poverty is nutrition-driven — evidence (Banerjee–Duflo) is mixed.
- Ignoring household allocation of food.

statements.s: Nutrition-based traps imply multiple equilibria.
statements.why: Low and high capacity–income combinations can both be stable.

statements.s: A one-time transfer can help escape a poverty trap.
statements.why: It can push someone over the threshold.

statements.s: Efficiency-wage theory says higher wages can raise productivity.
statements.why: Better-paid workers can be healthier and more motivated.

statements.s: Evidence shows nutrition traps explain all persistent poverty.
statements.why: Evidence is mixed.

quiz.why: Little capacity at low nutrition, rapid gains in the middle, flattening at the top.
Low income perpetuates itself.

quiz.q: Efficiency wage theory in development is associated with:
quiz.why: Harvey Leibenstein linked nutrition, wages and productivity.

scenes.text: In a Bangladeshi village, five women form a group; each borrows, and all are responsible.
Without collateral, peer pressure keeps repayment high — the Grameen idea.

steps.title: Rural credit problems
steps.body:
- **Information asymmetry**: adverse selection (unknown risk) and moral hazard (unobserved effort).
- **Enforcement**: weak legal recovery, no collateral.
- Result: credit rationing; moneylenders charge high rates reflecting monopoly power, default risk and screening costs; **interlinked contracts** (credit tied to labour or crop sales).

steps.title: Microfinance
steps.body:
- **Group lending with joint liability** (Grameen Bank, Muhammad Yunus): peer selection, peer monitoring, social sanctions.
- **Dynamic incentives**: repeat larger loans for good repayment.
- India: **SHG–bank linkage** (NABARD) and NBFC-MFIs.
- Evidence (RCTs): modest average effects on business and consumption; risk of over-indebtedness (Andhra Pradesh crisis 2010).

steps.title: Solved: lender's break-even rate
steps.body:
Lender's funds cost 10%; probability of default 20% (lose all).

Break-even: 0.8(1 + i) = 1.10 ⇒ 1 + i = 1.375 ⇒ **i = 37.5%** — high rates can reflect default risk, not only exploitation.

statements.s: Joint liability uses peer monitoring to improve repayment.
statements.why: Group members watch and pressure each other.

statements.s: Moneylenders' high rates can partly reflect default risk.
statements.why: Expected losses must be covered.

statements.s: RCTs show microfinance dramatically ends poverty.
statements.why: Average effects are modest.

statements.s: Interlinked contracts tie credit to other transactions like labour.
statements.why: Common in rural markets.

quiz.why: Yunus pioneered group lending in Bangladesh.

quiz.q: Adverse selection in credit markets arises from:
quiz.why: Lenders cannot tell safe from risky borrowers in advance.

questions.why: Inverted U against income.

questions.q: Income +2%, poverty 30% → 28.8%. Elasticity:
The Pigou–Dalton principle concerns:
questions.why: Such transfers should reduce measured inequality.

questions.why: No dispersion.

questions.q: Incomes 2, 6. CV (population SD):
questions.why: Mean 4, SD 2, CV 0.5.

questions.why: Threshold effects create multiple equilibria.

questions.q: Moral hazard in credit refers to:
questions.why: Borrowers may take risky actions after getting a loan.

Which is a microfinance feature?
questions.why: Group responsibility substitutes for collateral.

questions.q: SHG–bank linkage in India is promoted by:
questions.why: NABARD launched it in 1992.

options: East Asian growth with low inequality
questions.why: Fast growth without rising inequality.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Population, human capital and institutions
courses.summary: Malthusian theory and the demographic transition, the demographic dividend and dependency ratios, returns to education and health, and the role of institutions and the state in development.
outcomes: Explain Malthus and the demographic transition
Compute dependency ratios and doubling times
Explain the demographic dividend
Estimate returns to schooling (Mincer)
Assess the institutions view of development

scenes.text: Vaccines and clean water cut child deaths; families are still large for a generation.
Then, with schooling and urbanisation, families choose fewer children.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
- **Malthus (1798)**: population grows geometrically, food arithmetically ⇒ checks (positive: famine, disease; preventive: delayed marriage). Overtaken by technical progress in agriculture.
- **Demographic transition**: Stage 1 high birth and death rates; Stage 2 death rate falls (rapid population growth); Stage 3 birth rate falls; Stage 4 both low.
- India's total fertility rate has fallen to around replacement level (≈2.0 in NFHS-5, 2019–21).

steps.title: Solved: doubling time
steps.body:
Rule of 70: doubling time ≈ 70/growth rate (%).

- 2% growth ⇒ **35 years**.
- 1% growth ⇒ **70 years**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating Malthus as proven — technology raised food output faster than population.
- Confusing TFR with crude birth rate.

statements.s: In Stage 2 of the demographic transition, death rates fall while birth rates stay high.
statements.why: That produces rapid population growth.

statements.s: Malthus argued food grows geometrically.
statements.why: He argued food grows arithmetically.

statements.s: Replacement-level TFR is about 2.1.
statements.why: Slightly above 2 to allow for mortality.

statements.s: At 3.5% growth, population doubles in about 20 years.

quiz.why: Preventive checks lower births.
Both rates are low and population growth is slow.

scenes.text: India has one of the world's largest working-age populations.
The window of a demographic dividend is open — if jobs and skills keep pace.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Dependency ratio** = (population aged 0–14 + 65+)/(population 15–64) × 100.
- Falling dependency ⇒ more workers per dependant ⇒ higher saving and output per capita — the **demographic dividend**.
- Realising it requires employment, education, health and women's labour-force participation; otherwise a 'demographic burden'.

steps.title: Solved: dependency ratio
steps.body:
Ages 0–14: 36 crore; 15–64: 96 crore; 65+: 10 crore.

Dependency ratio = (36 + 10)/96 × 100 ≈ **47.9**. Child dependency = 37.5; old-age dependency ≈ 10.4.

steps.title: East Asia
steps.body: Studies attribute a meaningful part of East Asia's rapid growth to the demographic dividend combined with high saving and export-oriented jobs.

statements.s: The dependency ratio counts children and elderly relative to working-age people.
statements.why: That is its definition.

scenes.text: A girl completes secondary school instead of leaving at 14.
Her expected lifetime earnings and her children's health both improve.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Human capital** (Schultz, Becker): skills and health that raise productivity.
- **Mincer earnings equation**: ln(wage) = a + r·S + b·Exp − c·Exp²; r = return to a year of schooling (often 5–10%).
- Social returns include externalities (civic, health of children).
- Health: nutrition, disease burden; deworming and vaccination as cost-effective interventions.
- Quality matters: learning outcomes (ASER reports) not just enrolment.

steps.title: Solved: Mincer
steps.body:
r = 0.08. Worker A has 10 years of schooling; B has 14.

Wage ratio B/A = e^(0.08 × 4) = e^0.32 ≈ **1.377** ⇒ about 38% higher wages.

steps.title: Solved: private rate of return
steps.body:
One extra year costs ₹50,000 (fees + forgone earnings) and raises annual earnings by ₹6,000 for many years (approximate as perpetuity).

Return ≈ 6,000/50,000 = **12% per year**.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Trade, aid and sustainable development
courses.summary: Terms of trade and the Prebisch–Singer thesis, dependency theory, import substitution versus export orientation, foreign aid and the two-gap model, and sustainable development, the environmental Kuznets curve and the SDGs.
outcomes: Compute terms of trade and explain the Prebisch–Singer thesis

scenes.text: A coffee-exporting country finds it needs ever more sacks to buy one tractor.
Prebisch and Singer argued this was a long-run trend for primary exporters.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Net barter terms of trade** = (Px index / Pm index) × 100.
- **Income terms of trade** = NBTT × export volume index /100 (capacity to import).
- **Prebisch–Singer thesis (1950)**: long-run decline in primary-commodity prices relative to manufactures — low income elasticity of demand for primaries, market power in manufactures, technology gains passed on as higher wages in the centre.
- **Dependency theory** (Frank, Prebisch): core–periphery relations perpetuate underdevelopment.

steps.title: Solved: terms of trade
steps.body:
Export price index 90; import price index 120; export volume index 140 (base = 100).

- NBTT = 90/120 × 100 = **75** (deteriorated).
- Income ToT = 75 × 140/100 = **105** — capacity to import still rose because volumes grew.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Inverting the ratio.
- Concluding welfare fell whenever NBTT falls — check volumes and productivity.

statements.s: NBTT = export price index / import price index × 100.
statements.why: That is the definition.

statements.s: Prebisch–Singer predicted rising relative prices of primary commodities.
statements.why: They predicted a decline.

statements.s: Income terms of trade measure capacity to import based on exports.
statements.why: They combine price ratio and export volume.

statements.s: Dependency theory sees core–periphery relations as harmful to the periphery.
statements.why: That is its central claim.

options: low income elasticity of demand for primaries

scenes.text: India and Latin America protected domestic industry for decades.
South Korea and Taiwan pushed firms to export — and grew faster.

steps.title: Strategies
steps.body:
- **Import-substituting industrialisation (ISI)**: tariffs, quotas, overvalued exchange rates to build domestic industry. Problems: inefficiency, rent-seeking, foreign-exchange crises, anti-export bias.
- **Export-oriented industrialisation (EOI)**: competitive exchange rates, export incentives, discipline via world markets (East Asia).
- **Infant industry argument** (Hamilton, List): temporary protection justified if the industry can become competitive and learning spillovers exist.
- **Effective rate of protection** (ERP) = (VA at domestic prices − VA at world prices)/VA at world prices.

steps.title: Solved: ERP
steps.body:
World price of a shirt ₹1,000; imported cloth ₹600. Tariff on shirts 20%, on cloth 0%.

1. VA at world prices = 400.
2. Domestic VA = 1,200 − 600 = 600.
3. ERP = (600 − 400)/400 = **50%** — far above the 20% nominal tariff.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating nominal tariff with effective protection.
- Assuming EOI means no government role — East Asian states intervened heavily.

statements.s: ERP can exceed the nominal tariff when inputs face lower tariffs.
statements.why: Protection is concentrated on value added.

statements.s: ISI regimes often had an anti-export bias.
statements.why: Overvaluation and protection made exporting less attractive.

statements.why: States guided credit and industry.

statements.why: Protection should be temporary.

quiz.why: Domestic VA = 550 − 300 = 250 vs world VA 200; ERP = 25%.

quiz.why: List advocated temporary protection for developing industries.
Protected firms faced weak competitive pressure.

lessons.title: Foreign aid and the two-gap model

story.title: Short of savings, or short of dollars?

scenes.text: A developing country wants to grow 6% a year but saves too little.
It also lacks foreign exchange to import machinery — two different gaps.

steps.title: Two-gap model (Chenery–Strout)
steps.body:
- **Saving gap** = required investment − domestic saving (I − S).
- **Foreign-exchange gap** = required imports − exports (M − X).
- Ex post they are equal, but ex ante the **larger (binding) gap** determines foreign capital needed.
- Aid debates: Sachs (big push via aid) vs Easterly (aid ineffective, incentives); aid works better with good policies (Burnside–Dollar, contested).

steps.title: Solved: two gaps
steps.body:
Target growth 6%, ICOR 4 ⇒ I = 24% of GDP; domestic saving 18% ⇒ saving gap = **6%**.

Required imports 20% of GDP, exports 16% ⇒ forex gap = **4%**.

Binding gap = saving gap (6%) ⇒ foreign inflows of 6% of GDP needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding the two gaps — the binding one is the larger.
- Treating all aid as grants (much is concessional loans).

statements.s: In the two-gap model, the larger gap is binding.
statements.why: Filling it automatically covers the smaller.

statements.s: William Easterly is a leading critic of large-scale aid.
statements.why: 'The White Man's Burden' argues aid often fails.

statements.s: All official development assistance is in grants.
statements.why: Much is concessional lending.

statements.s: The saving gap equals investment minus domestic saving.
statements.why: That is its definition.

quiz.why: The larger gap binds.

quiz.q: The two-gap model is associated with:
quiz.why: Hollis Chenery and Alan Strout, 1966.

scenes.text: Cutting forests raises GDP this year but lowers future productivity and well-being.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:

- **Weak sustainability**: total capital (natural + man-made) non-declining; **strong**: critical natural capital must be preserved.
- **Environmental Kuznets curve**: pollution first rises then falls with income — holds for some local pollutants, not clearly for CO₂.
- **SDGs** (UN, 2015): 17 goals, 169 targets, horizon 2030.
- Climate: Paris Agreement (2015), nationally determined contributions; India's net-zero target 2070.

steps.title: Solved: genuine savings
steps.body:
Gross national saving 30% of GNI; depreciation of produced capital 10%; natural resource depletion 3%; pollution damage 1%; education spending 4%.

Adjusted net saving = 30 − 10 − 3 − 1 + 4 = **20% of GNI** (positive ⇒ wealth rising).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming the EKC proves growth will clean the environment automatically.
- Mixing up the MDGs (2000–2015, 8 goals) and SDGs (2015–2030, 17 goals).

Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA (Hons) Economics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Nature of econometrics and statistical foundations
courses.summary: What econometrics does and its methodology, types of data, random variables and expectation, sampling distributions, estimators and their properties, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests with t and z statistics.
outcomes: Describe the steps of econometric methodology and types of data
Compute expectation, variance and covariance
State properties of estimators: unbiasedness, efficiency, consistency
Construct confidence intervals for a mean
Conduct and interpret t and z tests, p-values and error types

scenes.text: Theory says education raises productivity and wages.
Econometrics turns that idea into a model, estimates it from data and tests it.

steps.title: Methodology (Gujarati's steps)
steps.body:
1. Statement of theory or hypothesis.
2. Mathematical model (e.g. W = β1 + β2·S).
3. Econometric model with a stochastic error u: W = β1 + β2·S + u.
4. Obtain data.
5. Estimate parameters.
6. Test hypotheses.
7. Forecast or predict.
8. Use for policy.

steps.title: Types of data
steps.body:
- **Cross-section**: many units at one time (households in PLFS 2023-24).
- **Time series**: one unit over time (India's GDP 1951–2024).
- **Pooled / panel (longitudinal)**: same units over time (state-level data for 20 years).
- Measurement scales: ratio, interval, ordinal, nominal.

steps.title: Why an error term?
steps.body: It captures omitted variables, measurement error, randomness in behaviour, wrong functional form and the principle of parsimony.

statements.s: Panel data follow the same units over time.
statements.why: That is the definition.

statements.s: An econometric model omits the error term.
statements.why: The stochastic error distinguishes it from a mathematical model.

statements.s: India's annual GDP from 1951 is time-series data.
statements.why: One unit observed over time.

statements.s: The error term captures omitted influences.
statements.why: Among other things.

quiz.q: Data on 5,000 households for one year are:
quiz.why: Many units observed at a single point in time.

quiz.q: The step after specifying the econometric model is:
quiz.why: Estimation requires data.
Categories have no natural order or magnitude.

scenes.text: More monsoon rain tends to go with bigger harvests.
Covariance and correlation measure how two variables move together.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- E(a + bX) = a + bE(X); Var(a + bX) = b²Var(X).
- Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X, Y).
- Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μX)(Y − μY)]; correlation ρ = Cov/(σXσY), −1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1.
- Sample variance s² = Σ(Xi − X̄)²/(n − 1).

statements.s: Var(a + bX) = b²Var(X).
statements.why: Adding a constant doesn't change spread.

statements.s: Correlation can exceed 1.
statements.why: It lies between −1 and 1.

statements.s: Independent variables have zero covariance.
statements.why: Though zero covariance does not imply independence.

statements.s: Sample variance divides by n − 1.
statements.why: For unbiasedness.

scenes.text: An archer whose arrows centre on the bull's-eye is unbiased.
One whose arrows cluster tightly is efficient. We want both.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- **Unbiased**: E(θ̂) = θ.
- **Efficient**: smallest variance among unbiased estimators.
- **Mean squared error** = Var + Bias².
- **Consistent**: θ̂ converges in probability to θ as n → ∞.
- **Sampling distribution** of X̄: mean μ, variance σ²/n; by the **central limit theorem**, approximately normal for large n.

steps.title: Solved: MSE comparison
steps.body:
Estimator A: bias 0, variance 4. Estimator B: bias 1, variance 2.

MSE_A = 4; MSE_B = 2 + 1 = **3** — B has lower MSE despite bias.

steps.title: Solved: standard error
steps.body:
Population σ = 12, n = 36.

SE(X̄) = 12/√36 = **2**. With n = 144, SE = 1 — quadrupling n halves the SE.

statements.s: An unbiased estimator has expected value equal to the parameter.
statements.why: Definition.

statements.s: A biased estimator can have smaller MSE than an unbiased one.
statements.why: If its variance is much smaller.

statements.s: Quadrupling sample size halves the standard error of the mean.
The central limit theorem requires the population to be normal.
statements.why: It holds for many distributions with finite variance.

quiz.why: It concerns behaviour as n grows.

scenes.text: A survey of 36 workers finds an average of ₹520.
Is that consistent with a true mean of ₹500, or evidence of more?

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
- H0 (null) vs H1 (alternative); choose α (e.g. 5%).
- Test statistic: z = (X̄ − μ0)/(σ/√n) if σ known/large n; **t = (X̄ − μ0)/(s/√n)** with n − 1 df otherwise.
- Reject H0 if |statistic| > critical value (two-tailed 5%: z = 1.96).
- **p-value**: probability, under H0, of a result at least as extreme.
- **Type I error**: rejecting a true H0 (prob α); **Type II**: failing to reject a false H0. **Power** = 1 − P(Type II).
- CI: X̄ ± critical × SE.

bands.text: Below 1.645: not significant even at 10%.
1.645–1.96: significant at 10% but not at 5%.
1.96–2.576: significant at 5% but not at 1%.
Above 2.576: significant at 1%.

quiz.why: Its probability is the significance level α.

courses.title: Unit 2 · The two-variable regression model and OLS
courses.summary: Population and sample regression functions, the meaning of linearity, the method of ordinary least squares with a fully worked example, the classical linear regression assumptions, the Gauss–Markov theorem, and R².
outcomes: Distinguish the PRF from the SRF and explain linearity in parameters
Derive and compute OLS estimates by hand
List the CLRM assumptions
State the Gauss–Markov theorem (BLUE)
Decompose TSS into ESS and RSS and compute R²

scenes.text: Among families earning ₹50,000 a month, consumption varies widely.
The population regression line traces average consumption at each income.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **PRF**: E(Y|Xi) = β1 + β2Xi; individual Yi = β1 + β2Xi + ui.
- **SRF**: Ŷi = b1 + b2Xi; Yi = b1 + b2Xi + ei (ei = residual).
- **Linear regression** means linear in **parameters** (not necessarily in variables): Y = β1 + β2X² + u is linear; Y = β1 + β2^2 X + u is not.
- β2 = slope = ΔE(Y)/ΔX; β1 = intercept.

steps.title: Solved: interpret
steps.body:
Estimated consumption Ĉ = 2,000 + 0.75·Income (₹/month).

- Slope 0.75 = estimated MPC: an extra ₹1,000 income raises average consumption by ₹750.
- At income ₹40,000: Ĉ = 2,000 + 30,000 = **₹32,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing the error u (unobservable) with the residual e (computed).
- Calling Y = β1 + β2 ln X + u non-linear — it is linear in parameters.

statements.s: Y = β1 + β2X² + u is a linear regression model.
statements.why: It is linear in the parameters.

statements.s: The residual ei is the same as the population error ui.
statements.why: ei estimates ui from the sample.

statements.s: The PRF gives the conditional mean of Y given X.
statements.why: E(Y|X).

statements.s: Y = β1 + β2² X + u is linear in parameters.
statements.why: β2 enters squared.

quiz.why: Change in consumption per unit change in income.

quiz.q: Which model is NOT linear in parameters?
options: Y = β1 + β2 ln X + u
quiz.why: β2 is raised to a power.

lessons.title: Ordinary least squares: a worked example

scenes.text: Many lines can be drawn through a scatter of points.
OLS picks the one that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
Minimise Σei² = Σ(Yi − b1 − b2Xi)². Normal equations give:
- **b2 = Σxiyi/Σxi²** (x, y = deviations from means)
- **b1 = Ȳ − b2X̄**
Properties of OLS fit: Σei = 0; ΣeiXi = 0; line passes through (X̄, Ȳ); mean of Ŷ = Ȳ.

statements.s: OLS residuals sum to zero when an intercept is included.
statements.why: From the first normal equation.

statements.s: The OLS line passes through the point of means.
statements.why: b1 = Ȳ − b2X̄.

statements.s: OLS minimises the sum of absolute residuals.
statements.why: It minimises squared residuals.

statements.s: In the example, b2 = 0.6.

scenes.text: Under a set of assumptions, OLS beats every other linear unbiased estimator.
Knowing the assumptions tells us when to worry.

steps.title: Classical assumptions
steps.body:
1. Linear in parameters.
2. X fixed in repeated samples (or independent of u).
3. **E(u|X) = 0**.
4. **Homoscedasticity**: Var(u|X) = σ².
5. **No autocorrelation**: Cov(ui, uj) = 0.
6. n > number of parameters; variation in X.
7. Correct specification; (multiple regression) no perfect multicollinearity.
8. For exact inference: u ~ Normal.

steps.title: Gauss–Markov theorem
steps.body:
Under assumptions 1–7, OLS estimators are **BLUE** — Best (minimum variance) Linear Unbiased Estimators. Normality is **not** needed for BLUE.

Variances: Var(b2) = σ²/Σx²; Var(b1) = σ²ΣX²/(nΣx²). σ̂² = Σe²/(n − 2).

statements.s: Gauss–Markov requires normally distributed errors.
statements.why: Normality is needed only for exact t and F tests.

statements.s: BLUE stands for Best Linear Unbiased Estimator.
statements.why: That is the acronym.

statements.s: Homoscedasticity means constant error variance.
statements.why: Var(u|X) = σ².

statements.s: More variation in X lowers Var(b2).
statements.why: Σx² is in the denominator.

quiz.why: Smallest variance among linear unbiased estimators.

scenes.text: Some of the variation in consumption is explained by income.
R² tells us what share.

steps.title: Decomposition
steps.body:
- **TSS** = Σy²; **ESS** = Σŷ² = b2²Σx²; **RSS** = Σe².
- TSS = ESS + RSS.
- **R²** = ESS/TSS = 1 − RSS/TSS, 0 ≤ R² ≤ 1.
- In simple regression, R² = r² (squared correlation between X and Y).
- A high R² does not prove causation or correct specification.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing R² across models with different dependent variables (Y vs ln Y).
- Thinking R² must be high for a useful model — in cross-section data low R² is common.

statements.s: TSS = ESS + RSS when an intercept is included.
statements.why: OLS decomposition.

statements.s: R² = 0.9 proves X causes Y.
statements.why: Correlation is not causation.

statements.s: In simple regression R² equals the squared correlation coefficient.
statements.why: A standard result.

statements.s: R² can be negative in OLS with an intercept.
statements.why: It lies between 0 and 1.

questions.why: Least squares.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Inference in the regression model
courses.summary: Sampling distributions of OLS estimators under normality, t-tests and confidence intervals for coefficients, the ANOVA table and F-test, mean and individual prediction intervals, and reporting regression results.
outcomes: Conduct two- and one-tailed t-tests on regression coefficients
Construct confidence intervals for β2

Report and interpret regression output correctly

story.title: Is the slope really different from zero?

scenes.text: Our five-point regression gave a slope of 0.6.
With only five observations, could that be pure chance?

steps.title: Test
steps.body:
Under normal errors: t = (b2 − β2*)/se(b2) ~ t with (n − 2) df.

- **Test of significance**: H0: β2 = 0.
- Two-tailed reject if |t| > t_{α/2, n−2}; one-tailed if t > t_{α, n−2} (in the hypothesised direction).
- **2-t rule of thumb**: with df ≥ 20, |t| > 2 is significant at about 5%.

steps.title: Solved: five-point example
steps.body:
b2 = 0.6, se(b2) = 0.283, n = 5 (df = 3).

1. t = 0.6/0.283 ≈ **2.12**.
2. Critical t(3), 5% two-tailed = 3.182 ⇒ **do not reject** H0.
3. One-tailed H1: β2 > 0, critical t(3, 5%) = 2.353 ⇒ still **not significant**.
Lesson: tiny samples need large t-values.

steps.title: Solved: testing a specific value
steps.body:
Consumption regression: b2 = 0.82, se = 0.04, n = 52. Test H0: MPC = 0.9.

t = (0.82 − 0.90)/0.04 = **−2.0**; critical t(50) ≈ 2.009 at 5% two-tailed ⇒ borderline, **do not reject** at 5% (|−2.0| < 2.009).

statements.s: The t-test for a slope in simple regression uses n − 2 degrees of freedom.
statements.why: Two parameters are estimated.

statements.s: With df = 3, a t of 2.12 is significant at 5% two-tailed.
statements.why: The critical value is 3.182.

statements.s: A one-tailed test has a smaller critical value than a two-tailed test at the same α.
statements.why: All of α is in one tail.

statements.s: Failing to reject H0 proves β2 = 0.
statements.why: It only means insufficient evidence against H0.

scenes.text: The slope is 0.6 — but how precise is that?
A confidence interval gives a plausible range for the true β2.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
100(1 − α)% CI: **b2 ± t_{α/2, n−2} × se(b2)**.

- If the CI excludes β2*, reject H0: β2 = β2* at level α (duality with two-tailed tests).
- Wider with smaller n, higher σ̂², less variation in X, higher confidence level.

steps.title: Solved: five-point example
steps.body:
95% CI = 0.6 ± 3.182 × 0.283 = 0.6 ± 0.900 ⇒ **(−0.30, 1.50)**.

It includes 0 ⇒ consistent with the t-test: not significant.

steps.title: Solved: larger sample
steps.body:
b2 = 0.82, se = 0.04, df = 50 (t ≈ 2.009).

95% CI = 0.82 ± 0.080 ⇒ **(0.740, 0.900)** — includes 0.9 only at the boundary (0.9004 upper limit before rounding), matching the borderline test.

statements.s: A 99% CI is wider than a 95% CI for the same data.
statements.why: A larger critical value is used.

statements.s: If a 95% CI for β2 excludes zero, β2 is significant at 5%.
statements.why: Duality with the two-tailed test.

statements.s: More variation in X widens the CI for β2.
statements.why: It reduces se(b2).

statements.s: A 95% CI contains the true β2 with probability 0.95 in repeated sampling.
statements.why: That is the frequentist interpretation.

quiz.why: 0 lies outside the interval.
More data reduce the standard error.

scenes.text: Regression software prints an analysis-of-variance table.
Its F statistic tests whether the model explains anything at all.

steps.title: ANOVA (simple regression)
steps.body:
| Source | SS | df | MSS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regression | ESS | 1 | ESS/1 |
| Residual | RSS | n − 2 | RSS/(n − 2) |
| Total | TSS | n − 1 | |

F = [ESS/1]/[RSS/(n − 2)] ~ F(1, n − 2). In simple regression **F = t²** for H0: β2 = 0.

Also F = [R²/1]/[(1 − R²)/(n − 2)].

statements.s: In simple regression, F equals t² for the slope.
statements.why: A standard identity.

statements.s: Residual df in simple regression are n − 1.
statements.why: They are n − 2.

statements.s: F can be computed from R².
A large F indicates the regression explains little.
statements.why: Large F means significant explanatory power.

quiz.why: F = t².

Predicting the average Y is more precise than predicting one particular outcome.

steps.title: Two predictions
steps.body:
At X0: Ŷ0 = b1 + b2X0.
- **Mean prediction** E(Y|X0): Var = σ̂²[1/n + (X0 − X̄)²/Σx²].
- **Individual prediction** Y0: Var = σ̂²[1 + 1/n + (X0 − X̄)²/Σx²].
- Intervals widen as X0 moves away from X̄.

Always report standard errors (or t), R², n and, where relevant, p-values.

statements.why: They add the error variance σ².

statements.s: Prediction is most precise at X0 = X̄.
statements.why: The (X0 − X̄)² term vanishes.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Multiple regression, functional forms and dummy variables
courses.summary: The three-variable model and partial regression coefficients, R² and adjusted R², the overall F-test and restricted least squares, log-linear, semi-log and reciprocal forms, and dummy-variable regression.
outcomes: Interpret partial regression coefficients
Compute adjusted R² and the overall F statistic
Test linear restrictions using restricted and unrestricted RSS
Interpret coefficients in log-log, log-lin and lin-log models
Use and interpret intercept and slope dummies and avoid the dummy trap

scenes.text: Wages depend on both schooling and experience.
Multiple regression estimates each effect holding the other fixed.

steps.title: Model
steps.body:
Yi = β1 + β2X2i + β3X3i + ui.

- β2 = **partial** effect of X2 on E(Y), holding X3 constant (ceteris paribus).
- OLS in deviation form: b2 = (Σyx2·Σx3² − Σyx3·Σx2x3)/(Σx2²·Σx3² − (Σx2x3)²).
- Additional assumption: **no perfect multicollinearity**.
- Omitting a relevant correlated variable biases the remaining coefficients (**omitted variable bias**).

steps.title: Solved: interpretation
steps.body:
ln(W) = 1.2 + 0.08S + 0.03Exp.

One more year of schooling, holding experience fixed, raises wages by about **8%**; one more year of experience by about 3%.

statements.s: A partial regression coefficient holds other regressors constant.
statements.why: That is its meaning.

statements.s: Perfect multicollinearity still allows OLS estimation of all coefficients.
statements.why: The normal equations cannot be solved uniquely.

statements.s: Omitting a relevant variable correlated with included ones causes bias.
statements.why: Omitted variable bias.

statements.why: RSS cannot rise when a regressor is added.

quiz.why: Coefficient × 100 in a log-lin model.

scenes.text: Adding any variable raises R² a little.
Adjusted R² penalises useless additions.

steps.title: Formulas (k = number of parameters incl. intercept)
steps.body:
- **Adjusted R²** = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − k).
- **Overall F** = [R²/(k − 1)]/[(1 − R²)/(n − k)] ~ F(k − 1, n − k): tests all slopes = 0.
- **Restricted least squares F** = [(RSS_R − RSS_UR)/m]/[RSS_UR/(n − k)], m = number of restrictions.
- Example restrictions: β2 + β3 = 1 (CRS in Cobb–Douglas).

statements.s: Adjusted R² can fall when a variable is added.
statements.why: If the gain in fit is smaller than the df penalty.

statements.s: The overall F-test tests whether all slope coefficients are zero.
statements.why: Joint significance.

statements.s: RSS_R is always less than RSS_UR.
statements.why: Restrictions can only raise RSS.

statements.s: Adjusted R² is always greater than R².
statements.why: It is less than or equal to R².

Logging both sides makes the slope an elasticity.

steps.title: Forms and interpretation
steps.body:
| Model | Form | Slope meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | Y = β1 + β2X | ΔY per unit ΔX |
| Log-log | ln Y = β1 + β2 ln X | **elasticity** |
| Log-lin | ln Y = β1 + β2X | 100β2 ≈ % change in Y per unit X (growth rate if X = time) |
| Lin-log | Y = β1 + β2 ln X | β2/100 = change in Y per 1% change in X |
| Reciprocal | Y = β1 + β2(1/X) | Y approaches β1 asymptotically |

steps.body:
ln GDP_t = 4.2 + 0.065t.

Instantaneous growth ≈ **6.5% per year**; compound growth = e^0.065 − 1 ≈ **6.72%**.

steps.title: Solved: Cobb–Douglas
steps.body:
ln Q = 0.5 + 0.7 ln L + 0.4 ln K.

Output elasticities 0.7 and 0.4; sum = 1.1 ⇒ **increasing returns to scale** (test formally with restricted least squares).

A 0/1 dummy measures the average wage gap between them.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- Dummy D = 1 for a category, 0 otherwise.
- **Intercept dummy**: Y = β1 + β2D + β3X ⇒ shifts the intercept.
- **Slope (interaction) dummy**: + β4(D·X) ⇒ different slopes.
- **Dummy variable trap**: with an intercept, use (m − 1) dummies for m categories; otherwise perfect multicollinearity.
- Seasonal dummies, structural-break dummies (alternative to Chow test).
- In ln Y models, % effect of a dummy = 100(e^β − 1).

statements.why: To avoid the dummy trap.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Multicollinearity, heteroscedasticity, autocorrelation and specification
courses.summary: Nature, consequences, detection and remedies for multicollinearity, heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation, and specification errors including omitted and irrelevant variables.
outcomes: Detect multicollinearity using correlations and VIF
Explain consequences of heteroscedasticity and apply Goldfeld–Quandt or White tests
Use the Durbin–Watson statistic and know its limits
Apply remedies: WLS, robust standard errors, GLS/Cochrane–Orcutt
Analyse omitted-variable bias and inclusion of irrelevant variables

scenes.text: A consumption model includes both income and wealth, which move almost together.
The overall fit is great, but neither coefficient is individually significant.

steps.title: Nature and consequences
steps.body:
- **Perfect** multicollinearity: exact linear relation ⇒ OLS impossible.
- **High (imperfect)**: OLS still BLUE but variances and standard errors are large ⇒ wide CIs, insignificant t's, high R² with few significant coefficients, estimates sensitive to small data changes.
- Detection: high pairwise correlations, **VIF = 1/(1 − R²_j)** (rule of thumb VIF > 10), tolerance = 1/VIF, condition index.
- Remedies: more data, drop a variable (beware omitted-variable bias), combine variables, use prior information, ratio or first-difference transformations.

steps.title: Solved: VIF
steps.body:
Auxiliary regression of X2 on X3 gives R²_2 = 0.9.

VIF = 1/(1 − 0.9) = **10**; tolerance = 0.1. The variance of b2 is 10 times what it would be with uncorrelated regressors ⇒ se is √10 ≈ 3.16 times larger.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

statements.s: High multicollinearity makes OLS biased.
statements.why: OLS remains unbiased; variances grow.

statements.s: A VIF above 10 is often taken as a sign of serious multicollinearity.
statements.why: Common rule of thumb.

statements.s: High R² with insignificant t-ratios is a classic symptom.
statements.why: Joint but not individual significance.

statements.s: Dropping a relevant variable is a cost-free remedy.
statements.why: It can cause omitted-variable bias.

quiz.q: VIF = 25. Factor by which se is inflated:

quiz.why: Tolerance = 1 − R²_j = 1/VIF.

scenes.text: Low-income families spend almost all their income in similar ways.
High-income families vary widely — the error variance grows with income.

steps.title: Consequences and tests
steps.body:
- Var(ui) = σi² (not constant), common in cross-section data.
- OLS still **unbiased and consistent**, but **not efficient**; usual standard errors are **biased** ⇒ t and F tests unreliable.
- Tests: graphical (e² vs X), **Park**, **Glejser**, **Goldfeld–Quandt** (order by X, drop middle, compare RSS), **Breusch–Pagan–Godfrey**, **White** (general).
- Remedies: **WLS/GLS** when variance form known (e.g. σi² = σ²Xi² ⇒ divide by Xi), **White heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors**, log transformation.

steps.title: Solved: Goldfeld–Quandt
steps.body:
n = 30 ordered by X; drop middle 10 ⇒ two groups of 10; each regression has df = 8. RSS_low = 20, RSS_high = 70.

λ = (70/8)/(20/8) = **3.5**; F-crit(8, 8) at 5% ≈ 3.44 ⇒ **reject homoscedasticity**.

steps.title: Solved: WLS transformation
steps.body:
Model Y = β1 + β2X + u with Var(u) = σ²X².

Divide by X: Y/X = β1(1/X) + β2 + u/X; Var(u/X) = σ² ⇒ homoscedastic. β2 becomes the **intercept** of the transformed regression.

statements.s: Under heteroscedasticity, OLS estimators remain unbiased.
statements.why: Unbiasedness needs only E(u|X) = 0.

statements.s: Usual OLS standard errors are valid under heteroscedasticity.
statements.why: They are biased.

statements.s: White's robust standard errors correct inference without knowing the variance form.
statements.why: They are consistent under general heteroscedasticity.

statements.s: Heteroscedasticity is most common in time-series data.
statements.why: It is typical of cross-section data.

quiz.q: GQ: RSS_high = 60, RSS_low = 15, equal df. λ =
If Var(u) = σ²X, the WLS weight divides the equation by:
quiz.why: Var(u/√X) = σ².

quiz.q: Which test is a general test not assuming a specific form?
quiz.why: White regresses e² on regressors, squares and cross-products.

scenes.text: A drought this year depresses farm output next year too.
Errors in time-series regressions are often correlated over time.

steps.title: AR(1) errors
steps.body:
- ut = ρut−1 + εt, |ρ| < 1.
- Causes: inertia, omitted variables, wrong functional form, data smoothing, lags.
- Consequences: OLS unbiased but inefficient; standard errors usually **underestimated** with positive ρ ⇒ inflated t's and R².
- **Durbin–Watson d** = Σ(et − et−1)²/Σet² ≈ 2(1 − ρ̂). d ≈ 2 no autocorrelation; d → 0 positive; d → 4 negative. Inconclusive zone between dL and dU; invalid with lagged dependent variable (use Durbin h or **Breusch–Godfrey LM**).
- Remedies: GLS via **Cochrane–Orcutt** or Prais–Winsten, first differences (if ρ ≈ 1), Newey–West (HAC) standard errors.

steps.title: Solved: DW
steps.body: ρ̂ = 0.6 ⇒ d ≈ 2(1 − 0.6) = **0.8**. With dL = 1.20 (say, n = 25, k' = 1), d < dL ⇒ **positive autocorrelation**.

steps.title: Solved: generalised difference
steps.body:
Known ρ = 0.7. Transform: Yt* = Yt − 0.7Yt−1, Xt* = Xt − 0.7Xt−1.

If Y_t = 120, Y_{t−1} = 100 ⇒ Y* = **50**; regress Y* on X* by OLS; intercept estimates β1(1 − 0.7).

bands.text: Negative ρ̂: d above about 2.6 — negative autocorrelation.
ρ̂ near 0: d near 2 — no first-order autocorrelation.
Positive ρ̂: d below about 1.4 — positive autocorrelation, typical in macro time series.

quiz.q: DW is not valid when the model includes:
quiz.why: Use Durbin's h or the Breusch–Godfrey test instead.

scenes.text: A wage regression omits ability, which raises both schooling and wages.
The schooling coefficient picks up part of ability's effect — upward bias.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Omitting a relevant variable** X3: E(b2) = β2 + β3·b32, where b32 is the slope from regressing X3 on X2 ⇒ biased and inconsistent unless β3 = 0 or X2, X3 uncorrelated.
- **Including an irrelevant variable**: estimators unbiased but less efficient.
- **Wrong functional form**, measurement error in X (attenuation bias), simultaneity.
- Tests: **Ramsey RESET**, t/F tests on added variables, LM tests.

steps.title: Solved: omitted-variable bias
steps.body:
True model: ln W = β1 + 0.06S + 0.04A + u. Regression of ability A on S gives slope 0.5.

Short regression slope on S ⇒ E(b2) = 0.06 + 0.04 × 0.5 = **0.08** — overstates the return to schooling by 2 percentage points.

steps.title: Solved: attenuation
steps.body:
Measurement error in X with Var(X_true) = 9, Var(error) = 3.

plim b2 = β2 × 9/(9 + 3) = **0.75β2** — biased towards zero.

statements.why: Omitted variable bias.

statements.s: Including an irrelevant variable makes OLS biased.
statements.why: Estimates stay unbiased but lose efficiency.

statements.s: Measurement error in X biases the slope towards zero.
statements.why: Attenuation bias.

statements.s: Ramsey's RESET is a test for specification error.
statements.why: It adds powers of fitted values.

quiz.why: Variances rise.

questions.why: Inference becomes unreliable.

questions.why: Var(u/X) = σ².

uni-ba-eco-indian-economy.title: Indian Economy — structure, sectors, policy
uni-ba-eco-indian-economy.description: Colonial legacy and planning, the 1991 reforms, agriculture, industry and services, poverty, employment and human development, and fiscal, monetary and external-sector policy in India. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA (Hons) Economics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · From colonial economy to planning and reforms
courses.summary: The colonial legacy, the Nehru–Mahalanobis strategy and Five-Year Plans, the licence-permit regime, the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis and LPG reforms, and the shift from the Planning Commission to NITI Aayog.
outcomes: Describe India's economic condition at independence
Explain the Mahalanobis heavy-industry strategy
Identify causes of the 1991 crisis
Summarise liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation measures
Compare the Planning Commission and NITI Aayog

story.title: An economy shaped for export of raw materials

scenes.text: Railways linked ports to cotton and jute fields more than to Indian markets.
Handicrafts declined while machine-made British textiles flooded in.

steps.title: Features at independence (1947)
steps.body:
- Stagnant agriculture: low productivity, zamindari and other exploitative land tenure, commercialisation without investment.
- **De-industrialisation** of handicrafts; limited modern industry (textiles, jute).
- Weak infrastructure geared to trade; high illiteracy and mortality.
- **Drain of wealth** theory (Dadabhai Naoroji): transfer of resources to Britain via home charges and profits.
- Very low growth of per capita income in the first half of the 20th century.

steps.title: Exam framing
steps.body: Structure answers as agriculture → industry → trade → infrastructure → demography, and link each to the post-1947 policy response (land reform, industrial policy, import substitution, public investment).

steps.title: Occupational structure
steps.body: A very large majority of the workforce depended on agriculture at independence, a feature that has changed only gradually since.

statements.s: Dadabhai Naoroji is associated with the drain of wealth theory.
statements.why: He argued that India's resources were transferred to Britain.

statements.s: Colonial railways were built mainly to integrate Indian domestic markets.
statements.why: They mainly served raw-material exports and imports of British goods.

statements.s: India's handicraft industry declined during colonial rule.
statements.why: Competition from machine-made goods and colonial policies hurt artisans.

statements.s: At independence most Indians worked in industry.
statements.why: The large majority depended on agriculture.

options: transfer of resources from India to Britain
quiz.why: Naoroji described the outflow of wealth through home charges and remitted profits.

quiz.q: De-industrialisation in colonial India mainly affected:
quiz.why: Traditional crafts lost markets to British factory goods.

quiz.q: A key agrarian problem at independence was:
options: high exports of grain to India
quiz.why: Zamindari and similar systems extracted rent without investment.

scenes.text: In the Second Plan, public-sector steel plants came up at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur.
The idea: build capital goods first to grow faster later.

steps.title: Planning framework
steps.body:
- Planning Commission set up in **1950**; First Five-Year Plan 1951–56 focused on agriculture and irrigation (Harrod–Domar inspired).
- **Second Plan (1956–61)**: Mahalanobis model — priority to heavy/capital-goods industries in the public sector.
- Industrial Policy Resolution **1956**: reserved key industries for the state.
- Instruments: industrial licensing, import substitution, public sector, administered prices.

steps.title: Achievements and problems
steps.body:
- Achievements: industrial base, self-reliance in many capital goods, institutions (IITs, research), Green Revolution later.
- Problems: **licence-permit raj**, inefficiency of public enterprises, slow growth (the so-called 'Hindu rate of growth' ~3.5% coined by Raj Krishna), neglect of exports and labour-intensive manufacturing.

steps.title: Solved: Harrod–Domar planning logic
steps.body: If the capital–output ratio is 3 and the target growth is 5%, required investment = 5 × 3 = **15% of GDP**. With domestic saving of 10%, the gap of 5% must come from foreign savings or higher domestic saving.

statements.s: The Second Five-Year Plan was based on the Mahalanobis model.
statements.why: It prioritised heavy industry.

statements.s: The Planning Commission was set up in 1950.
statements.why: It was established by a cabinet resolution in March 1950.

statements.s: The First Plan gave top priority to heavy industry.
statements.why: It focused on agriculture, irrigation and power.

statements.s: The term 'Hindu rate of growth' refers to India's slow growth of about 3.5% before the 1980s.
statements.why: Raj Krishna coined the phrase.

quiz.q: The Industrial Policy Resolution that reserved key sectors for the state was issued in:
quiz.why: IPR 1956 created schedules reserving industries for the public sector.

quiz.q: Capital–output ratio 4, growth target 6%. Required investment rate:

quiz.why: Protection was used to build domestic industry in place of imports.

scenes.text: In 1991 India pledged gold to raise emergency foreign exchange.
Within weeks a new government announced sweeping reforms.

steps.title: Causes of the crisis
steps.body:
- Large fiscal deficits through the 1980s and rising public debt.
- Widening current-account deficit; rising short-term external debt.
- Gulf War (1990–91): oil price spike, fall in remittances.
- Political uncertainty; downgrade of credit rating; reserves fell to a level covering only a few weeks of imports.

steps.title: Reforms (LPG)
steps.body:
- **Stabilisation**: fiscal correction, rupee devaluation (July 1991), IMF support.
- **Liberalisation**: abolition of industrial licensing for most industries (New Industrial Policy, July 1991), reduction of reservations.
- **Privatisation**: disinvestment in public enterprises.
- **Globalisation**: tariff cuts, FDI liberalisation, current-account convertibility (1994).
- Financial-sector reforms (Narasimham Committee), tax reforms (Chelliah Committee).

steps.title: Outcomes
steps.body: Faster growth, especially in services; rise in foreign reserves; greater integration with world trade. Critiques: jobless growth concerns, agrarian distress, rising inequality.

statements.s: The Gulf War contributed to India's 1991 crisis.
statements.why: Oil prices rose and remittances fell.

statements.s: The New Industrial Policy of 1991 expanded industrial licensing.
statements.why: It abolished licensing for most industries.

statements.s: Current-account convertibility of the rupee was introduced in 1994.
statements.why: India accepted IMF Article VIII obligations in 1994.

statements.s: Privatisation in India mainly took the form of disinvestment.
statements.why: The government sold part of its stakes in public enterprises.

quiz.q: Which committee is associated with financial-sector reforms in 1991?
quiz.why: The Narasimham Committee recommended banking reforms.

lessons.title: From Planning Commission to NITI Aayog

story.title: A think tank replaces a planner

scenes.text: On 1 January 2015 the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog.
The new body emphasised cooperative federalism rather than allocating funds.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
- **Planning Commission** (1950–2014): formulated Five-Year Plans, allocated plan funds to states; top-down.
- **NITI Aayog** (National Institution for Transforming India, 2015): policy think tank, no fund allocation power, promotes **cooperative and competitive federalism**, indices ranking states (e.g. SDG India Index).
- Twelfth Plan (2012–17) was the last Five-Year Plan.

steps.title: Growth phases (stylised)
steps.body:
- 1950–80: slow growth.
- 1980s: acceleration with partial reforms but rising deficits.
- 1991 onwards: higher growth, services-led.
- 2003–08: high-growth phase; global financial crisis 2008–09; pandemic contraction in 2020–21 followed by recovery.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: When asked to compare, use a two-column table: role, finance powers, approach (top-down vs cooperative), output (plans vs strategy documents and indices).

statements.s: NITI Aayog allocates plan funds to states.
statements.why: Fund allocation moved to the Finance Ministry; NITI is a think tank.

statements.s: The Twelfth Five-Year Plan was the last.
statements.why: Five-Year Plans ended in 2017.

statements.s: NITI Aayog promotes cooperative federalism.
statements.why: States participate through its Governing Council.

statements.s: The Planning Commission was abolished in 1991.
statements.why: It was replaced in 2015.

quiz.why: It replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.

quiz.why: It advises and coordinates rather than allocating resources.
