courses.title: Unit 2 · Indian agriculture
courses.summary: Land reforms, the Green Revolution and its effects, agricultural pricing (MSP, procurement), food security and PDS, rural credit and the problems of small and marginal farmers.
outcomes: Evaluate land reform measures and outcomes
Explain the Green Revolution and its regional and ecological effects
Describe MSP, procurement and the cost concepts used
Explain the National Food Security Act and PDS
Assess institutional credit and recent farmer-support schemes

scenes.text: A tenant in 1950 paid half his crop as rent to an absentee landlord.
Land reform laws aimed to abolish intermediaries and give tillers security.

steps.title: Components
steps.body:
- **Abolition of intermediaries** (zamindari) — largely achieved in the 1950s.
- **Tenancy reforms**: regulation of rent, security of tenure, ownership rights.
- **Ceilings on landholdings** and redistribution of surplus land.
- **Consolidation of holdings** to reduce fragmentation.
- Success varied: notable in West Bengal (Operation Barga, 1978) and Kerala; weak in many states due to evasion (benami transfers).

steps.title: Small farms today
steps.body: Agricultural Census data show a steadily falling average holding size; the large majority of holdings are marginal (< 1 hectare) or small (1–2 hectares).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming land ceilings redistributed most farmland — the amount redistributed was modest.
- Confusing consolidation (merging scattered plots) with ceilings.

statements.s: Operation Barga was a West Bengal programme to register sharecroppers.
statements.why: It gave bargadars security of tenure.

statements.s: Land ceiling laws redistributed the majority of India's farmland.
statements.why: Evasion limited redistribution.

statements.s: Most Indian landholdings are marginal or small.
statements.why: Agricultural Census data show this consistently.

statements.s: Abolition of zamindari removed intermediaries between the state and the cultivator.
statements.why: That was its purpose.

quiz.why: It merges scattered plots into compact holdings.

quiz.q: A marginal holding is smaller than:
quiz.why: Marginal holdings are below 1 hectare.

quiz.q: Land reforms were most successful in:
quiz.why: Political commitment produced effective tenancy and ceiling reforms there.

scenes.text: In the mid-1960s India relied on imported US wheat under PL-480.
High-yielding varieties, irrigation and fertiliser made Punjab a granary within a decade.

steps.title: Package
steps.body:
- Introduced mid-1960s: **HYV seeds** (wheat varieties developed from Norman Borlaug's work; M.S. Swaminathan led adaptation in India), assured irrigation, chemical fertilisers, pesticides, credit, MSP and procurement.
- Concentrated in **wheat** and in **Punjab, Haryana, western UP**; rice gains came later.

steps.title: Effects
steps.body:
- Positive: food self-sufficiency, higher farm incomes, buffer stocks.
- Negative: **regional and inter-crop disparities** (pulses, oilseeds lagged), interpersonal inequality (large farmers gained first), **groundwater depletion**, soil degradation, chemical overuse, monocropping (wheat–rice).
- Need for a 'second' / evergreen revolution emphasising sustainability and dryland farming.

steps.title: Solved: productivity
steps.body:
Output 4,800 tonnes from 1,200 hectares.

Yield = 4,800/1,200 = **4 tonnes per hectare**. If yield rises to 5 t/ha on the same area, output = 6,000 t (+25%).

statements.s: The Green Revolution initially benefited wheat more than rice or pulses.
statements.why: HYV wheat spread fastest.

statements.s: It reduced regional inequality in agriculture.
statements.why: Gains concentrated in irrigated north-western regions.

statements.s: Groundwater depletion in Punjab is linked to the wheat–rice cycle.
statements.why: Paddy needs heavy irrigation.

statements.s: M.S. Swaminathan is associated with the Green Revolution in India.
statements.why: He led the scientific adaptation of HYVs.

quiz.q: The Green Revolution's key input was:
quiz.why: HYV seeds, used with irrigation and fertiliser, raised yields.

quiz.q: Which crops lagged during the Green Revolution?
quiz.why: HYV technology for these crops was weaker.

scenes.text: At a mandi, wheat is bought by the Food Corporation of India at the Minimum Support Price.
That grain later reaches ration shops under the National Food Security Act.

steps.title: MSP and procurement
steps.body:
- **Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)** recommends MSPs for 22 mandated crops (plus FRP for sugarcane).
- Cost concepts: **A2** (paid-out costs), **A2 + FL** (plus imputed family labour), **C2** (comprehensive, including rent and interest on owned land/capital).
- Since 2018-19 the government has fixed MSPs at least **1.5 times A2 + FL** for kharif and rabi crops.
- Procurement is concentrated in wheat and rice and in a few states.

steps.title: Food security
steps.body:
- **National Food Security Act, 2013**: legal entitlement to subsidised grains for up to 75% of rural and 50% of urban population; 5 kg per person per month for priority households, 35 kg per household for Antyodaya families.
- Delivered through the **Targeted PDS**; reforms include Aadhaar-linked ration cards and One Nation One Ration Card portability.
- Free foodgrains under PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana have been extended for NFSA beneficiaries.

steps.title: Solved: MSP formula
steps.body:
A2 + FL cost of wheat = ₹1,400 per quintal.

Minimum MSP under the 1.5× rule = 1.5 × 1,400 = **₹2,100 per quintal**. Margin over A2 + FL = 50%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying MSP is based on C2 — the 1.5× rule uses A2 + FL.
- Saying all farmers benefit from MSP — benefit depends on procurement reach.

statements.s: CACP recommends Minimum Support Prices.
statements.why: Its recommendations go to the government.

statements.s: The 1.5× MSP rule is based on C2 cost.
statements.why: It is based on A2 + FL.

statements.s: NFSA 2013 provides 5 kg of grain per person per month for priority households.
statements.why: That is the entitlement.

statements.s: Procurement is evenly spread across all crops and states.
statements.why: It is concentrated in wheat and rice and in a few states.

quiz.q: A2 + FL = ₹1,800/quintal. Minimum MSP under the 1.5× rule:

options: rent and interest on owned land and capital as well
quiz.why: C2 is the comprehensive cost measure.
These are the coverage ceilings in the Act.

scenes.text: A farmer once borrowed from a moneylender at very high monthly interest.
With a Kisan Credit Card from a bank, she now borrows at subsidised rates.

steps.title: Institutions and schemes
steps.body:
- Sources: cooperatives, commercial banks (after 1969 nationalisation), Regional Rural Banks (1975), **NABARD** (1982, apex refinance).
- **Priority sector lending** includes agriculture targets for banks.
- **Kisan Credit Card** (1998) for short-term crop credit; interest subvention for prompt repayment.
- Microfinance and self-help groups (SHG–bank linkage).
- **PM-KISAN** (2019): income support of ₹6,000 per year to eligible farmer families in three instalments.
- **PMFBY** (2016): crop insurance with low farmer premiums.

steps.title: Persistent problems
steps.body: Small holdings, dependence on monsoon, low irrigation in many regions, indebtedness, low value addition, fragmented markets (APMC system), climate risk.

steps.title: Solved: cost of informal credit
steps.body:
Loan ₹50,000 from a moneylender at 3% per month simple interest for 12 months vs a KCC at 7% per year.

- Moneylender interest = 50,000 × 0.03 × 12 = **₹18,000**.
- KCC interest = 50,000 × 0.07 = **₹3,500**.
Saving = ₹14,500.

statements.s: NABARD was established in 1982.
statements.why: It took over agricultural refinance functions from RBI.

statements.s: PM-KISAN provides ₹6,000 per year to eligible farmer families.
statements.why: Paid in three instalments of ₹2,000.

statements.s: Regional Rural Banks were set up after 2000.
statements.why: They began in 1975.

statements.s: Kisan Credit Cards provide short-term crop credit.
statements.why: That is their main purpose.

quiz.q: Apex institution for rural credit refinance:
quiz.why: NABARD refinances rural lending institutions.

quiz.why: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana insures crops.

questions.why: It recorded sharecroppers' rights in West Bengal.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Industry and services
courses.summary: Evolution of industrial policy, public sector and disinvestment, MSMEs, manufacturing initiatives (Make in India, PLI), measurement of industrial output, and the services-led growth pattern.
outcomes: Trace industrial policy from 1948 to post-1991
Evaluate the role of public sector enterprises and disinvestment
Explain the importance and problems of MSMEs
Describe Make in India and the PLI scheme
Analyse why India's growth has been services-led

lessons.title: Industrial policy and the public sector

story.title: From commanding heights to strategic sale

scenes.text: In the 1950s the state built steel, power and heavy engineering — the 'commanding heights'.
Decades later, the government began selling stakes, and in 2022 Air India was handed to a private group.

steps.title: Milestones
steps.body:
- **IPR 1948**: mixed economy framework.
- **IPR 1956**: Schedule A (state monopoly), B (state-led), C (private).
- **MRTP Act 1969**, FERA 1973 — controls on large firms and foreign exchange.
- **New Industrial Policy 1991**: abolished licensing except for a short list, reduced public-sector reservation, liberalised FDI; MRTP later replaced by the **Competition Act, 2002**; FERA by **FEMA, 1999**.

steps.title: PSEs and disinvestment
steps.body:
- Roles: infrastructure, regional balance, employment, self-reliance.
- Problems: low returns, political interference, soft budget constraints.
- Disinvestment: minority stake sales (from 1991-92), strategic sales (e.g. early 2000s; Air India 2022).
- Maharatna/Navratna/Miniratna status gives autonomy to better performers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying FEMA replaced the MRTP Act (FEMA replaced FERA; the Competition Act replaced MRTP).
- Treating disinvestment and privatisation as identical — minority stake sales do not transfer control.

statements.s: FEMA 1999 replaced FERA 1973.
statements.why: It shifted from regulating to managing foreign exchange.

statements.s: The Competition Act 2002 replaced the MRTP Act.
statements.why: It moved from size-based controls to behaviour-based competition law.

statements.s: All disinvestment transfers management control to private buyers.
statements.why: Minority stake sales leave control with the government.

statements.s: IPR 1956 divided industries into three schedules.
statements.why: Schedules A, B and C.

quiz.why: Key sectors were placed under public ownership.

quiz.q: Air India's strategic sale was completed in:
quiz.why: Ownership passed to the Tata group in January 2022.
Delicensing was its central reform.

scenes.text: A small auto-parts workshop in Pune employs 25 people and supplies a large carmaker.
Its biggest worries: delayed payments and access to credit.

steps.title: Role
steps.body:
- Large share of manufacturing employment, exports and enterprises; mostly micro units.
- Classified (since 2020) by **both investment in plant and machinery and turnover** into micro, small and medium; thresholds have since been revised upward.
- **Udyam registration** online since 2020.

steps.title: Problems and support
steps.body:
- Problems: credit access, delayed payments, technology, informality, competition from imports and large firms.
- Support: priority-sector lending, credit guarantee (CGTMSE), Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (pandemic), TReDS platform for invoice discounting, public procurement preference.

steps.title: Solved: working-capital cost of delayed payment
steps.body:
An MSME has ₹40 lakh of receivables delayed by 90 extra days and borrows at 12% per year to fill the gap.

Extra interest = 40 × 0.12 × 90/365 ≈ **₹1.18 lakh** — why payment discipline matters.

statements.s: Since 2020, MSMEs are classified using both investment and turnover.
statements.why: The composite criterion replaced the investment-only rule.

statements.s: Most MSMEs in India are medium-sized enterprises.
statements.why: The vast majority are micro enterprises.

statements.s: TReDS helps MSMEs discount invoices.
statements.why: It is an electronic platform for trade receivables.

statements.s: Delayed payments raise MSMEs' working-capital costs.
statements.why: They must borrow to bridge the gap.

quiz.why: It is the online registration system for MSMEs.

quiz.q: ₹10 lakh delayed 73 days at 10% p.a. Extra interest:

quiz.why: It guarantees collateral-free loans to micro and small enterprises.

lessons.title: Manufacturing push: Make in India and PLI

scenes.text: A decade ago most smartphones sold in India were imported.
Now large assembly plants export phones, helped by production-linked incentives.

steps.title: Policies
steps.body:
- **Make in India** (2014): raise manufacturing share, ease of doing business, FDI promotion.
- **Production Linked Incentive (PLI)** schemes (from 2020): incentives as a percentage of incremental sales over a base year in sectors such as mobile phones, pharmaceuticals, electronics, automobiles, textiles, solar modules.
- Supporting reforms: corporate tax cut (2019), labour codes, logistics policy, industrial corridors.

steps.title: Debates
steps.body:
- Manufacturing's share of GDP has remained in the mid-teens percent — 'premature deindustrialisation' concern (Rodrik).
- PLI critiques: assembly-heavy, low domestic value addition in some sectors, fiscal cost; supporters point to scale and export gains.

steps.title: Solved: PLI payout
steps.body:
A firm's base-year sales ₹1,000 crore; this year ₹1,600 crore; incentive rate 5% on incremental sales.

Incentive = 5% × (1,600 − 1,000) = **₹30 crore**.

statements.s: PLI incentives are linked to incremental sales.
statements.why: Payouts depend on sales above a base year.

statements.s: Make in India was launched in 1991.
statements.why: It was launched in 2014.

statements.s: Premature deindustrialisation refers to manufacturing's share peaking at low income levels.
statements.why: Rodrik's term.

statements.s: Mobile phones are one of the PLI sectors.
statements.why: Large-scale electronics manufacturing was among the first.

quiz.q: Base sales 500, current 800, PLI rate 4%. Incentive:
A criticism of PLI in electronics is:
quiz.why: Much activity is assembly of imported components.

quiz.q: Corporate tax rates were cut significantly in:
quiz.why: September 2019 reduced base rates for domestic companies.

scenes.text: IT and business services became India's signature export after the 1990s.
But most services workers are in low-productivity trade, transport and personal services.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body:
- Services account for over half of GVA, a larger share than in many economies at similar income.
- Drivers: IT/ITeS and telecom liberalisation, financial services, skilled English-speaking workforce, time-zone advantage, Global Capability Centres.
- Contrast with the East Asian model of manufacturing-led growth.

steps.title: Issues
steps.body:
- Modern services are skill-intensive and employ relatively few; most low-skilled workers remain in agriculture, construction and informal services.
- **Structural transformation** from agriculture has been slower in employment than in output.
- Digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI) supports fintech and services.

steps.title: Solved: sectoral productivity
steps.body:
Sector shares: services 55% of GVA with 30% of workers; agriculture 18% of GVA with 45% of workers.

Relative productivity (GVA share ÷ employment share): services 55/30 ≈ **1.83**; agriculture 18/45 = **0.40**. Moving workers from farms to services raises average productivity.

statements.s: Services contribute more than half of India's GVA.
statements.why: This has been true for many years.

statements.s: India followed the East Asian manufacturing-led growth model closely.
statements.why: India's growth has been services-led.

statements.s: Agriculture's share of employment is higher than its share of output.
statements.why: Hence low output per worker.

statements.s: UPI is part of India's digital public infrastructure.
statements.why: It is a public payments platform built by NPCI.

quiz.q: GVA share 20%, employment share 40%. Relative productivity:
A reason for India's IT boom:
quiz.why: Skilled labour at competitive cost drove offshoring.

options: workers shifting from low- to high-productivity sectors
quiz.why: Development involves moving resources to more productive sectors.

questions.why: Schedule A covered state monopolies.

questions.why: FEMA 1999.

questions.why: Strategic sale passes control to the buyer.

questions.why: A composite criterion.

questions.why: September 2014.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Poverty, employment and human development
courses.summary: Measuring poverty (poverty lines, headcount ratio, poverty gap, multidimensional poverty), inequality measures, employment structure and informality, anti-poverty programmes, and education and health outcomes.
outcomes: Compute headcount ratio and poverty-gap index
Explain the Tendulkar and Rangarajan methodologies and the MPI
Describe India's employment structure using PLFS concepts
Evaluate MGNREGA and other anti-poverty programmes
Discuss human development in health and education

scenes.text: Experts debate what monthly spending is the minimum for a decent life.
Where the line is drawn changes how many Indians count as poor.

steps.title: Approaches
steps.body:
- **Consumption-based poverty line** using household consumer expenditure surveys.
- Expert groups: Lakdawala (calorie-based, state-specific), **Tendulkar** (2009; broader basket incl. health and education) — 2011-12 poverty ratio **21.9%**; **Rangarajan** (2014) — 2011-12 ratio **29.5%**.
- **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)**: health, education, living standards (Alkire–Foster); NITI Aayog publishes a national MPI.
- International: World Bank extreme poverty line in PPP dollars per day.

steps.title: Indices
steps.body:
- **Headcount ratio (HCR)** H = q/n (share below the line).
- **Poverty gap index** PG = (1/n) Σ (z − yi)/z over the poor — depth.
- **Squared poverty gap** — severity, weights poorest more (FGT family).

steps.title: Solved: HCR and PG
steps.body:
Poverty line z = ₹100. Ten people; three are poor with incomes 60, 80, 90.

1. H = 3/10 = **0.30**.
2. Gaps: 0.40, 0.20, 0.10 ⇒ sum 0.70 ⇒ PG = 0.70/10 = **0.07**.
3. Transfer ₹10 to the person at 60: H unchanged, PG falls to 0.06 — HCR ignores depth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing the poverty gap sum by the number of poor instead of total population.
- Mixing figures from different methodologies when comparing over time.

statements.s: The Tendulkar methodology put 2011-12 poverty at 21.9%.
statements.why: This was the official estimate for 2011-12.

statements.s: The headcount ratio captures how far below the line the poor are.
statements.why: It only counts them; the poverty gap measures depth.

statements.s: MPI includes health, education and living standards.
statements.why: These are its three dimensions.

statements.s: A transfer from a poor person to a richer poor person can leave HCR unchanged.
statements.why: HCR is insensitive to distribution among the poor.

quiz.why: Two of five are below 50.
Gaps 0.4 and 0.2 sum to 0.6; divided by 5 gives 0.12.
The Rangarajan group's estimate was 29.5%.

scenes.text: Luxury towers rise beside informal settlements in Mumbai.
The Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient summarise how unequal incomes are.

steps.title: Measures
steps.body:
- **Lorenz curve**: cumulative share of income vs cumulative share of population; the diagonal = perfect equality.
- **Gini coefficient** = area between diagonal and Lorenz curve ÷ total area under the diagonal; 0 (equal) to 1 (one person has all).
- Others: income share of top 10%/1%, Palma ratio (top 10% ÷ bottom 40%), Kuznets ratio.

steps.title: Solved: Gini from a simple Lorenz curve
steps.body:
Two equal groups: poorer half has 20% of income.

Lorenz points: (0,0), (0.5, 0.2), (1,1). Area under Lorenz = ½·0.5·0.2 + 0.5·(0.2 + 1)/2 = 0.05 + 0.30 = 0.35.

Gini = (0.5 − 0.35)/0.5 = **0.30**.

steps.title: India
steps.body: Consumption-based Gini estimates for India are lower than income- or wealth-based ones, because consumption is more evenly distributed than income and wealth.

statements.s: A Gini coefficient of 0 means perfect equality.
statements.why: Lorenz curve coincides with the diagonal.

statements.s: Consumption inequality is usually higher than wealth inequality.
statements.why: Wealth is far more concentrated.

statements.s: The Palma ratio compares the top 10% with the bottom 40%.
statements.why: That is its definition.

statements.s: A Lorenz curve further from the diagonal indicates more inequality.
statements.why: The gap area is larger.

quiz.q: Poorer half holds 25% of income (two groups). Gini:
Top 10% share 30%, bottom 40% share 20%. Palma ratio:

quiz.why: As a ratio of areas it lies between 0 and 1.

scenes.text: A construction worker in Delhi works without a written contract or social security.
PLFS surveys count him as employed — but in the informal sector.

steps.title: Concepts (PLFS)
steps.body:
- **Periodic Labour Force Survey** (NSO, from 2017-18) replaced the quinquennial employment–unemployment rounds.
- **LFPR** = labour force / population; **WPR** = employed / population; **UR** = unemployed / labour force.
- Status: usual status (ps + ss) and current weekly status (CWS).
- Employment types: self-employed, regular wage/salaried, casual labour.
- Large majority of workers are **informal** (no written contract, paid leave or social security).

steps.title: Solved: rates
steps.body:
Population (15+) 1,000; labour force 560; employed 530.

- LFPR = 56%.
- WPR = 53%.
- UR = 30/560 = **5.4%**.

steps.title: Female LFPR
steps.body: Female LFPR in India has been low by international standards, though PLFS rounds since 2017-18 show a rise, much of it in rural self-employment. Factors: social norms, care work, lack of suitable jobs, safety, education effects.

statements.s: PLFS is conducted by the National Statistics Office.
statements.why: It began in 2017-18.

statements.s: The unemployment rate uses population as the denominator.
statements.why: It uses the labour force.

statements.s: Most Indian workers are in informal employment.
statements.why: They lack formal contracts or social security.

statements.s: WPR is always at least as large as LFPR.
statements.why: WPR ≤ LFPR since employed ≤ labour force.

quiz.q: Casual labour refers to workers who:
options: are hired daily/periodically without regular contracts
quiz.why: Casual workers are engaged on a daily or periodic basis.

scenes.text: A woman with an MGNREGA job card demands work during a dry season.
She earns wages building a village water tank — a safety net and an asset.

steps.title: Programmes
steps.body:
- **MGNREGA (2005)**: legal guarantee of up to 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year; demand-driven; one-third of beneficiaries to be women; wages paid via bank accounts.
- **NRLM / DAY-NRLM**: self-help groups for livelihoods.
- **PM Awas Yojana** (housing), **Jan Dhan** (bank accounts, 2014), **Ujjwala** (LPG), **Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY** (health insurance up to ₹5 lakh per family per year).
- **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)** using the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile).

steps.title: Human development
steps.body:
- Education: Right to Education Act (2009) for ages 6–14; National Education Policy 2020; learning outcomes remain a concern.
- Health: National Health Mission; improvements in infant and maternal mortality; persistent child stunting.
- India's HDI places it in the 'medium human development' group.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Fiscal, financial and external-sector policy
courses.summary: The Union Budget and deficit concepts, FRBM, GST and fiscal federalism through Finance Commissions, banking reforms, NPAs and the IBC, and India's balance of payments, FDI and exchange-rate management.
outcomes: Compute revenue, fiscal and primary deficits
Explain FRBM and GST
Describe the role of Finance Commissions
Explain NPAs, recapitalisation and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code
Analyse India's balance of payments, capital flows and reserves

scenes.text: On 1 February the Finance Minister presents the Union Budget in Parliament.
Analysts jump straight to one number: the fiscal deficit.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
- **Effective revenue deficit** = revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets.
- **Fiscal deficit** = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) = borrowing requirement.
- **Primary deficit** = fiscal deficit − interest payments.
- **FRBM Act, 2003**: rules to reduce deficits; targets revised several times (N.K. Singh committee review 2017).

steps.title: Solved: deficits (₹ lakh crore)
steps.body:
Revenue receipts 25; non-debt capital receipts 1; revenue expenditure 37 (interest 10); capital expenditure 8.

1. Revenue deficit = 37 − 25 = **12**.
2. Total expenditure = 45 ⇒ fiscal deficit = 45 − 25 − 1 = **19**.
3. Primary deficit = 19 − 10 = **9**.
4. With GDP 300: fiscal deficit = 6.3% of GDP.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including borrowings in receipts when computing fiscal deficit.
- Subtracting capital expenditure when computing revenue deficit.

statements.s: Fiscal deficit measures the government's total borrowing requirement.
statements.why: It is the gap financed by debt.

statements.s: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit + interest payments.
statements.why: It is fiscal deficit minus interest.

statements.s: Disinvestment proceeds are non-debt capital receipts.
statements.why: They do not create liabilities.

statements.s: The FRBM Act was passed in 2003.
statements.why: Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003.

Total expenditure 40, revenue receipts 28, non-debt capital receipts 2. Fiscal deficit:

scenes.text: Trucks once waited for hours at state check-posts.
From 1 July 2017, GST replaced a web of central and state indirect taxes.

steps.title: GST
steps.body:
- Introduced **1 July 2017** after the 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016).
- Destination-based, multi-stage tax with **input tax credit** (tax only on value added).
- Components: CGST + SGST (intra-state), IGST (inter-state).
- **GST Council** (Union Finance Minister + state finance ministers) decides rates; rate structure has been rationalised over time.
- Some items (e.g. petroleum crude, alcohol for human consumption) remain outside GST.

steps.title: Solved: input tax credit
steps.body:
18% GST. Manufacturer sells for ₹1,000 (tax 180). Retailer sells for ₹1,500 (tax 270).

Retailer pays 270 − 180 = **₹90** = 18% of value added (500). Total tax collected = 270 = 18% of final price — no cascading.

steps.title: Finance Commissions
steps.body:
- Constitutional body under **Article 280**, every five years.
- Recommends vertical sharing (states' share of divisible pool) and horizontal distribution among states (by population, area, income distance, forest cover, demographic performance, etc.).
- The 15th Finance Commission recommended **41%** of the divisible pool for states (2021–26).

statements.s: GST was introduced on 1 July 2017.
statements.why: That was the rollout date.

statements.s: IGST applies to inter-state supplies.
statements.why: Integrated GST is levied by the Centre on inter-state trade.

statements.s: Input tax credit causes cascading of taxes.
statements.why: It removes cascading by taxing only value added.

statements.s: The Finance Commission is constituted under Article 280.
statements.why: It is a constitutional body.

quiz.why: Output tax 300 − input credit 240 = ₹60.

quiz.why: It recommended 41% of the divisible pool.

quiz.why: The GST Council recommends rates.

lessons.title: Banking reforms, NPAs and the IBC

scenes.text: After the 2000s investment boom, many infrastructure firms could not repay loans.
Banks' bad loans soared; the 2016 bankruptcy code aimed to clean up.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **NPA**: loan where interest/principal is overdue for more than **90 days**.
- Gross NPA ratio = gross NPAs/gross advances; net NPA = gross NPA − provisions.
- **Twin balance sheet problem** (Economic Survey 2016-17): over-leveraged corporates + stressed banks.
- Responses: Asset Quality Review (2015), recapitalisation of public sector banks, bank mergers, **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016** (time-bound resolution through NCLT), National Asset Reconstruction Company.

steps.title: Solved: NPA ratios
steps.body:
Gross advances ₹10,000 crore; gross NPAs ₹800 crore; provisions ₹500 crore.

- Gross NPA ratio = **8%**.
- Net NPA = 300 ⇒ net NPA ratio = 300/(10,000 − 500) ≈ **3.2%**.
- Provision coverage ratio = 500/800 = **62.5%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a 30-day threshold for NPAs.
- Computing net NPA ratio over gross instead of net advances.

statements.s: A loan becomes an NPA after 90 days overdue.
statements.why: That is the standard RBI norm.

statements.s: The IBC was enacted in 2016.
statements.why: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.

statements.s: Provision coverage ratio = provisions / gross NPAs.
statements.why: It shows how much of bad loans is provided for.

statements.s: The twin balance sheet problem concerns households and the government.
statements.why: It concerns corporates and banks.

lessons.title: External sector: BoP, FDI and the rupee

scenes.text: In 1991 reserves covered only a few weeks of imports.
Today India holds large reserves that RBI uses to smooth rupee volatility.

steps.title: BoP pattern
steps.body:
- Persistent **merchandise trade deficit** (oil, electronics, gold).
- **Services surplus** (software, business services) and large **remittances** (India is the world's largest recipient).
- Current-account deficit usually modest; financed by FDI, portfolio flows, ECBs.
- **Forex reserves** cover many months of imports.

steps.title: FDI and exchange rate
steps.body:
- FDI via **automatic route** (no prior approval) or **government route**; sectoral caps apply (e.g. defence, insurance, media).
- **Managed float**: RBI intervenes to curb excess volatility, no fixed target.
- Full capital-account convertibility not adopted; liberalised remittance scheme allows resident individuals to remit up to a limit per year.

steps.title: Solved: import cover
steps.body:
Reserves $600 billion; annual merchandise imports $720 billion.

Monthly imports = 60 ⇒ import cover = 600/60 = **10 months**.

statements.s: India typically runs a merchandise trade deficit.
statements.why: Imports of oil, gold and electronics exceed goods exports.

statements.s: India is the world's largest recipient of remittances.
statements.why: World Bank data have ranked India first for years.

statements.s: FDI under the automatic route needs prior government approval.
statements.why: Only the government route needs approval.

statements.s: India's exchange-rate regime is a managed float.
statements.why: RBI intervenes to curb volatility.

quiz.why: Monthly imports = 54; 540/54 = 10.

quiz.why: IT and business services exports exceed services imports.
Capital flows are liberalised but with limits.

uni-ba-eco-international.title: International Economics — trade theory, policy and finance
uni-ba-eco-international.description: Ricardian and Heckscher–Ohlin trade theory, new trade theory, tariffs and trade policy, balance-of-payments adjustment and exchange rates, and international institutions and economic integration. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA (Hons) Economics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Classical trade theory
courses.summary: Mercantilism, Smith's absolute advantage, Ricardo's comparative advantage with labour-cost numericals, opportunity cost and the PPF, the range of mutually beneficial terms of trade, gains from trade and offer curves.
outcomes: Distinguish absolute and comparative advantage
Determine the pattern of trade from labour requirements
Find the range of mutually beneficial terms of trade
Measure gains from trade
Explain reciprocal demand and offer curves

scenes.text: A senior lawyer types faster than her assistant.
She still hires the assistant to type — her time is worth more in court. That is comparative advantage.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Mercantilism**: wealth = gold; maximise exports, minimise imports — zero-sum view.
- **Absolute advantage (Smith, 1776)**: a country produces a good with fewer resources.
- **Comparative advantage (Ricardo, 1817)**: a country has a lower **opportunity cost**; trade benefits both even if one has absolute advantage in both goods.
- Assumptions: two countries, two goods, labour only factor, constant costs, full employment, no transport costs, labour immobile internationally.

steps.title: Solved: Ricardian table
steps.body:
Labour hours per unit: India — cloth 2, wheat 4; UK — cloth 3, wheat 9.

1. India has absolute advantage in both.
2. Opportunity cost of cloth: India 2/4 = 0.5 wheat; UK 3/9 = 0.33 wheat ⇒ **UK has comparative advantage in cloth**.
3. Opportunity cost of wheat: India 2 cloth; UK 3 cloth ⇒ **India in wheat**.
4. India exports wheat, UK exports cloth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding no trade happens when one country has absolute advantage in both.
- Comparing labour hours directly instead of opportunity costs.

statements.s: Trade can benefit both countries even if one has absolute advantage in both goods.
statements.why: Comparative advantage drives gains.

statements.s: In the example, India has comparative advantage in cloth.
statements.why: UK's opportunity cost of cloth is lower.

statements.s: Ricardo's model uses labour as the only factor.
statements.why: Labour theory of value.

statements.s: Mercantilists saw trade as positive-sum.
statements.why: They saw it as zero-sum.

quiz.q: Country A: 1 hr/cloth, 2 hrs/wine; B: 3 hrs/cloth, 4 hrs/wine. A's comparative advantage is in:
quiz.why: A's opportunity cost of cloth is 0.5 wine, below B's 0.75 wine.
B's opportunity cost of wine is 4/3 ≈ 1.33 cloth, lower than A's 2 cloth, so B specialises in wine.
It depends on what a country gives up to produce a good.

scenes.text: India and the UK must agree how much cloth trades for a unit of wheat.
Any rate between their opportunity costs makes both better off.

steps.title: Range of mutually beneficial ToT
steps.body:
- Terms of trade (ToT) must lie **between the two countries' domestic opportunity-cost ratios**.
- In the example: 1 wheat = 2 cloth in India, 3 cloth in the UK ⇒ ToT between **2 and 3 cloth per wheat**.
- Gains: each country consumes beyond its PPF.
- Where exactly ToT settle depends on **reciprocal demand** (J.S. Mill).

steps.title: Solved: gains
steps.body:
ToT 1 wheat = 2.5 cloth. India has 400 labour hours.

1. Autarky: to get 1 wheat India gives up 2 cloth.
2. Specialise: 400/4 = 100 wheat. Trade 40 wheat for 100 cloth ⇒ consumes 60 wheat + 100 cloth.
3. In autarky, 60 wheat (240 hrs) leaves 160 hrs ⇒ only 80 cloth. **Gain = 20 cloth**.

steps.title: Offer curves
steps.body: An offer curve shows how much of its export a country will offer for various quantities of imports. The intersection of the two countries' offer curves gives equilibrium ToT and volumes.

activity.label: Terms of trade (cloth per wheat) — India exports wheat

bands.text: Below 2: India gets fewer cloth per wheat than at home — India won't trade.
Between 2 and 3: both gain; closer to 3 favours India, closer to 2 favours the UK.
Above 3: the UK pays more cloth than its own cost — the UK won't trade.

quiz.q: Domestic ratios: A 1 wine = 2 cloth, B 1 wine = 1.33 cloth. Feasible ToT range (cloth per wine):
quiz.why: Terms of trade must lie between the two countries' opportunity costs, here 1.33 and 2 cloth per wine.

quiz.q: Where ToT settle within the range depends on:
quiz.why: Mill's reciprocal demand determines how the gains are split.

quiz.q: ToT equal to one country's domestic ratio means that country:
quiz.why: It could achieve the same outcome by domestic transformation, so it gains nothing from trade.

scenes.text: With constant labour costs, each country's PPF is a straight line.
Trade leads to complete specialisation at one end of the line.

steps.title: Analysis
steps.body:
- PPF intercepts: L/a_cloth and L/a_wheat; slope = opportunity cost.
- Constant costs ⇒ **complete specialisation** under free trade (unless a country is large).
- With increasing costs (concave PPF), specialisation is **incomplete**.
- Small country takes world ToT as given and captures most gains.

steps.title: Solved: PPF
steps.body:
UK has 900 hours; cloth 3 hrs, wheat 9 hrs.

- Max cloth = 300; max wheat = 100.
- PPF: 3C + 9W = 900 ⇒ slope −1/3 (wheat per cloth).
- Under trade the UK specialises in cloth: **300 units**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing a concave PPF for a Ricardian model.
- Forgetting that the slope is the opportunity cost.

statements.s: Ricardian PPFs are straight lines.
statements.why: Constant opportunity costs.

statements.s: Increasing opportunity costs lead to complete specialisation.
statements.why: They lead to incomplete specialisation.

statements.s: The slope of the PPF equals the opportunity cost.
statements.why: Rate of transformation.

statements.s: A small country can take world prices as given.
statements.why: It cannot influence ToT.

quiz.q: Country with 600 hours, 2 hrs/cloth, 6 hrs/wheat. Max wheat:
quiz.why: 600 hours divided by 6 hours per unit gives 100 units of wheat.
One wheat takes 6 hours, enough for 3 units of cloth at 2 hours each.
Factors are not equally suited to both goods, so each extra unit costs more.

story.title: Many goods, wages and exchange rates

scenes.text: Real countries trade thousands of goods.
Wages and exchange rates decide which goods each country exports.

steps.title: Many goods (chain of comparative advantage)
steps.body:
- Rank goods by relative labour productivity aL*/aL. A country exports goods where its relative productivity exceeds the relative wage w/w*.
- Empirical support: MacDougall (1951) — US–UK export shares correlated with relative labour productivity.
- Critiques: single factor, constant costs, ignores demand differences, transport costs, scale economies, unemployment.

steps.title: Solved: wage cut-off
steps.body:
India/foreign labour hours per unit (a_I, a_F): A (1, 4), B (2, 4), C (3, 3), D (4, 2). Relative wage w_I/w_F = 1.5.

India exports where a_F/a_I > 1.5: A (4), B (2) ⇒ **A and B**; foreign exports C (1) and D (0.5).

steps.title: Answer structure
steps.body: State assumptions, derive pattern of trade, show gains, then list empirical tests and limitations.

statements.s: MacDougall's study supported the Ricardian model.
statements.why: Export shares tracked relative productivity.

statements.s: In the many-goods model, a country exports goods where its relative productivity exceeds the relative wage.
statements.why: Those goods are cheaper to produce there.

statements.s: Ricardo's model includes capital as a factor.
statements.why: Only labour.

statements.s: Scale economies are central to the Ricardian model.
statements.why: It assumes constant costs.

quiz.q: In the wage cut-off example, if w_I/w_F rose to 2.5, India would export:
quiz.why: Only good A has a_F/a_I = 4, above the new relative wage of 2.5.
On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation appeared in 1817.

quiz.q: A limitation of the Ricardian model is:
quiz.why: It ignores capital and land, so it cannot explain factor-based trade.

questions.q: Absolute advantage is due to:
questions.why: Smith set it out in the Wealth of Nations, 1776.

questions.q: A: 4 hrs/rice, 2 hrs/cloth. B: 6 hrs/rice, 6 hrs/cloth. A's OC of rice:
questions.why: 4/2 = 2 cloth per rice.

questions.q: B's OC of rice:
questions.why: 6/6 = 1 cloth per rice.

questions.q: So B has comparative advantage in:
questions.why: B's opportunity cost of rice (1) is below A's (2).

questions.q: Mutually beneficial ToT (cloth per rice):
questions.why: ToT must lie between the two domestic ratios, 1 and 2.

questions.q: Reciprocal demand was developed by:
questions.why: Mill extended Ricardo by explaining how demand sets the terms of trade.

questions.q: Constant opportunity costs imply PPFs that are:
questions.why: A constant slope gives a straight line.

questions.q: 500 hours, 5 hrs/cloth, 10 hrs/wheat. Max cloth:
Under trade with constant costs, specialisation is:
questions.why: No rising costs stop the move to one good.

questions.q: India in the lesson: 400 hours, ToT 2.5 cloth/wheat, trades 40 wheat. Cloth received:
Gain in cloth in that example:
questions.why: India gets 100 cloth instead of the 80 it could make in autarky alongside 60 wheat.

questions.why: Mercantilists measured national wealth in bullion.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Factor endowments and new trade theory
courses.summary: The Heckscher–Ohlin model, factor-price equalisation, Stolper–Samuelson and Rybczynski theorems, the Leontief paradox, specific-factors model, and new trade theory with scale economies, intra-industry trade and gravity.
outcomes: State and apply the Heckscher–Ohlin theorem
Explain factor-price equalisation and Stolper–Samuelson
Apply the Rybczynski theorem
Explain the Leontief paradox and its resolutions
Explain intra-industry trade, the Grubel–Lloyd index and the gravity model

scenes.text: Bangladesh, with abundant labour, exports garments.
Germany, with abundant capital, exports machinery. Endowments shape trade.

steps.title: Assumptions and theorem
steps.body:
- 2×2×2: two countries, two goods, two factors (L, K); identical technologies and tastes; CRS; perfect competition; factors mobile within, immobile between countries; no factor-intensity reversal.
- **H–O theorem**: a country exports the good that uses its **abundant factor** intensively.
- Factor abundance: physical definition (K/L ratio) or price definition (r/w).

steps.title: Solved: abundance and pattern
steps.body:
India: K = 200, L = 800 (K/L = 0.25). Germany: K = 400, L = 400 (K/L = 1).

India is **labour-abundant** ⇒ exports the labour-intensive good (textiles); Germany exports the capital-intensive good (machinery).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using absolute quantities instead of ratios for abundance.
- Forgetting that H–O assumes identical technology (unlike Ricardo).

statements.s: H–O predicts countries export goods intensive in their abundant factor.
statements.why: That is the theorem.

statements.s: H–O assumes technologies differ across countries.
statements.why: It assumes identical technology.

statements.s: Factor abundance is measured by relative ratios.
statements.why: K/L compared across countries.

statements.s: H–O is a two-factor model.
statements.why: Labour and capital.

quiz.q: Country X: K/L = 2; Y: K/L = 0.5. X exports:
quiz.why: X is capital-abundant, so it exports the capital-intensive good.

quiz.q: The price definition of abundance compares:
quiz.why: A lower relative rental rate signals capital abundance.

quiz.q: A key difference from Ricardo is that H–O assumes:
quiz.why: Trade arises from endowments, not technology differences.

scenes.text: When a labour-abundant country opens to trade, demand for its labour-intensive exports rises.
Wages rise and returns to capital fall — trade creates winners and losers.

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
- **Factor-price equalisation** (Samuelson): free trade equalises factor prices across countries under H–O assumptions.
- **Stolper–Samuelson**: a rise in the relative price of a good raises the real return of the factor used intensively in it and lowers the real return of the other factor (**magnification effect**).
- **Rybczynski**: at constant goods prices, an increase in one factor raises output of the good intensive in it **more than proportionately** and reduces output of the other good.

steps.title: Solved: magnification
steps.body:
Price of textiles (labour-intensive) rises 10%, machinery price unchanged.

Stolper–Samuelson: wage rises **more than 10%** (e.g. 15%); rental on capital **falls**. Workers gain in terms of both goods; capital owners lose.

steps.title: Specific-factors model
steps.body: With one factor specific to each sector and labour mobile: a price rise in sector X raises the return to X's specific factor, lowers the return to Y's specific factor, and raises the wage by less than the price rise (ambiguous real wage).

statements.s: Stolper–Samuelson implies trade benefits the abundant factor.
statements.why: Exports raise demand for it.

statements.s: Rybczynski says more capital raises output of both goods.
statements.why: The labour-intensive good's output falls.

statements.s: FPE requires H–O assumptions including no transport costs.
statements.why: Otherwise prices differ.

statements.s: In the specific-factors model, the mobile factor's real wage change is ambiguous.
statements.why: It rises in terms of one good and falls in terms of the other.

quiz.q: Price of the capital-intensive good rises 5%. The rental rate:
quiz.why: The magnification effect makes the intensive factor's return rise more than the price.

quiz.q: A rise in labour supply (Rybczynski) at constant prices:
options: raises labour-intensive output, lowers capital-intensive output
quiz.why: Extra labour is absorbed by expanding the labour-intensive sector, pulling capital from the other.
Paul Samuelson (1948–49).

scenes.text: In 1953 Leontief found US exports were less capital-intensive than its import substitutes.
The world's most capital-rich country seemed to export labour-intensive goods.

steps.title: The paradox and explanations
steps.body:
- Leontief's input–output data (1947): K/L in US import-competing production > K/L in exports.
- Explanations: **human capital/skills** (US labour highly skilled), natural resources ignored, factor-intensity reversals, US tariffs protecting labour-intensive industries, demand bias, three or more factors.
- Later tests with multiple factors (Leamer, Trefler) give mixed support for H–O; 'missing trade'.

steps.title: Solved: computing Leontief's ratio
steps.body:
Per $1 million: exports use K = $2.5 m, L = 180 person-years; import substitutes use K = $3.1 m, L = 170.

K/L exports = 13,889 $/worker; imports = 18,235 $/worker. Ratio (imports/exports) ≈ **1.31** > 1 ⇒ paradox.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

statements.s: Leontief found US exports were relatively labour-intensive.
statements.why: Contrary to H–O expectations.

statements.s: Human capital is one explanation of the paradox.
statements.why: US labour embodied high skills.

statements.s: Leontief used input–output tables.
statements.why: He pioneered the technique.

statements.s: Later multi-factor tests strongly confirm H–O.
statements.why: Results are mixed.

quiz.q: Exports K/L = 10,000; imports K/L = 12,000. Leontief ratio:
Which is NOT an explanation of the paradox?
quiz.why: A perfect fit would mean no paradox.

quiz.q: Leontief's study used US data for:
quiz.why: The 1953 paper used 1947 data.

scenes.text: Germany exports cars to France, and France exports cars to Germany.
Comparative advantage alone can't explain this — scale economies and variety can.

steps.title: Ideas
steps.body:
- **Krugman (1979–80)**: increasing returns + love of variety ⇒ **intra-industry trade** between similar countries; firms specialise in varieties.
- **Home-market effect**: countries export goods with large domestic demand.
- **Melitz (2003)**: heterogeneous firms; only the most productive export.
- **Grubel–Lloyd index** = 1 − |X − M|/(X + M) (1 = all intra-industry).
- **Gravity model**: trade ∝ (GDP_i × GDP_j)/distance.

steps.title: Solved: Grubel–Lloyd
steps.body:
Car exports 80, car imports 60.

GL = 1 − 20/140 = **0.857** ⇒ highly intra-industry.

steps.title: Solved: gravity
steps.body: T = G × Y1 × Y2/D. Pair A: Y 10 and 5, D 2 ⇒ 25G. Pair B: Y 10 and 5, D 4 ⇒ 12.5G. Doubling distance **halves** predicted trade.

statements.s: Intra-industry trade is common between similar rich countries.
statements.why: Variety and scale economies drive it.

statements.s: A Grubel–Lloyd index of 0 means pure intra-industry trade.
statements.why: 0 means pure inter-industry trade.

statements.s: The gravity model predicts more trade between larger, closer economies.
statements.why: Trade rises with GDP and falls with distance.

statements.s: Melitz showed only the most productive firms export.
statements.why: Exporting has fixed costs.

quiz.why: |X − M| = 0, so GL = 1.
Krugman's models rest on scale economies and differentiated products.

questions.q: H–O theorem: a capital-abundant country exports:
questions.why: Exports use the abundant factor intensively.

questions.q: Country A: K 300, L 600; B: K 500, L 500. Capital-abundant country:

courses.title: Unit 3 · Trade policy
courses.summary: Partial-equilibrium welfare effects of tariffs and quotas in small and large countries, the optimal tariff, export subsidies, non-tariff barriers and anti-dumping, arguments for protection, and the WTO.
outcomes: Compute consumer, producer, revenue and deadweight effects of a tariff
Compare tariffs and quotas
Explain the terms-of-trade gain and optimal tariff for a large country
Analyse export subsidies and anti-dumping duties
State WTO principles and evaluate arguments for protection

story.title: A duty on imported edible oil

scenes.text: India raises the import duty on edible oil to support domestic oilseed farmers.
Farmers gain, consumers lose, the government collects revenue — and some value simply disappears.

steps.title: Effects
steps.body:
Small country takes world price Pw as given. Tariff t raises domestic price to Pw + t.
- **Consumption effect**: Qd falls.
- **Production (protective) effect**: Qs rises.
- **Revenue effect**: t × imports.
- **Welfare**: ΔCS = −(a + b + c + d); ΔPS = +a; revenue = c; **DWL = b + d** (production and consumption distortions).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting tariff revenue as a loss — it is a transfer to the government.
- Forgetting the production distortion triangle.

activity.label: Tariff t (₹) with Qd = 100 − P, Qs = P, Pw = 20

bands.text: Free trade: imports 60, no deadweight loss.
Tariff t: imports 60 − 2t, revenue t(60 − 2t), DWL = t² (e.g. t = 10 gives DWL 100).
t = 30: prohibitive — price reaches autarky level 50, imports and revenue fall to zero.

quiz.q: In the example, a tariff of 20 gives imports of:
quiz.why: P = 40 gives Qd = 60 and Qs = 40, so imports are 20.
Each triangle is ½ × 20 × 20 = 200, so DWL = 400.

quiz.q: The prohibitive tariff in the example is:
quiz.why: At P = 50, Qd = Qs = 50, so imports stop when t = 30.

scenes.text: Instead of a tariff, a country allows only 40 units of imports via licences.
Whoever holds the licences pockets the price gap — quota rents.

steps.title: Quota vs tariff
steps.body:
- A quota restricting imports to the tariff-level volume raises domestic price by the same amount (**equivalence** in static, competitive case).
- Difference: the rectangle 'c' becomes **quota rent** to licence holders (or foreign exporters under a **voluntary export restraint**) instead of government revenue.
- Non-equivalence: with demand growth a quota raises price further; with domestic monopoly a quota creates more market power.
- NTBs: standards, licensing, local-content rules, sanitary measures.

steps.title: Solved: quota
steps.body:
Same market (Pw = 20). Quota 40 units.

Domestic price where Qd − Qs = 40: (100 − P) − P = 40 ⇒ **P = 30**. Quota rent = (30 − 20) × 40 = **400** — same size as tariff revenue.

steps.title: Solved: demand growth
steps.body:
Demand rises to Qd = 120 − P with quota still 40.

120 − 2P = 40 ⇒ **P = 40** (vs P = 30 under a ₹10 tariff, where imports would rise to 60) — quotas give more protection when demand grows.

statements.s: Under a VER, quota rents usually go to foreign exporters.
statements.why: Exporters restrict supply and raise their prices.

statements.s: A quota and an equivalent tariff always have identical effects.
statements.why: They differ with demand growth or monopoly.

statements.s: Quota rents replace tariff revenue in welfare analysis.
statements.why: Rectangle 'c' goes to licence holders.

statements.s: Sanitary and phytosanitary standards can act as NTBs.
statements.why: They can restrict imports.

quiz.q: Quota 20 with Qd = 100 − P, Qs = P. Domestic price:
With growing demand, a quota compared with a tariff gives:
quiz.why: Imports cannot rise, so the domestic price rises further.

lessons.title: Large country, optimal tariff and subsidies

story.title: When a big buyer taxes imports

scenes.text: A large importer's tariff cuts world demand and pushes down the world price.
Part of the tariff is paid by foreign exporters — a terms-of-trade gain.

steps.title: Large-country tariff
steps.body:
- Tariff lowers the world (foreign) price ⇒ **terms-of-trade gain** (area e) may exceed DWL (b + d).
- **Optimal tariff** t* = 1/ε*, ε* = elasticity of foreign export supply. Risk of **retaliation** (tariff wars).
- **Export subsidy** (small country): domestic price rises by the subsidy; consumers lose, producers gain, government pays; net DWL. For a large country, ToT worsen as well.

steps.title: Solved: optimal tariff
steps.body:
Foreign export supply elasticity ε* = 4.

t* = 1/4 = **25%**. If foreign supply is perfectly elastic (small country case), t* = 0.

statements.s: A large country's tariff can improve its terms of trade.
statements.why: It lowers the world price of imports.

statements.s: The optimal tariff for a small country is positive.
statements.why: It cannot affect world prices, so t* = 0.

statements.s: Export subsidies reduce national welfare for a small country.
statements.why: Costs exceed producer gains net of consumer losses.

statements.s: Retaliation can wipe out gains from an optimal tariff.
statements.why: Both countries may end up worse off.

quiz.q: Export subsidy of 5 with exports rising to 30. Subsidy cost:
Terms-of-trade gain from a tariff falls on:
quiz.why: Foreign exporters receive a lower price, so they bear part of the tariff.

lessons.title: Arguments for protection and the WTO

scenes.text: In 1947, 23 countries signed GATT.
In 1995 the WTO took over, covering services and intellectual property too.

steps.title: Arguments
steps.body:
- Valid (with caveats): **infant industry**, terms of trade (large country), national security, externalities/market failures (second-best), strategic trade (Brander–Spencer), revenue in poor tax systems.
- Weak: 'cheap foreign labour', protecting jobs at any cost, BoP correction (better via exchange rate).
- **Anti-dumping**: duty when exports are priced below normal value and cause injury; India's DGTR investigates.

steps.title: WTO
steps.body:
- Established **1 January 1995** (Uruguay Round).
- Principles: **MFN** (non-discrimination), **national treatment**, transparency, binding tariffs, special and differential treatment for developing countries.
- Agreements: GATT (goods), GATS (services), TRIPS (IP), Agreement on Agriculture, dispute settlement (Appellate Body non-functional since 2019 due to blocked appointments).

steps.title: Solved: dumping margin
steps.body:
Normal value in exporter's home market ₹500; export price to India ₹400.

Dumping margin = (500 − 400)/400 = **25%** of export price; anti-dumping duty cannot exceed this margin.

statements.s: The WTO was established on 1 January 1995.
statements.why: After the Uruguay Round.

statements.s: MFN means treating all WTO members equally.
statements.why: Non-discrimination among members.

statements.s: National treatment allows discriminating against imports after they clear customs.
statements.why: Imports must be treated like domestic goods.

statements.s: TRIPS deals with intellectual property.
statements.why: Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights.

Strategic trade policy is associated with:
quiz.why: Brander and Spencer's 1985 model showed export subsidies can shift oligopoly profits.
It is the General Agreement on Trade in Services.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Exchange rates and balance-of-payments adjustment
courses.summary: The foreign exchange market, spot and forward rates, covered interest parity, the elasticities approach and Marshall–Lerner condition, the J-curve, the absorption and monetary approaches, and fixed versus flexible regimes.
outcomes: Compute forward rates using covered interest parity
Apply the Marshall–Lerner condition
Explain the J-curve
Use the absorption approach to analyse devaluation
Compare exchange-rate regimes and the monetary approach

scenes.text: A Chennai importer must pay $1 million in three months.
She buys dollars forward today to lock in the rate.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Spot rate**: for immediate delivery; **forward rate**: agreed today for future delivery.
- Forward premium/discount on a currency.
- **Covered interest parity (CIP)**: F/S = (1 + i)/(1 + i*), where i is domestic and i* foreign interest, S and F in domestic currency per foreign unit.
- Approximation: forward premium on foreign currency ≈ i − i*.
- Participants: hedgers, speculators, arbitrageurs; central bank.

steps.title: Solved: forward rate
steps.body:
S = ₹80/$, annual i (India) = 7%, i* (US) = 4%, one-year forward.

F = 80 × 1.07/1.04 ≈ **₹82.31/$** ⇒ dollar at a forward premium of about 2.9% (≈ 7 − 4).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Inverting the interest ratio.
- Confusing covered parity (forward rate, arbitrage) with uncovered parity (expected spot, risk).

statements.s: Covered interest parity uses the forward rate.
statements.why: Forward cover removes exchange risk.

statements.s: If domestic interest exceeds foreign interest, the foreign currency trades at a forward premium.
statements.why: F > S when i > i*.

statements.s: Hedgers seek to profit from exchange-rate bets.
statements.why: That describes speculators.

statements.s: CIP violations create arbitrage opportunities.
statements.why: Riskless profit is possible.

quiz.why: The interest differential sets the forward premium.

quiz.q: Someone covering a future payment in forex is a:
quiz.why: Hedgers reduce exposure to exchange-rate risk.

story.title: A weaker rupee, a worse deficit — at first

scenes.text: The rupee depreciates, but the trade deficit widens for a few months.
Then exports pick up and imports fall — the J-curve.

steps.title: Marshall–Lerner
steps.body:
- Starting from balanced trade, a depreciation improves the trade balance if **|εx| + |εm| > 1** (sum of export and import demand elasticities).
- Short run elasticities are low (contracts, habits) ⇒ trade balance first **worsens** then improves — **J-curve**.
- Pass-through: exporters may absorb part of the change in margins.

steps.title: Solved: check M–L
steps.body:
|εx| = 0.6, |εm| = 0.7 ⇒ sum 1.3 > 1 ⇒ depreciation **improves** the balance.

Short run: |εx| = 0.2, |εm| = 0.3 ⇒ sum 0.5 < 1 ⇒ balance **worsens** initially (bottom of the J).

steps.title: Solved: approximate change
steps.body:
Balanced trade, exports = imports = ₹100 (domestic currency). 10% depreciation; |εx| = 0.8, |εm| = 0.5.

ΔTB ≈ 100 × 0.10 × (0.8 + 0.5 − 1) = **+₹3**.

bands.text: Below 1: depreciation worsens the trade balance (Marshall–Lerner fails).
Exactly 1: no change in the balance from a small depreciation.
Above 1: depreciation improves the trade balance; bigger elasticities, bigger improvement.

quiz.why: The sum 0.7 is below 1, so the Marshall–Lerner condition fails.

quiz.q: Exports = imports = 200, 5% depreciation, elasticities sum 1.6. ΔTB ≈

quiz.why: Volumes adjust slowly while prices change at once.

scenes.text: A country consumes and invests more than it produces — the gap is its trade deficit.
The monetary approach adds: BoP deficits mirror excess money supply.

steps.title: Absorption (Alexander, 1952)
steps.body:
- B = Y − A, A = C + I + G (absorption).
- Devaluation improves B only if it raises Y more than A, or lowers A (expenditure-switching vs expenditure-reducing).
- At full employment, devaluation needs accompanying **expenditure reduction**.
- ΔB = (1 − a)ΔY − ΔA_d, where a = marginal propensity to absorb, ΔA_d = direct absorption effect.

steps.title: Solved: absorption
steps.body:
Devaluation raises Y by 50; marginal propensity to absorb a = 0.9; direct absorption effect ΔA_d = +2.

ΔB = 0.1 × 50 − 2 = **+3**.

steps.title: Monetary approach
steps.body:
- BoP is a monetary phenomenon: excess money supply ⇒ deficit (reserves flow out) under fixed rates; ⇒ depreciation under flexible rates.
- Under fixed rates, money supply is endogenous; devaluation only temporarily improves BoP by raising money demand.

statements.s: In the absorption approach, B = Y − A.
statements.why: Trade balance equals output minus domestic absorption.

statements.s: At full employment, devaluation alone always improves the balance.
statements.why: Absorption must also fall.

statements.s: The monetary approach links BoP deficits to excess money supply.
statements.why: Reserves flow out to restore money-market equilibrium.

statements.s: Expenditure-switching policies change the composition of spending between home and foreign goods.
statements.why: Devaluation and tariffs are examples.

quiz.q: Tight fiscal policy to cut a deficit is:
quiz.why: It lowers total absorption.

quiz.q: The absorption approach was developed by:
quiz.why: Alexander's 1952 IMF paper.

scenes.text: In 1944 delegates at Bretton Woods set fixed but adjustable pegs to the dollar, itself tied to gold.
In 1971 the gold link ended; by 1973 major currencies floated.

steps.title: Regimes
steps.body:
- **Gold standard**: price–specie-flow mechanism (Hume) automatic adjustment.
- **Bretton Woods (1944–71/73)**: adjustable peg, IMF, dollar convertible to gold at $35/oz; ended by the 'Nixon shock' (1971).
- **Floating**: market-determined; insulation and monetary independence vs volatility.
- **Intermediate**: crawling peg, bands, managed float (India), currency boards, dollarisation.
- **Currency crises**: first-generation (fiscal deficits, Krugman), second-generation (self-fulfilling expectations), third-generation (banking/balance sheets — Asian crisis 1997).

steps.title: Solved: defending a peg
steps.body: Peg ₹80/$. Market pressure would move it to ₹84/$. RBI must sell dollars; if it sells $5 billion and buys ₹400 billion (at 80), domestic money supply falls by ₹400 billion unless sterilised (offset by buying government bonds).

steps.title: Pros and cons
steps.body: Fixed: certainty, discipline, but loss of monetary independence and speculative attacks. Flexible: automatic adjustment and independence, but volatility and possible overshooting (Dornbusch).

statements.s: Bretton Woods fixed the dollar at $35 per ounce of gold.
statements.why: The anchor of the system.

statements.s: The Nixon shock ended dollar–gold convertibility in 1971.
statements.why: August 1971.

statements.s: Sterilisation offsets the money-supply effect of forex intervention.
statements.why: Through opposite open-market operations.

statements.s: The 1997 Asian crisis is a classic first-generation crisis.
statements.why: It is usually seen as third-generation (banking/balance-sheet).

quiz.why: Hume (1752) described gold flows adjusting prices.
Rudiger Dornbusch, 1976.

quiz.q: India's exchange-rate regime is best described as:
quiz.why: RBI intervenes to curb volatility without a target.

questions.why: Sum of elasticities above one.

Exports = imports = 500, 4% depreciation, sum of elasticities 1.5. ΔTB ≈
The J-curve shows the trade balance after depreciation:
questions.why: Low short-run elasticities.

questions.why: Alexander's framework.

questions.q: Under the monetary approach with fixed rates, excess money supply causes:
questions.why: Residents spend excess money on foreign goods and assets.

questions.why: July 1944.

questions.why: OMOs offset the reserve change.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Economic integration, FDI and global institutions
courses.summary: Stages of economic integration, Viner's trade creation and diversion, optimum currency areas, FDI and multinationals, the IMF and World Bank, and India's trade agreements.
outcomes: List Balassa's stages of integration
Distinguish trade creation from trade diversion numerically
Explain optimum currency area criteria
Analyse determinants and effects of FDI
Describe the roles of the IMF and World Bank and India's main trade agreements

story.title: A cheaper partner, not the cheapest

scenes.text: Two neighbours form a customs union and drop tariffs on each other.
Imports shift to the partner — sometimes away from a cheaper outside supplier.

steps.title: Balassa's stages
steps.body:
1. **Preferential trade area** (reduced tariffs among members).
2. **Free trade area**: zero internal tariffs, own external tariffs (rules of origin needed).
3. **Customs union**: FTA + common external tariff.
4. **Common market**: + free factor mobility.
5. **Economic union**: + harmonised policies (e.g. single currency in the euro area).

steps.title: Viner (1950)
steps.body:
- **Trade creation**: higher-cost domestic production replaced by lower-cost partner imports ⇒ welfare gain.
- **Trade diversion**: imports shift from a low-cost outside supplier to a higher-cost partner ⇒ welfare loss (lost tariff revenue, higher real cost).
- A customs union is beneficial if creation outweighs diversion.

steps.title: Solved: creation vs diversion
steps.body:
Costs: partner 90, rest of world (ROW) 80. Home tariff 50% on all imports before the union ⇒ ROW price 120, partner 135.

- **Case A (home cost 110)**: before, home produces at 110; after union, buys from partner at 90 ⇒ **trade creation** (saves 20 per unit).
- **Case B (home cost 130)**: before, imports from ROW at 120 (real cost 80, tariff 40 to government); after, imports from partner at 90 ⇒ **trade diversion** — real resource cost rises from 80 to 90.

statements.s: A customs union has a common external tariff.
statements.why: That distinguishes it from an FTA.

statements.s: Trade diversion always raises welfare.
statements.why: It shifts imports to a higher-cost source.

statements.s: Free trade areas need rules of origin.
statements.why: To prevent trade deflection through the low-tariff member.

statements.s: A common market allows free movement of labour and capital.
statements.why: That is the step beyond a customs union.

quiz.q: Replacing costly domestic output with cheaper partner imports is:
quiz.why: Production shifts to a lower-cost source, which raises welfare.

quiz.q: Which stage adds free factor mobility to a customs union?
quiz.why: A common market allows labour and capital to move freely.

quiz.q: In Case B, the real cost per unit rises by:
quiz.why: The source changes from ROW at 80 to the partner at 90.

scenes.text: Twenty European countries share the euro.
When Greece fell into crisis, it could not devalue its own currency.

steps.title: Mundell's criteria (1961)
steps.body:
- **Labour mobility** across regions.
- **Wage and price flexibility**.
- **Fiscal transfers** (federal budget).
- **Openness** and trade integration (McKinnon); **diversification** (Kenen).
- **Symmetric shocks** and similar business cycles.

Benefits: lower transaction costs, no exchange risk, price transparency. Costs: loss of independent monetary policy and exchange-rate adjustment.

steps.title: Solved: transaction-cost saving
steps.body:
Trade between two members ₹10 lakh crore a year; conversion and hedging cost 0.4%.

Annual saving from a common currency ≈ 0.004 × 10 = **₹4,000 crore**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a single currency eliminates all shocks.
- Ignoring the absence of a large fiscal union in the euro area.

statements.s: High labour mobility makes a currency union more workable.
statements.why: Workers move to where jobs are.

statements.s: Members of a currency union keep independent monetary policy.
statements.why: They share one central bank.

statements.s: Asymmetric shocks are a cost for a currency union.
statements.why: One interest rate cannot suit all.

statements.s: Mundell pioneered OCA theory.
statements.why: His 1961 paper.

quiz.why: 0.0025 × 20 lakh crore = ₹5,000 crore.

quiz.why: Flexible wages substitute for exchange-rate adjustment.

quiz.why: Ronald McKinnon, 1963.

scenes.text: A foreign electronics firm sets up a plant in Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body:
- **FDI**: lasting interest with control (commonly ≥ 10% equity); vs **FPI** (portfolio, < 10%).
- **Dunning's OLI (eclectic) paradigm**: Ownership advantages, Location advantages, Internalisation advantages.
- Horizontal (market-seeking) vs vertical (efficiency-seeking) FDI.
- Effects on host: capital, technology, jobs, exports, spillovers; concerns: profit repatriation, crowding out, transfer pricing.

steps.title: Solved: classification
steps.body:
A foreign fund buys 6% of an Indian listed company: **FPI**. A foreign firm buys 26% with board seats: **FDI** (≥ 10%).

BoP: both are financial-account inflows; FDI is generally more stable.

steps.title: India
steps.body: Most sectors allow FDI under the automatic route; sectoral caps and government approval apply in sensitive areas. Major sources include Singapore, Mauritius and the US.

steps.title: Institutions
steps.body:
- **IMF** (1944): short-term BoP support, surveillance, conditionality; quotas determine voting and access; **SDRs** as reserve asset.
- **World Bank Group**: IBRD (loans), IDA (concessional credits), IFC (private sector), MIGA, ICSID.
- Critiques: conditionality (austerity), governance dominated by advanced economies.
- Others: Asian Development Bank, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (2016), New Development Bank (BRICS).

steps.title: India's agreements
steps.body:
- **SAFTA** (2006), India–ASEAN FTA in goods (2010), CEPAs with South Korea and Japan.
- **India–UAE CEPA** (2022), **India–Australia ECTA** (2022), India–EFTA TEPA (signed 2024).
- India withdrew from **RCEP** negotiations in 2019.

A country's quota is SDR 13 billion out of total quotas of SDR 476 billion.

Quota share ≈ 13/476 = **2.7%** — roughly its voting-power share (plus basic votes).

uni-ba-eco-macro-1.title: Macroeconomics I — income, money and short-run fluctuations
uni-ba-eco-macro-1.description: National income accounting, the Keynesian income-expenditure model, money and banking, IS–LM, and AD–AS with inflation and unemployment. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA (Hons) Economics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · National income accounting
courses.summary: Circular flow, GDP and its aggregates, the three methods of measurement, nominal versus real GDP and the deflator, and limits of GDP as a welfare measure, with India's base-year conventions.
outcomes: Explain the circular flow and leakages/injections
Move between GDP, GNP, NDP and NNP at market price and factor cost
Compute national income by value added, income and expenditure methods
Compute real GDP, the GDP deflator and growth rates
Discuss limitations of GDP as a welfare measure

scenes.text: Households supply labour to firms and get wages; they spend those wages on goods the firms make.
Add banks, government and the rest of the world and you get the full circular flow.

steps.title: Circular flow
steps.body:
- Two-sector: households ↔ firms; income = expenditure = output.
- **Leakages**: saving (S), taxes (T), imports (M). **Injections**: investment (I), government spending (G), exports (X).
- Equilibrium: S + T + M = I + G + X.

steps.title: Aggregates
steps.body:
- **GDP** = value of final goods and services produced within the domestic territory in a year.
- **GNP** = GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA).
- **NDP** = GDP − depreciation (consumption of fixed capital).
- **Factor cost (FC)** = market price (MP) − net indirect taxes (indirect taxes − subsidies).
- **National income** = NNP at factor cost.
- In India's current series (base 2011-12), GVA at basic prices is the main sectoral measure; GDP = GVA + product taxes − product subsidies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding imports instead of subtracting them.
- Forgetting that NFIA can be negative (as for India).
- Treating subsidies as adding to market price.

statements.s: GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad.
statements.why: It counts income of residents wherever earned.

statements.s: National income is NNP at market prices.
statements.why: It is NNP at factor cost.

statements.s: Imports are an injection into the circular flow.
statements.why: They are a leakage.

statements.s: Net indirect taxes = indirect taxes − subsidies.
statements.why: Subsidies lower market prices relative to factor cost.

quiz.why: Saving is income not spent on domestic output.
Net measures subtract consumption of fixed capital.

scenes.text: A farmer sells wheat for ₹100 to a miller, who sells flour for ₹150 to a baker.
The baker sells bread for ₹220. Counting all sales would triple-count the wheat.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
- **Value-added (product) method**: Σ(value of output − intermediate consumption).
- **Income method**: compensation of employees + operating surplus (rent, interest, profit) + mixed income of self-employed.
- **Expenditure method**: C + I + G + (X − M), final expenditure only.
- All three give the same total (with statistical discrepancy in practice).

steps.title: Solved: value added
steps.body:
Farmer 100 (no inputs), miller 150 (input 100), baker 220 (input 150).

1. VA: 100 + 50 + 70 = **220** = value of the final good ✓.
2. Summing all sales (470) would double count.

steps.title: Solved: income method
steps.body:
Compensation of employees 400, rent 50, interest 40, profit 110, mixed income 200, depreciation 30, net indirect taxes 70, NFIA −10.

1. NDP_FC = 400 + 50 + 40 + 110 + 200 = **800**.
2. NNP_FC (NI) = 800 − 10 = 790.
3. GDP_MP = 800 + 30 + 70 = **900**.

steps.title: What to exclude
steps.body: Exclude transfer payments (pensions, scholarships), sale of second-hand goods (only the dealer's commission counts), purchase of shares/bonds, and intermediate goods. Include imputed rent of owner-occupied houses and own-account production of goods.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting old-age pensions as factor income.
- Including the full price of a used car sold this year.

statements.s: Value of intermediate goods is included in GDP separately.
statements.why: Only value added or final goods are counted.

statements.s: Imputed rent of owner-occupied housing is included in GDP.
statements.why: It values housing services consumed.

statements.s: Government scholarships are transfer payments.
statements.why: No current production is exchanged.

statements.s: A broker's commission on selling a used flat is part of GDP.
statements.why: It is a current service.

quiz.q: Output 500, intermediate consumption 300. Gross value added:
quiz.why: GVA = output − intermediate consumption = 200.

quiz.q: Which is included in national income?
quiz.why: Interest by firms is a factor payment for capital used in production.

quiz.q: Mixed income refers to income of:
quiz.why: Self-employed income mixes labour and capital returns that cannot be separated.

lessons.title: Nominal vs real GDP and price indices

scenes.text: Nominal GDP rose 12% this year. Prices rose 5%.
Real growth is closer to 6.7% — the rest was just inflation.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Nominal GDP**: current-year prices. **Real GDP**: base-year (constant) prices.
- **GDP deflator** = (Nominal/Real) × 100 — covers all domestic output.
- **CPI**: fixed basket of consumer goods (Laspeyres); India's headline inflation target uses CPI (combined).
- **WPI**: wholesale prices; no services.
- Real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation (exact: (1 + g_n)/(1 + π) − 1).

steps.title: Solved: deflator
steps.body:
Nominal GDP 1,320; real GDP 1,200.

Deflator = 1,320/1,200 × 100 = **110** ⇒ prices 10% above base year.

steps.title: Solved: real growth
steps.body:
Nominal growth 12%, deflator inflation 5%.

Exact real growth = 1.12/1.05 − 1 = **6.67%** (approximation 7%).

steps.title: Solved: two-good economy
steps.body:
Base year: 10 apples @ ₹2, 5 pens @ ₹10. Current: 12 apples @ ₹3, 6 pens @ ₹12.

1. Nominal current = 36 + 72 = 108.
2. Real current (base prices) = 24 + 60 = 84.
3. Deflator = 108/84 × 100 ≈ **128.6**.

statements.s: Real GDP is measured at constant base-year prices.
statements.why: This removes the effect of price changes.

statements.s: WPI in India includes services.
statements.why: WPI covers goods only.

statements.s: The GDP deflator includes prices of imported goods.
statements.why: It covers domestically produced output.

statements.s: If the deflator is 125, prices are 25% above the base year.
statements.why: Base year = 100.

quiz.q: India's RBI inflation target is defined on:
quiz.why: The flexible inflation-targeting framework uses headline CPI (combined) inflation.
All the nominal rise is price increase.

scenes.text: A city's GDP soars as factories expand.
Air quality worsens, commutes lengthen and unpaid care work goes unnoticed in the numbers.

steps.title: Limitations
steps.body:
- Ignores **non-market work** (household and care work).
- Ignores **distribution** — average income can rise while many are left behind.
- Ignores **externalities** and depletion of natural capital.
- Ignores **leisure** and quality of goods.
- Informal sector is hard to measure.
- Defensive expenditures (pollution clean-up) add to GDP.

steps.title: Alternatives
steps.body:
- **Per capita GDP** at PPP for cross-country comparison.
- **Human Development Index** (UNDP): health (life expectancy), education (expected and mean years of schooling), income (GNI per capita PPP); geometric mean of dimension indices.
- Green GDP / genuine savings; multidimensional poverty index.

steps.title: Solved: per capita
steps.body:
GDP ₹300 lakh crore, population 140 crore.

Per capita = 300 × 10^12 / (140 × 10^7) ≈ **₹2.14 lakh** per year.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating GDP growth as equal to welfare growth.
- Comparing countries' GDP at market exchange rates when PPP is more apt for living standards.

statements.s: Unpaid household work is included in GDP.
statements.why: GDP covers market (and some own-account) production, not unpaid services.

statements.s: HDI combines health, education and income.
statements.why: These are its three dimensions.

statements.s: Spending on cleaning up pollution raises GDP.
statements.why: It is market expenditure, even though welfare may not rise.

statements.s: Per capita GDP shows how income is distributed.
statements.why: It is an average and hides inequality.

quiz.q: HDI uses which mean of its dimension indices?
quiz.why: Since 2010 UNDP aggregates the three indices by geometric mean.

quiz.q: For comparing living standards across countries, GDP is best expressed in:
quiz.why: PPP adjusts for differences in price levels.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a limitation of GDP?
quiz.why: Measuring final market output is what GDP is designed to do.

questions.why: Pensions are transfer payments.
