Nominal growth 9%, inflation 4%. Exact real growth:

questions.why: The series launched in 2015 uses 2011-12 as base.

options: S + T + M = I + G + X
questions.why: That is the equilibrium condition of the four-sector flow.

questions.q: GDP at factor cost plus net indirect taxes equals:
questions.why: Market price = factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Classical and Keynesian income determination
courses.summary: The classical full-employment model (Say's law, flexible wages, loanable funds), Keynes' critique, the consumption function, the Keynesian cross, investment, government and foreign-trade multipliers, and the paradox of thrift.
outcomes: Outline the classical model and Say's law
Explain the consumption function, APC and MPC
Solve for equilibrium income in two-, three- and four-sector Keynesian models
Compute investment, tax, balanced-budget and open-economy multipliers
Explain inflationary and deflationary gaps and the paradox of thrift

lessons.title: The classical model and Keynes' critique

scenes.text: In the 1930s a quarter of American workers were jobless for years.
Classical theory said wages should fall and clear the market. Keynes asked: what if demand itself is too low?

steps.title: Classical building blocks
steps.body:
- **Say's law**: supply creates its own demand — income from production is spent.
- **Flexible wages and prices**: labour market clears at full employment; output fixed by the production function.
- **Saving = investment** via a flexible interest rate (loanable funds).
- **Quantity theory**: MV = PY ⇒ money affects only prices (**money neutrality**, classical dichotomy).
- Unemployment is voluntary or frictional.

steps.title: Keynes' critique
steps.body:
- Saving and investment depend on different things (S on income, I on expectations/animal spirits).
- Money wages are sticky downward; even if they fell, lower incomes reduce demand.
- Equilibrium can occur **below full employment** — involuntary unemployment.
- Output is determined by **aggregate demand** in the short run.

steps.title: Solved: quantity theory
steps.body:
M = ₹50 lakh crore, V = 2, Y (real) = ₹100 lakh crore.

1. P = MV/Y = 100/100 = **1**.
2. If M rises 10% with V and Y fixed ⇒ P rises **10%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying classical economists denied all unemployment — they allowed frictional and voluntary unemployment.
- Treating V as always constant in modern data.

statements.s: Say's law states that supply creates its own demand.
statements.why: Production generates income sufficient to buy the output.

statements.s: In the classical model, money supply changes real output.
statements.why: Money is neutral; only prices change.

statements.s: Keynes argued that equilibrium could exist with involuntary unemployment.
statements.why: Deficient aggregate demand can keep output below full employment.

statements.s: In the classical model, the interest rate equates saving and investment.
statements.why: This is the loanable-funds mechanism.

quiz.q: MV = PY with M = 200, V = 4, Y = 400. P =

quiz.why: Real variables are determined independently of money, which only sets nominal values.

quiz.q: Keynes stressed that investment depends heavily on:
quiz.why: Investment is driven by uncertain expected returns.

lessons.title: Consumption function and the Keynesian cross

story.title: A bonus and a shopping spree

scenes.text: A worker gets a ₹10,000 bonus and spends ₹8,000 of it.
The shopkeeper who receives ₹8,000 spends ₹6,400 — and the ripples continue.

steps.title: Consumption
steps.body:
- C = a + bY, a = autonomous consumption, b = **MPC** (0 < b < 1).
- APC = C/Y falls as Y rises (a > 0). MPS = 1 − MPC.
- Saving S = −a + (1 − b)Y.
- Keynes' psychological law: as income rises, consumption rises but by less.

steps.title: Equilibrium
steps.body:
Two-sector: Y = C + I (aggregate demand = output) or S = I.

Y* = (a + I)/(1 − b). **Investment multiplier** k = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS.

steps.title: Gaps and the paradox of thrift
steps.body:
- **Deflationary gap**: AD falls short of AD needed at full-employment output. **Inflationary gap**: AD exceeds it.
- Gap needed = (Yf − Y*)/k.
- **Paradox of thrift**: if all households try to save more (a falls), income falls; with induced investment total saving may not rise.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing k = 1/MPC.
- Measuring the deflationary gap as the output gap instead of the demand shortfall.

bands.text: Low MPC: multiplier only 2–2.5; demand shocks have muted effects.
Moderate MPC: multiplier 2.9–5 in a closed economy without taxes.
High MPC: multiplier up to 20 in theory — real-world taxes and imports cut it sharply.

quiz.why: k = 1/MPS = 4.

quiz.q: Full employment Y = 2,000, actual 1,500, k = 5. Deflationary gap:
quiz.why: Extra demand needed = 500/5 = 100.

scenes.text: The government spends ₹1 lakh crore on roads during a slowdown.
Contractors, workers and suppliers spend their new incomes — national income rises by more.

steps.title: Three-sector model
steps.body:
Y = C + I + G, C = a + b(Y − T).

- Lump-sum tax: Y* = (a − bT + I + G)/(1 − b).
- **Government spending multiplier** = 1/(1 − b).
- **Tax multiplier** = −b/(1 − b).
- **Balanced-budget multiplier** (ΔG = ΔT) = 1.
- **Transfer multiplier** = b/(1 − b).
- Proportional tax T = tY: multiplier = 1/[1 − b(1 − t)] — automatic stabiliser.

steps.title: Solved: lump-sum taxes
steps.body:
C = 100 + 0.8(Y − T), I = 200, G = 100, T = 100.

1. Y = 100 + 0.8Y − 80 + 200 + 100 ⇒ 0.2Y = 320 ⇒ **Y = 1,600**.
2. Compared with Y = 1,500 without G and T: ΔY = 100 = ΔG ⇒ balanced-budget multiplier 1 ✓.
3. Tax multiplier = −0.8/0.2 = −4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the spending multiplier for tax cuts (the tax multiplier is smaller in size).
- Forgetting that proportional taxes reduce the multiplier.

statements.s: The balanced-budget multiplier in the simple model equals 1.
A tax cut raises income by more than an equal rise in government spending.
statements.why: Part of the tax cut is saved, so its multiplier is smaller.

statements.s: Proportional income taxes act as automatic stabilisers.
statements.why: Tax receipts rise in booms and fall in slumps, damping fluctuations.

statements.s: With MPC 0.9, the tax multiplier is −9.

scenes.text: When Indian households get extra income, part is spent on imported phones and oil.
That spending boosts foreign, not domestic, income — the multiplier shrinks.

steps.title: Four-sector model
steps.body:
Y = C + I + G + X − M, M = M0 + mY (m = marginal propensity to import).

- Multiplier = 1/(1 − b + m) (lump-sum taxes) or 1/[1 − b(1 − t) + m].
- Exports are autonomous injections; a rise in X raises Y and worsens/improves trade balance by less than ΔX.

steps.title: Solved: export boom
steps.body:
X rises by 30.

1. ΔY = 3.33 × 30 = 100.
2. ΔM = 0.1 × 100 = 10.
3. ΔNX = 30 − 10 = **+20** — trade balance improves by less than the export rise.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding m in the numerator instead of the denominator.
- Ignoring induced imports when computing the trade-balance change.

statements.s: A higher marginal propensity to import lowers the multiplier.
statements.why: Imports are an extra leakage.

statements.s: A rise in exports improves the trade balance by the full amount of the rise.
statements.why: Higher income raises imports, offsetting part of it.

statements.s: Open-economy multiplier = 1/(1 − MPC + MPM) with no taxes.
statements.why: Leakages are saving and imports.

statements.s: Exports are a leakage from the circular flow.
statements.why: They are an injection.

quiz.q: Multiplier 2.5, exports rise by 40, m = 0.2. Change in net exports:
Which reduces the size of the multiplier?
quiz.why: More of each rupee of income leaks abroad.

questions.q: Money neutrality means money affects:
questions.why: In the classical model money changes nominal but not real variables.

questions.q: APC at Y = 800 in that model:
MPC 0.9. Investment multiplier:
Balanced-budget multiplier in the simple Keynesian model:
questions.why: Spending and tax multipliers sum to one.

questions.q: Transfer-payment multiplier with MPC 0.8:
MPC 0.8, tax rate 0.25, MPM 0.1. Multiplier:
Inflationary gap arises when:
options: AD at full employment exceeds full-employment output
savings exceed investment at full employment
questions.why: Excess demand at full capacity pushes up prices.

questions.q: Paradox of thrift implies an attempt to save more can:
options: lower income without raising total saving
questions.why: Lower consumption reduces income, which reduces saving again.

questions.q: Proportional taxes make the economy:
questions.why: They lower the multiplier and act as automatic stabilisers.

questions.q: Deflationary gap with Yf = 1,200, Y* = 1,000, MPC 0.75:
questions.why: k = 4, so needed extra demand = 200/4 = 50.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Money, banking and monetary policy
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Introductory Macroeconomics; Money and Banking)
courses.summary: Functions and measures of money, credit creation by banks, the money multiplier, demand for money (Fisher, Cambridge, Keynes), and the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy instruments and framework.
outcomes: List functions of money and RBI's monetary aggregates
Compute credit creation and the money multiplier
Compare Fisher, Cambridge and Keynesian demand for money
Explain RBI's policy instruments and the inflation-targeting framework
Trace the transmission of a repo rate change

scenes.text: A weaver wanting rice must find a rice farmer who wants cloth — the double coincidence of wants.
Today a UPI payment settles in seconds; money removes the barter problem.

steps.title: Functions
steps.body:
- Primary: **medium of exchange**, **unit of account**.
- Secondary: **store of value**, **standard of deferred payment**.
- Fiat money: legal tender by government decree; bank deposits are money because they are accepted for payment.

steps.title: RBI measures
steps.body:
- **Reserve money (M0)** = currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI. Also called high-powered money (H).
- **M1 (narrow money)** = currency with the public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with RBI.
- **M3 (broad money)** = M1 + time deposits with banks.
- M3 is the most commonly used broad measure in India.

steps.title: Solved: aggregates
steps.body:
Currency with public 30, demand deposits 20, other deposits with RBI 1, time deposits 150 (₹ lakh crore).

M1 = 30 + 20 + 1 = **51**; M3 = 51 + 150 = **201**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including time deposits in M1.
- Confusing reserve money (a liability of the RBI) with broad money.

statements.s: M3 includes time deposits with banks.
statements.why: M3 = M1 + time deposits.

statements.s: Store of value is a primary function of money.
statements.why: It is usually classed as a secondary function.

statements.s: Reserve money is also called high-powered money.
statements.why: Bank deposits are built on it via the multiplier.

statements.s: Barter requires a double coincidence of wants.
statements.why: Each party must want what the other has.

quiz.why: M1 is currency with the public plus demand deposits plus other deposits with RBI.

quiz.q: Money as a 'unit of account' means:
options: it is used to settle debts later
quiz.why: Money provides the common yardstick in which values are measured.
Reserve money is the monetary base on which deposits are created.

lessons.title: Credit creation and the money multiplier

scenes.text: A farmer deposits ₹1,000. The bank keeps ₹200 as reserves and lends ₹800.
The ₹800 is spent and redeposited elsewhere; the process repeats.

steps.title: Process
steps.body:
- With reserve ratio r and no cash drain: total deposits = initial deposit × **1/r**.
- With currency ratio c = C/D and reserve ratio r = R/D: M = C + D, H = C + R.
- **Money multiplier** m = M/H = **(1 + c)/(c + r)**.
- Limits: cash leakage, excess reserves, lack of creditworthy borrowers, CRR/SLR.

steps.title: Solved: simple multiplier
steps.body:
Initial deposit ₹1,000, r = 0.2.

1. Total deposits = 1,000/0.2 = **₹5,000**.
2. Credit created = 5,000 − 1,000 = **₹4,000**.
3. Rounds: 1,000 + 800 + 640 + … (geometric series ratio 0.8).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 1/r when the public holds cash.
- Counting the initial deposit as created credit.

bands.text: Low reserves: m = 1.2/(0.2 + r) is about 4.3–5; credit expands strongly.
Moderate reserves: m roughly 3.3–4.
High reserves: m falls towards 2.4; a CRR hike is a contractionary tool.

quiz.q: r = 0.25, no cash drain, deposit ₹2,000. Total deposits:
A higher currency–deposit ratio makes the money multiplier:
quiz.why: More cash held outside banks reduces deposits available for lending.

story.title: Why hold cash that earns nothing?

scenes.text: People keep some money for daily purchases and emergencies.
When bond prices look set to fall, investors hold even more money.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
- **Fisher**: MV = PT — transactions approach; V institutionally fixed.
- **Cambridge (cash balance)**: Md = kPY, k = fraction of income held as money (k = 1/V).
- **Keynes (liquidity preference)**: transactions + precautionary motives depend on Y; **speculative** motive depends inversely on interest rate r: L = L1(Y) + L2(r).
- **Liquidity trap**: at very low r, everyone expects r to rise (bond prices to fall) ⇒ money demand perfectly elastic; monetary policy ineffective.

steps.title: Bond prices and interest
steps.body: A consol paying ₹50 a year: price = 50/r. At r = 5% price = 1,000; at r = 10% price = 500. Bond prices and interest rates move inversely — the basis of the speculative motive.

statements.s: In the Cambridge equation, k is the inverse of velocity.
statements.why: Md = kPY and MV = PY give k = 1/V.

statements.s: Speculative demand for money rises when interest rates rise.
statements.why: It falls: higher r makes bonds more attractive.

statements.s: In a liquidity trap, increases in money supply do not lower interest rates.
statements.why: Money demand is perfectly elastic at the floor rate.

statements.s: Bond prices rise when interest rates fall.
statements.why: Price = coupon/r for a perpetuity.

quiz.q: Precautionary demand for money mainly depends on:
quiz.why: Keynes linked transactions and precautionary balances to income.

scenes.text: Six members of RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meet every two months.
Their repo rate decision ripples through bank loans, EMIs and inflation.

steps.title: Framework
steps.body:
- Flexible inflation targeting (amended RBI Act, 1934; framework since 2016): CPI inflation target **4% ± 2%**.
- **Monetary Policy Committee**: six members (three RBI, three external); governor has a casting vote.
- **Policy (repo) rate**: rate at which RBI lends to banks against government securities.
- **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)** (introduced 2022) is the floor of the liquidity corridor; **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)** is the ceiling.

steps.title: Instruments
steps.body:
- **Quantitative**: repo/reverse repo, SDF, MSF, **CRR** (cash reserve ratio with RBI), **SLR** (liquid assets banks hold), **open market operations** (buy/sell government securities), bank rate.
- **Qualitative**: margin requirements, moral suasion, selective credit controls.

steps.title: Solved: transmission
steps.body:
Repo rate is raised by 0.50 percentage point.

1. Banks' cost of funds rises; external-benchmark-linked loans reset higher.
2. A ₹30 lakh, 20-year home loan at 8.5% vs 9.0%: EMI rises from about ₹26,035 to about ₹26,992 (≈ ₹957 more per month).
3. Borrowing and spending slow ⇒ aggregate demand eases ⇒ inflation pressure falls (with lags).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the repo rate the rate at which banks lend to the public.
- Thinking an OMO purchase reduces liquidity — buying securities injects money.

statements.s: RBI's inflation target is 4% CPI inflation with a ±2% band.
statements.why: This is the flexible inflation-targeting mandate.

statements.s: An open market sale of government securities injects liquidity.
statements.why: Selling securities absorbs money from banks.

statements.s: Raising CRR reduces banks' lendable resources.
statements.why: More deposits must be kept with RBI.

statements.s: Moral suasion is a quantitative instrument.
statements.why: It is a qualitative, persuasion-based tool.

quiz.q: To curb inflation RBI would most likely:
quiz.why: A higher policy rate raises borrowing costs and dampens demand.

quiz.q: The MPC has how many members?
quiz.why: It has three RBI members and three external members.

options: specified liquid assets such as government securities
quiz.why: SLR is a share of net demand and time liabilities kept in liquid assets.

questions.q: Currency with public 40, demand deposits 30, other deposits with RBI 2, time deposits 180. M3:
r = 0.1, no cash drain. Deposit multiplier:
c = 0.25, r = 0.15, H = 80. Money supply:
Velocity 4, money stock 500, real output 1,000. Price level:
The liquidity trap makes monetary policy:
questions.why: Extra money is simply held, so interest rates do not fall.

questions.q: Perpetual bond coupon ₹60, interest rate 8%. Price:
Speculative motive relates money demand to:
questions.why: It depends inversely on the interest rate.

questions.q: Which absorbs liquidity?
questions.why: Selling securities drains bank reserves.

questions.q: The floor of RBI's liquidity corridor since 2022 is:
questions.why: The Standing Deposit Facility replaced fixed-rate reverse repo as the floor.

questions.q: An increase in excess reserves held by banks makes the multiplier:
questions.why: It raises the effective reserve ratio.

questions.q: Which is a qualitative tool of RBI?
questions.why: Margin requirements target credit for specific purposes.

courses.title: Unit 4 · The IS–LM model
courses.summary: Derivation of the IS and LM curves, their slopes and shifts, general equilibrium in goods and money markets, fiscal and monetary policy effectiveness, crowding out, and the special cases of the liquidity trap and the classical range.
outcomes: Derive IS and LM algebraically and explain their slopes
Solve for simultaneous equilibrium income and interest rate
Measure the effect of fiscal and monetary policy including crowding out
Explain the liquidity trap and classical cases
Discuss the policy mix

scenes.text: When loan rates fall, more factory projects pass the profitability test.
More investment raises income through the multiplier — that link is the IS curve.

steps.title: Goods-market equilibrium
steps.body:
- IS: combinations of (Y, r) where planned spending = output (I + G = S + T in a closed economy).
- Investment falls as r rises: I = I0 − d·r.
- **Downward sloping**: lower r ⇒ more I ⇒ higher Y.
- **Slope** flatter when investment is more interest-sensitive (d large) or multiplier larger.
- **Shifts**: rightward with higher G, lower T, higher autonomous C or I0.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Horizontal shift of IS = multiplier × change in autonomous spending. Vertical shift = that change ÷ d.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling IS upward sloping.
- Thinking a change in r shifts IS — it moves along IS.

statements.s: The IS curve slopes downward.
statements.why: Lower interest rates raise investment and income.

statements.s: A tax cut shifts IS to the left.
statements.why: It raises consumption and shifts IS right.

statements.s: More interest-sensitive investment makes IS flatter.
statements.why: A small r change causes a big change in Y.

statements.s: A change in the interest rate shifts the IS curve.
statements.why: It is a movement along IS.

quiz.q: In the example IS, at r = 5, Y =

quiz.why: More autonomous investment raises spending at every r.
A larger multiplier magnifies the income response to r.

scenes.text: As incomes rise, people need more money for transactions.
With money supply fixed, interest rates must rise to persuade others to hold less — the LM curve.

steps.title: Money-market equilibrium
steps.body:
- LM: (Y, r) where real money demand = real money supply: M/P = kY − hr.
- **Upward sloping**: higher Y raises money demand ⇒ r must rise.
- Flatter when money demand is interest-sensitive (h large); horizontal in a **liquidity trap**; vertical in the **classical case** (h = 0).
- Shifts right with higher M or lower P.

steps.title: Solved: price level effect
steps.body: M = 1,600, P = 2 ⇒ M/P = 800. If P rises to 2.5 ⇒ M/P = 640 ⇒ LM: Y = 1,280 + 100r — shifts left.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using nominal instead of real money balances.
- Forgetting that a price rise shifts LM left.

statements.s: The LM curve slopes upward.
statements.why: Higher income raises money demand and thus the interest rate.

statements.s: An increase in money supply shifts LM to the right.
statements.why: At each r, higher Y is consistent with money-market equilibrium.

statements.s: In the classical case, LM is horizontal.
statements.why: It is vertical when money demand does not depend on r.

statements.s: A rise in the price level shifts LM to the right.
statements.why: Real balances fall, shifting LM left.

quiz.why: Infinite interest-elasticity of money demand at the floor rate gives a flat LM.
Real money supply M/P falls.

scenes.text: The finance ministry raises spending; interest rates edge up and some private investment is postponed.
If the RBI accommodates with more liquidity, income rises more.

steps.title: Joint equilibrium
steps.body:
Solve IS and LM together for (Y*, r*).

- **Fiscal expansion**: IS right ⇒ Y↑, r↑; higher r reduces I (**crowding out**).
- **Monetary expansion**: LM right ⇒ Y↑, r↓.
- **Policy mix**: fiscal expansion + monetary accommodation can raise Y without raising r.

steps.title: Solved: fiscal policy and crowding out
steps.body:
G rises by 40 ⇒ IS: Y = 2,300 − 100r.

1. 2,300 − 100r = 1,600 + 100r ⇒ r = 3.5, **Y = 1,950**.
2. ΔY = 100 vs simple-multiplier ΔY = 200.
3. Investment falls from 250 to 230 (−20); times multiplier 5 = 100 of output **crowded out**.

statements.s: Fiscal expansion in IS–LM raises both income and the interest rate.
statements.why: IS shifts right along an upward-sloping LM.

statements.s: Monetary expansion raises the interest rate.
statements.why: LM shifts right, lowering r.

statements.s: Crowding out is larger when investment is very interest-sensitive.
statements.why: A given rise in r cuts more investment.

statements.s: A fiscal expansion with matching monetary accommodation can keep r unchanged.
statements.why: Shifting LM right offsets the rise in r.

quiz.why: 600 = 150r gives r = 4.

options: higher G reducing private investment via higher r
quiz.why: Higher interest rates caused by fiscal expansion discourage private investment.

scenes.text: After 2008, several central banks cut rates near zero, yet lending stayed weak.
Governments turned to fiscal stimulus — the liquidity-trap lesson of IS–LM.

steps.title: Effectiveness rules
steps.body:
- **Fiscal policy most effective**: steep IS? No — fiscal is most effective with a **flat LM** (liquidity trap) and/or **steep IS**; no crowding out in the trap.
- **Monetary policy most effective**: **steep (vertical) LM** and **flat IS**.
- **Classical case** (vertical LM): fiscal policy fully crowds out; only money changes Y.
- **Keynesian extreme** (vertical IS, interest-inelastic investment): monetary policy cannot change Y.

steps.title: Solved: horizontal LM
steps.body:
Liquidity trap at r = 1. IS: Y = 2,100 − 100r ⇒ Y = 2,000.

G +40 ⇒ Y = 2,200: full multiplier effect (ΔY = 200), **no crowding out**. Raising M leaves Y unchanged.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing the slope conditions for policy effectiveness.
- Forgetting that IS–LM holds P fixed (short run).

statements.s: In a liquidity trap, fiscal policy has its full multiplier effect.
statements.why: Interest rates do not rise, so there is no crowding out.

statements.s: With a vertical LM curve, fiscal expansion raises output.
statements.why: It only raises r; private spending is fully crowded out.

statements.s: Monetary policy is ineffective when investment is completely interest-inelastic.
statements.why: IS is vertical, so lower r does not raise Y.

statements.s: IS–LM assumes a flexible price level.
statements.why: It is a fixed-price, short-run model.

quiz.why: A steep LM means money mainly changes income rather than being absorbed by interest-sensitive money demand.
With vertical LM, output is pinned by money supply.

quiz.why: Investment responds little to r, so crowding out is small.

questions.why: Higher interest rates reduce investment and income.

courses.title: Unit 5 · AD–AS, inflation and unemployment
courses.summary: Aggregate demand from IS–LM, short- and long-run aggregate supply, demand and supply shocks, types, causes and costs of inflation, types of unemployment and Okun's law, and the Phillips curve with expectations.
outcomes: Derive AD and explain its slope
Distinguish classical, Keynesian and short-run AS
Analyse demand-pull and cost-push inflation and stagflation
Classify unemployment and apply Okun's law
Use the expectations-augmented Phillips curve and the sacrifice ratio

scenes.text: Crude oil prices double. Transport and fertiliser costs rise across the economy.
Output falls while prices rise — a supply shock, not a demand shock.

steps.title: AD
steps.body:
- AD: combinations of P and Y where goods and money markets clear (IS–LM at each P).
- Slopes down: higher P ⇒ lower M/P ⇒ LM left ⇒ higher r ⇒ lower I and Y (**Keynes effect**); also wealth (Pigou) effect and, in open economies, net exports.
- Shifts right with higher G, lower T, higher M, higher confidence.

steps.title: AS
steps.body:
- **Classical/long-run AS**: vertical at potential output Yf (flexible wages).
- **Keynesian AS**: horizontal at fixed P below full employment.
- **Short-run AS**: upward sloping because of sticky wages or misperceptions.
- Equilibrium where AD meets AS; in the long run Y returns to Yf.

steps.title: Shocks
steps.body:
- Demand shock: P and Y move in the **same** direction.
- Adverse supply shock: P up, Y down — **stagflation**.
- Policy dilemma: stimulating demand worsens inflation; tightening worsens output.

statements.s: An adverse supply shock raises prices and lowers output.
statements.why: SRAS shifts left along AD.

statements.s: Long-run aggregate supply is vertical at potential output.
statements.why: Output depends on resources and technology, not P.

statements.s: AD slopes down only because of substitution between goods.
statements.why: It reflects interest-rate (Keynes), wealth and trade effects of the price level.

statements.s: A rise in money supply shifts AD to the left.
statements.why: It shifts AD right.

quiz.why: 600 = 300P gives P = 2.
Higher costs push prices up while output falls.

quiz.q: The Keynes effect links a lower price level to:
options: lower interest rates and higher investment
quiz.why: Higher real balances reduce r and stimulate investment.

scenes.text: Vegetable prices spike after unseasonal rain; fuel prices rise with global crude.
CPI inflation jumps, and RBI must judge whether it is temporary or broad-based.

steps.title: Types and causes
steps.body:
- By rate: creeping, walking, galloping, **hyperinflation** (often defined as > 50% per month, Cagan).
- **Demand-pull**: excess demand (monetary/fiscal expansion).
- **Cost-push**: rising wages, raw-material/oil prices, profit mark-ups.
- **Structural** (relevant to India): supply bottlenecks in food, infrastructure.
- Headline vs **core** inflation (excluding food and fuel).

steps.title: Costs
steps.body:
- **Anticipated**: shoe-leather costs, menu costs, tax distortions.
- **Unanticipated**: redistribution from creditors to debtors and from fixed-income earners; uncertainty reduces investment.
- Inflation acts as a regressive 'tax' on cash holders.

steps.title: Solved: inflation rate
steps.body:
CPI: 180 last year, 189 this year.

Inflation = (189 − 180)/180 × 100 = **5%**. Real value of a ₹10,000 pension falls to 10,000/1.05 ≈ ₹9,524.

steps.title: Solved: debtor gain
steps.body:
Loan ₹1 lakh at 8% nominal; actual inflation 10% (expected 4%).

Real rate paid = 1.08/1.10 − 1 ≈ **−1.8%**: the borrower gains, the lender loses from unanticipated inflation.

statements.s: Unanticipated inflation redistributes wealth from lenders to borrowers.
statements.why: Debts are repaid in money of lower real value.

statements.s: Core inflation includes food and fuel prices.
statements.why: Core excludes these volatile items.

statements.s: Menu costs arise even with fully anticipated inflation.
statements.why: Prices must still be changed physically.

statements.s: A rise in oil prices is a source of cost-push inflation.
statements.why: It raises production costs across sectors.

quiz.why: Spending exceeds what the economy can produce at current prices.

quiz.q: Who loses most from unanticipated inflation?
quiz.why: Their nominal income does not rise with prices.

scenes.text: Some graduates are between jobs; some lack the skills firms want; others lose jobs in a slowdown.
Each type needs a different policy.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Frictional**: search between jobs.
- **Structural**: mismatch of skills or location.
- **Cyclical**: from deficient demand in recessions.
- **Natural rate** = frictional + structural (no cyclical).
- Indian context: **disguised unemployment** in agriculture (MP of extra workers ≈ 0), seasonal unemployment; PLFS reports unemployment by usual status and current weekly status.

steps.title: Okun's law
steps.body: Output gap is negatively related to cyclical unemployment: roughly (Y − Y*)/Y* = −β(u − un), with β about 2 in Okun's original US estimates.

steps.title: Solved: Okun
steps.body:
β = 2, un = 5%, actual u = 7%.

Output gap = −2 × (7 − 5) = **−4%** of potential output. With potential ₹200 lakh crore, lost output ≈ ₹8 lakh crore.

steps.title: Solved: unemployment rate
steps.body:
Labour force 50 crore, employed 46 crore.

Unemployment rate = 4/50 × 100 = **8%**.

statements.s: The natural rate of unemployment includes cyclical unemployment.
statements.why: It includes only frictional and structural unemployment.

statements.s: Disguised unemployment means extra workers add almost nothing to output.
statements.why: Their marginal product is close to zero.

statements.s: Okun's law links unemployment above the natural rate to an output gap.
statements.why: Higher cyclical unemployment means output below potential.

statements.s: Retraining programmes mainly address frictional unemployment.
statements.why: They target structural mismatch.

quiz.q: Workers laid off in a recession are:
quiz.why: Their job loss comes from weak aggregate demand.

scenes.text: In the 1960s, data suggested lower unemployment could be bought with a little more inflation.
In the 1970s, inflation and unemployment rose together. Expectations had changed the game.

steps.title: Original and augmented curves
steps.body:
- **Phillips (1958)**: inverse relation between wage inflation and unemployment (UK data).
- **Friedman–Phelps**: π = πe − β(u − un). Short-run trade-off exists only while expectations lag.
- **Long run**: π = πe ⇒ u = un — vertical long-run Phillips curve (**natural rate hypothesis**).
- Under rational expectations, anticipated policy has no real effect even in the short run.

steps.title: Solved: short-run trade-off
steps.body:
π = πe − 0.5(u − 6), πe = 4%.

1. u = 4% ⇒ π = 4 + 1 = **5%**.
2. Next year with adaptive expectations πe = 5 ⇒ holding u = 4 needs π = **6%** — accelerating inflation.

steps.title: Solved: sacrifice ratio
steps.body:
Disinflation from 8% to 4% costs a cumulative 6 percentage points of output.

Sacrifice ratio = 6/4 = **1.5** (output points per point of inflation reduction).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the original Phillips curve as stable in the long run.
- Forgetting that credible policy can lower the sacrifice ratio.

activity.label: Unemployment rate u (%) with πe = 4, un = 6, β = 0.5

bands.text: u below 6%: inflation exceeds expectations (π = 4 + 0.5 × (6 − u)); expectations will drift up.
u = natural rate: π = πe = 4% — stable inflation.
u above 6%: inflation falls below expectations — the cost of disinflation.

quiz.why: Once expectations adjust, unemployment returns to its natural rate whatever the inflation rate.

quiz.why: They argued the trade-off holds only while inflation expectations lag.

questions.why: Cagan's threshold is 50% per month.

uni-ba-eco-macro-2.title: Macroeconomics II — consumption, investment, growth, open economy, policy
uni-ba-eco-macro-2.description: Theories of consumption and investment, Harrod–Domar and Solow growth, open-economy macroeconomics with Mundell–Fleming, and modern macro policy debates. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA (Hons) Economics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Consumption and investment
courses.summary: Kuznets' puzzle and the absolute, relative, life-cycle and permanent income hypotheses; investment appraisal with NPV and MEC, the accelerator, Tobin's q and the user cost of capital.
outcomes: Explain Kuznets' consumption puzzle
Apply the life-cycle and permanent income hypotheses numerically
Compute NPV and the marginal efficiency of capital
Use the accelerator model
Interpret Tobin's q and the user cost of capital

scenes.text: Household surveys showed richer families save a larger share of income.
Yet Kuznets found that over decades the national saving rate barely changed. Two facts, one puzzle.

steps.title: Keynes and Kuznets
steps.body:
- **Absolute income hypothesis (Keynes)**: C = a + bY, APC falls as Y rises.
- **Short-run / cross-section**: APC > MPC, falling APC.
- **Long-run time series (Kuznets)**: APC roughly constant ⇒ C = bY.
- The puzzle motivated new theories.

steps.title: Duesenberry's relative income
steps.body:
- **Demonstration effect**: consumption depends on income relative to others.
- **Ratchet effect**: consumption depends on past peak income; when income falls, households cut consumption only slowly.
- C/Y = a − b(Y/Y_peak).

steps.title: Solved: APC vs MPC
steps.body:
C = 200 + 0.75Y.

- Y = 800: C = 800, APC = 1.00.
- Y = 2,000: C = 1,700, APC = 0.85.
MPC stays 0.75 < APC; APC falls as Y rises — consistent with cross-section data but not with Kuznets' long-run series.

statements.s: Kuznets found a roughly constant long-run APC.
statements.why: Long-run time series showed stable saving rates.

statements.s: The ratchet effect implies consumption falls quickly when income falls.
statements.why: It falls slowly because habits are tied to past peak income.

statements.s: With C = a + bY and a > 0, APC exceeds MPC.
statements.why: APC = a/Y + b > b.

statements.s: The demonstration effect links consumption to others' spending.
statements.why: Households emulate the living standards of those around them.

quiz.q: The ratchet effect is due to:
quiz.why: Duesenberry's relative income hypothesis includes the ratchet effect.

quiz.q: Kuznets' long-run consumption function passes through:
quiz.why: A constant APC implies C = bY.

scenes.text: A 30-year-old engineer saves part of every salary for life after 60.
A one-time Diwali bonus barely changes her monthly spending.

steps.title: Life-cycle (Modigliani)
steps.body:
- People smooth consumption over their lifetime: save while working, dissave in retirement.
- With no initial wealth and zero interest: C = (working years × Y)/(remaining life years).
- Aggregate C = αW + βY; APC = α(W/Y) + β — constant in the long run if W/Y stable, falling in the short run.

steps.title: Permanent income (Friedman)
steps.body:
- Y = Yp + Yt (permanent + transitory). C = k·Yp; MPC out of transitory income ≈ 0.
- Yp estimated as a weighted average of current and past incomes (adaptive expectations).
- Explains why temporary tax cuts have small effects.

steps.title: Solved: life cycle
steps.body:
Age 25, works until 65 (40 years) earning ₹6 lakh/year, expects to live to 85. No wealth, zero interest.

1. Lifetime resources = 40 × 6 = 240.
2. Years of life remaining = 60 ⇒ **C = ₹4 lakh/year**.
3. Saving while working = ₹2 lakh/year; wealth at 65 = 80 lakh, run down over 20 years.

statements.s: According to PIH, a one-time lottery win has a large effect on current consumption.
statements.why: It is transitory income with MPC near zero.

statements.s: The life-cycle hypothesis predicts dissaving in retirement.
statements.why: Retirees consume out of accumulated wealth.

statements.s: In the life-cycle model, wealth affects consumption.
statements.why: C = αW + βY.

statements.s: PIH implies the short-run MPC is larger than the long-run MPC.
statements.why: The short-run MPC is smaller because current income gets a partial weight in Yp.

quiz.q: Works 30 years at ₹10 lakh; lives 50 more years. LCH consumption:
quiz.why: 300/50 = ₹6 lakh per year.

quiz.q: The life-cycle hypothesis is associated with:
quiz.why: Franco Modigliani (with Brumberg and Ando) developed it.

story.title: Should the mill buy a new loom?

scenes.text: A loom costs ₹10 lakh and will add ₹6 lakh of net revenue in each of the next two years.
Whether to buy it depends on the interest rate.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **NPV** = −C + Σ Rt/(1 + r)^t. Invest if NPV > 0.
- **MEC (Keynes)**: the discount rate m that makes PV of returns equal to cost (internal rate of return). Invest if m > r.
- The MEC schedule slopes down (diminishing returns, rising supply price of capital) ⇒ investment demand falls with r.
- Keynes stressed volatile **expectations** (animal spirits) shifting MEC.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing undiscounted returns with cost.
- Confusing MEC (expected return) with the interest rate (cost of funds).

activity.label: Market interest rate r (%) for the loom project (MEC ≈ 13.1%)

bands.text: r below MEC: NPV is positive — the loom is worth buying.
r close to 13.1%: NPV is about zero — the firm is indifferent.
r above MEC: NPV is negative — postpone the purchase.

quiz.q: C = 500, one return of 550 next year, r = 8%. NPV:
MEC of the project in the previous question:
A rise in r with unchanged MEC causes investment to:
quiz.why: Fewer projects have MEC above the cost of funds.

lessons.title: Accelerator, Tobin's q and user cost

scenes.text: When car sales grow quickly, component makers order many new machines.
When sales growth merely slows, machine orders collapse — the accelerator.

steps.title: Accelerator
steps.body:
- Desired capital K* = vY ⇒ net investment I = v(Yt − Yt−1); v = capital–output ratio.
- Investment depends on the **change** in output, so it is more volatile than output.
- **Flexible accelerator**: I = λ(K* − K₋₁), 0 < λ < 1.
- **Multiplier–accelerator interaction** (Samuelson) can generate cycles.

steps.title: Solved: accelerator
steps.body:
v = 3. Output: 100, 110, 115, 115.

Net I: 3(10) = **30**, 3(5) = **15**, 3(0) = **0** — output growth slows from 10 to 5 and investment halves; output levels off and net investment stops.

steps.title: Tobin's q and user cost
steps.body:
- **q** = market value of installed capital / replacement cost. q > 1 ⇒ invest; q < 1 ⇒ don't.
- **Jorgenson user cost**: c = Pk(r + δ) (ignoring taxes and capital gains). Firms add capital until MPK × P = c.

steps.title: Solved: user cost
steps.body:
Machine price ₹5 lakh, r = 8%, depreciation 12%.

User cost = 5 × (0.08 + 0.12) = **₹1 lakh per year**.

statements.s: The accelerator makes investment depend on the change in output.
statements.why: I = v·ΔY.

statements.s: If output stops growing, accelerator net investment becomes zero.
statements.why: ΔY = 0 means no new capital is needed.

statements.s: Tobin's q below 1 encourages firms to invest.
statements.why: Capital is valued below its replacement cost, so investing destroys value.

statements.s: A higher depreciation rate raises the user cost of capital.
statements.why: c = Pk(r + δ).

quiz.q: v = 4, Y rises from 200 to 215. Net investment:
Tobin's q = market value ₹150 crore / replacement cost ₹100 crore =
quiz.why: 150/100 = 1.5, so expansion is attractive.

quiz.q: Pk = ₹10 lakh, r = 6%, δ = 10%. User cost:
quiz.why: 10 × 0.16 = ₹1.6 lakh per year.

options: constant long-run APC vs falling short-run APC
questions.why: Cross-section and long-run data gave different consumption patterns.

questions.why: Transitory income is mostly saved.

NPV of cost 2,000 and returns 1,100 in years 1 and 2 at 5%:

questions.why: Expected return must exceed the cost of funds.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Economic growth models
courses.summary: Harrod–Domar growth and the knife-edge problem, the Solow–Swan model with steady state, golden rule and technical progress, growth accounting, convergence and endogenous growth.
outcomes: Compute Harrod–Domar growth and explain warranted vs natural growth
Solve for the Solow steady state
Find the golden-rule saving rate
Do growth accounting for TFP
Contrast exogenous and endogenous growth and explain convergence

scenes.text: Early Five-Year Plans asked: how much must we save to grow at a target rate?
Harrod–Domar gave a simple answer: growth = saving rate ÷ capital–output ratio.

steps.title: The model
steps.body:
- Fixed capital–output ratio v = K/Y; saving S = sY; I = S.
- **Warranted growth** gw = s/v: growth that keeps capacity fully used.
- **Natural growth** gn = n (+ labour-augmenting progress): growth needed to employ the growing labour force.
- **Actual growth** g.
- **Knife-edge instability**: if g ≠ gw, deviations are self-reinforcing; full employment with steady growth needs gw = gn = g — a fluke.

steps.title: Solved: growth target
steps.body:
s = 30%, v = 4.

1. gw = 0.30/4 = **7.5%**.
2. Target 9% with v = 4 ⇒ required s = 0.09 × 4 = **36%**.
3. With population growth 1%, per capita growth ≈ 7.5 − 1 = 6.5%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing g = v/s.
- Treating knife-edge as a prediction of stable growth.

bands.text: Low saving: warranted growth only 2.5–4%.
Moderate saving: warranted growth 4.5–7.5%.
High saving: warranted growth 8–10% — only if capital productivity (v) stays constant.

quiz.q: Target growth 6% with v = 5. Required saving:

quiz.why: With fixed coefficients, a gap between actual and warranted growth widens.

story.title: Why saving more doesn't grow you forever

scenes.text: A country raises its saving rate and grows faster for a while.
Then diminishing returns bite and growth returns to the old rate — at a higher income level.

steps.title: Set-up
steps.body:
- Y = K^α (AL)^(1−α), CRS, diminishing returns to capital, smooth substitution.
- Per worker: y = k^α (with A = 1).
- Capital accumulation: Δk = s·y − (n + δ)k.
- **Steady state**: s·f(k*) = (n + δ)k* ⇒ k* = [s/(n + δ)]^(1/(1−α)).
- In steady state, per-capita output is constant (without technical progress); total output grows at n.

steps.title: Solved: population growth
steps.body: Same model, n rises to 0.05 (s = 0.2): k* = (0.2/0.08)^2 = 6.25, y* = 2.5 — faster population growth lowers steady-state income per worker.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying higher saving raises the long-run growth rate in Solow.
- Forgetting depreciation in break-even investment.

statements.s: In the Solow model a higher saving rate permanently raises the growth rate of output per worker.
statements.why: It raises the steady-state level; long-run growth comes from technology.

statements.s: Higher population growth lowers steady-state capital per worker.
statements.why: Break-even investment (n + δ)k rises.

statements.s: In steady state, sy = (n + δ)k.
statements.why: Investment just offsets depreciation and dilution.

statements.s: Without technical progress, output per worker grows at n in steady state.
statements.why: Output per worker is constant; total output grows at n.

quiz.q: Long-run growth of output per worker in Solow comes from:
quiz.why: Only exogenous technical progress sustains per-capita growth.

scenes.text: Saving everything leaves nothing to eat; saving nothing leaves no capital.
The golden rule finds the saving rate that maximises steady-state consumption.

steps.title: Golden rule
steps.body:
- Steady-state c = f(k) − (n + δ)k. Maximise: **MPK = n + δ**.
- For Cobb–Douglas y = k^α: golden-rule saving rate **s_gold = α**.
- If s > α (dynamic inefficiency), lowering saving raises consumption now and later.

steps.title: Growth accounting (Solow residual)
steps.body: gY = gA + α·gK + (1 − α)·gL. TFP growth gA = residual.

statements.s: At the golden rule, MPK equals n + δ.

scenes.text: East Asian economies grew far faster than rich countries for decades.
But many poor countries did not catch up — ideas, skills and institutions matter.

steps.title: Convergence
steps.body:
- **Absolute convergence**: poorer countries grow faster regardless of characteristics — weak evidence globally.
- **Conditional convergence**: countries converge to their own steady states (given s, n, δ, technology) — better supported.
- Club convergence among similar economies.

steps.title: Endogenous growth
steps.body:
- Growth explained within the model: knowledge spillovers (Romer), human capital (Lucas), R&D.
- **AK model**: Y = AK (no diminishing returns) ⇒ g = sA − δ — higher saving raises growth permanently.
- Policy matters: education, research, openness, institutions.

steps.title: Solved: AK

g = 0.25 × 0.4 − 0.05 = **5%**. If s rises to 0.3: g = 7% — a permanent growth effect, unlike Solow.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating conditional convergence as meaning all countries reach the same income.
- Forgetting that AK removes diminishing returns to capital.

courses.summary: Balance of payments accounting, nominal and real exchange rates, purchasing power and interest parity, the Mundell–Fleming model under fixed and flexible exchange rates, and the impossible trinity.

lessons.title: Balance of payments and national saving

scenes.text: India earns heavily from software services and remittances.
It spends heavily on oil and gold imports. The BoP records it all.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
- **Current account**: merchandise trade, services (invisibles), primary income (investment income, wages), secondary income (remittances, transfers).
- **Capital and financial account**: FDI, portfolio investment, loans (ECBs), banking capital, and changes in official reserves.
- BoP always balances: CA + KA + errors and omissions + reserve change = 0 (sign conventions vary).
- India typically runs a **merchandise deficit** partly offset by a **services and remittance surplus**.

steps.title: Saving–investment identity
steps.body:
Y = C + I + G + NX ⇒ (S_private + (T − G)) − I = NX ≈ CA.

A current-account deficit means domestic investment exceeds national saving, financed by foreign capital.

steps.title: Solved: CA
steps.body:
National saving 30% of GDP, investment 32%.

CA = S − I = **−2% of GDP** (deficit) financed by net capital inflows.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing remittances in the capital account (they are secondary income in the CA).
- Saying the BoP can be in deficit overall without reserve changes.

statements.s: Workers' remittances are recorded in the current account.
statements.why: They are secondary income transfers.

statements.s: FDI inflows appear in the current account.
statements.why: They are financial-account flows.

statements.s: A current-account deficit implies investment exceeds national saving.
statements.why: CA = S − I.

statements.s: India's services trade usually shows a surplus.
statements.why: Software and business services exports are large.

quiz.why: Lower national saving widens S − I negatively (twin deficits).

lessons.title: Exchange rates, PPP and interest parity

story.title: The rupee and the Big Mac

scenes.text: The rupee trades around ₹80-something per dollar.
If a burger costs far less in India at that rate, the rupee looks undervalued by PPP.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Nominal rate** e = ₹ per $ (rise = rupee depreciation).
- **Real exchange rate** ε = e·P*/P — price of foreign goods relative to domestic goods; a rise means real depreciation (domestic goods cheaper).
- **Absolute PPP**: e = P/P*. **Relative PPP**: %Δe ≈ π − π*.
- **Uncovered interest parity**: i = i* + expected depreciation of the home currency.

steps.title: Solved: real exchange rate
steps.body:
e = 80 ₹/$, US price index 100, Indian price index 120.

ε = 80 × 100/120 = **66.7**. If India's prices rise 10% with e fixed, ε = 80 × 100/132 = 60.6 ⇒ real appreciation (Indian goods dearer).

steps.title: Solved: relative PPP and UIP
steps.body:
- Indian inflation 5%, US 2% ⇒ rupee expected to depreciate ≈ **3%** per year.
- US interest 4% ⇒ UIP Indian interest ≈ 4 + 3 = **7%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading a rise in ₹/$ as rupee appreciation.
- Expecting PPP to hold in the short run.

statements.why: More rupees are needed per dollar.

statements.s: Relative PPP predicts high-inflation countries' currencies depreciate.
statements.why: %Δe ≈ π − π*.

statements.s: A real depreciation makes domestic goods more expensive abroad.
statements.why: It makes them relatively cheaper.

statements.why: Returns must be equal in a common currency.

scenes.text: A small open economy boosts government spending under a floating rate.
Capital flows in, the currency appreciates, and exports fall until the stimulus fizzles.

steps.title: Set-up
steps.body:
- Small open economy, **perfect capital mobility**: r = r*.
- IS*: Y = C(Y − T) + I(r*) + G + NX(e). LM*: M/P = L(r*, Y).
- Under perfect mobility, LM* is vertical in (Y, e) space — Y is pinned by money market at r = r*.

steps.title: Policy under floating rates
steps.body:
- **Fiscal expansion**: IS* shifts right ⇒ upward pressure on r ⇒ capital inflow ⇒ currency **appreciates** ⇒ NX falls ⇒ **Y unchanged** (full crowding out via net exports).
- **Monetary expansion**: LM* right ⇒ r falls below r* ⇒ outflow ⇒ **depreciation** ⇒ NX rises ⇒ **Y rises** — monetary policy is powerful.
- **Tariffs/import quotas**: appreciation offsets; Y unchanged, trade balance unchanged.

steps.title: Solved: monetary expansion
steps.body:
LM*: M/P = 0.25Y − 10r, r* = 5, M/P = 450.

1. 450 = 0.25Y − 50 ⇒ **Y = 2,000**.
2. M/P rises to 500 ⇒ 0.25Y = 550 ⇒ **Y = 2,200** — currency depreciates enough to raise NX by the required amount.
3. G rise: Y stays 2,000 because LM* fixes Y at r*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying closed-economy IS–LM crowding out via interest rates; here crowding out works through the exchange rate.
- Forgetting the small-open-economy assumption r = r*.

statements.s: Under floating rates and perfect capital mobility, fiscal policy cannot change output.
statements.why: Appreciation crowds out net exports fully.

statements.s: Monetary expansion under floating rates leads to currency depreciation.
statements.why: Lower domestic interest rates trigger outflows.

statements.s: A tariff under floating rates improves the trade balance.
statements.why: Appreciation offsets it; NX unchanged.

statements.s: In Mundell–Fleming, the domestic interest rate equals the world rate.
statements.why: Perfect capital mobility.

quiz.why: Monetary policy works through depreciation and net exports.

quiz.why: Capital inflows bid up the currency, crowding out exports.

lessons.title: Fixed exchange rates and the impossible trinity

scenes.text: A central bank promises a fixed rate to the dollar.
To keep that promise it must buy or sell reserves — and loses control of money supply.

steps.title: Policy under fixed rates
steps.body:
- **Fiscal expansion**: pressure to appreciate ⇒ central bank buys foreign currency, **expanding money supply** ⇒ LM* shifts right ⇒ **Y rises strongly**.
- **Monetary expansion**: pressure to depreciate ⇒ central bank sells reserves, reversing the expansion ⇒ **Y unchanged**.
- **Devaluation**: raises NX and Y (expansionary).
- Lesson: fiscal policy powerful, monetary policy impotent under fixed rates.

steps.title: Impossible trinity
steps.body: A country cannot simultaneously have (1) **fixed exchange rate**, (2) **free capital mobility**, and (3) **independent monetary policy**. It can choose two. India operates a managed float with partial capital controls — a middle path.

steps.title: Solved: choose two
steps.body:
- Hong Kong: fixed rate + capital mobility ⇒ gives up monetary independence.
- US: floating + capital mobility ⇒ keeps monetary independence.
- China (historically): fixed/managed + capital controls ⇒ keeps monetary independence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing the policy effectiveness results between regimes.
- Claiming a country can have all three of the trinity.

statements.why: Reserve operations to defend the peg reverse it.

statements.s: Fiscal policy is powerful under fixed exchange rates.
statements.why: Defending the peg forces monetary accommodation.

statements.why: That violates the impossible trinity.

statements.why: It shifts NX up at each income.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Expectations, rules and monetary policy debates
courses.summary: Adaptive and rational expectations, the Lucas critique and policy ineffectiveness, rules versus discretion and time inconsistency, central bank independence, inflation targeting and the Taylor rule.
outcomes: Contrast adaptive and rational expectations
Explain the policy ineffectiveness proposition and the Lucas critique
Show why discretionary policy suffers from inflation bias
Compute a Taylor-rule policy rate
Evaluate inflation targeting and central bank independence

scenes.text: A household expects next year's inflation to equal this year's — adaptive expectations.
A bond trader reads the RBI's guidance and the budget too — rational expectations.

steps.title: Two models
steps.body:
- **Adaptive**: πe_t = πe_{t−1} + λ(π_{t−1} − πe_{t−1}); backward-looking, systematic errors possible.
- **Rational (Muth, Lucas, Sargent)**: agents use all available information and the correct model; forecast errors are random with mean zero.
- **Policy ineffectiveness (Sargent–Wallace)**: with RE and flexible prices, anticipated monetary policy cannot affect real output; only surprises matter.

steps.title: Solved: adaptive expectations
steps.body:
λ = 0.5, πe last year 4%, actual inflation last year 8%.

πe this year = 4 + 0.5(8 − 4) = **6%**.

steps.title: Lucas critique
steps.body: Estimated relationships (like the Phillips curve) depend on policy regime; when policy changes, people's behaviour and the parameters change. Policy evaluation must use models with deep (structural) parameters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking RE means perfect foresight — errors happen but are not systematic.
- Forgetting that with sticky prices (New Keynesian) anticipated policy can still matter.

statements.s: Under rational expectations, forecast errors are systematic.
statements.why: They are random with zero mean.

statements.s: The Lucas critique says estimated parameters may change when policy changes.
statements.why: Behaviour responds to the policy regime.

statements.s: Policy ineffectiveness says unanticipated monetary shocks have no real effects.
statements.why: Only anticipated policy is ineffective; surprises matter.

statements.s: Adaptive expectations are backward-looking.
statements.why: They update from past errors.

quiz.why: They showed anticipated money has no real effect under RE and flexible prices.
Forecasts are the best possible given information, though not perfect.

lessons.title: Rules vs discretion and time inconsistency

scenes.text: A teacher announces an exam so students study, then cancels it the night before — it is optimal ex post.
Next term no one studies. Central banks face the same temptation with inflation.

steps.title: Time inconsistency (Kydland–Prescott)
steps.body:
- An optimal plan announced today may not be optimal to carry out later.
- A central bank that promises low inflation is tempted, once wages are set, to create surprise inflation to cut unemployment.
- Agents anticipate this ⇒ expected inflation rises ⇒ **inflation bias** with no output gain (Barro–Gordon).

steps.title: Solutions
steps.body:
- **Rules** instead of discretion (e.g. money growth or Taylor rule).
- **Central bank independence** and appointing a conservative central banker (Rogoff).
- **Inflation targeting** with transparency and accountability.
- Reputation in repeated settings.

steps.title: Solved: Barro–Gordon outcome
steps.body:
Loss function makes the discretionary inflation rate π = a·b, where a = weight on output, b = Phillips slope (illustrative a = 2, b = 1.5).

1. Discretion: π = **3%**, output at natural level (no surprise).
2. Credible rule: π = **0%**, same output ⇒ the rule is strictly better.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking discretion always beats rules because it is more flexible.
- Confusing time inconsistency with incompetence.

statements.s: Discretionary policy can create an inflation bias without lowering unemployment.
statements.why: Agents anticipate the temptation.

statements.s: Time inconsistency was formalised by Kydland and Prescott.
statements.why: Their 1977 paper introduced it.

statements.s: Central bank independence aims to reduce inflation bias.
statements.why: It insulates policy from short-term political pressure.

statements.s: A credible rule leads to higher average inflation than discretion.
statements.why: It lowers average inflation.

quiz.why: Expected surprise inflation raises actual inflation.

quiz.q: A 'conservative central banker' places more weight on:
quiz.why: Rogoff's idea is to appoint someone more inflation-averse than society.

story.title: A recipe for the policy rate

scenes.text: John Taylor noticed the US Fed's rate followed a simple formula.
Analysts now use it to judge whether policy is too loose or too tight.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
i = r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5(y − y*)

- r* = neutral real rate; π* = inflation target; (y − y*) = output gap (%).
- **Taylor principle**: nominal rates should rise more than one-for-one with inflation (coefficient on π > 1) so real rates rise.

steps.title: Solved: response to inflation
steps.body: Inflation rises from 6% to 7% (gap unchanged): i rises by 1 + 0.5 = **1.5 points** to 10% — satisfying the Taylor principle.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to add current inflation π before the deviation term.
- Treating the rule as mechanically followed by any central bank — it is a benchmark.

At target: rate = 6% (2% real + 4% inflation).
Above target: rate rises 1.5 points per point of inflation; π = 8 gives 12%.

scenes.text: In 2016 India formally adopted flexible inflation targeting, with a Monetary Policy Committee.
The aim: anchor inflation expectations around 4%.

steps.title: Features
steps.body:
- Explicit numerical target (India: CPI 4% ± 2%), set by the government in consultation with RBI, reviewed every five years.
- Committee decisions, published minutes, regular communication.
- If inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, RBI must report reasons and remedial action to the government.
- 'Flexible': growth and financial stability also considered.

steps.title: Debates
steps.body:
- Pros: credibility, anchored expectations, transparency.
- Cons: supply shocks (food, fuel) dominate CPI in India; limited control over food prices; possible neglect of growth; transmission lags.
- Alternatives: nominal GDP targeting, price-level targeting.

steps.body:
Repo rate 6.5%, expected CPI inflation 4.5%.

Real policy rate ≈ 6.5 − 4.5 = **2%** — positive, indicating a moderately tight stance if neutral real rate is around 1–1.5%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying RBI targets WPI.
- Saying the target is a hard 4% with no tolerance band.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Fiscal policy, public debt and business cycles
courses.summary: Government budget constraint and debt dynamics, Ricardian equivalence, phases and theories of business cycles — multiplier–accelerator, real business cycle and New Keynesian views — and stabilisation policy lags.
outcomes: Use the debt-dynamics equation to judge sustainability

story.title: Can the debt ratio fall while borrowing continues?

scenes.text: A government runs a deficit every year, yet its debt-to-GDP ratio falls.
The secret: nominal GDP grows faster than the interest rate on debt.

steps.title: Equation
steps.body:
Δb ≈ (r − g)·b − ps

- b = debt/GDP, r = nominal interest rate on debt, g = nominal GDP growth, ps = primary surplus/GDP (negative if primary deficit).
- If r < g, debt ratio can stabilise even with primary deficits.
- Debt-stabilising primary balance: ps* = (r − g)·b.

steps.title: Solved: danger zone
steps.body:
Same debt, but growth slows to g = 6%.

Δb = (0.07 − 0.06) × 80 + 2 = 0.8 + 2 = **+2.8 points** ⇒ ratio rises. Debt-stabilising primary surplus = 0.01 × 80 = 0.8% of GDP.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing real and nominal r and g.
- Forgetting that the primary balance excludes interest payments.

statements.s: If r < g, a primary deficit can coexist with a stable debt ratio.
statements.why: Growth erodes the ratio faster than interest adds to it.

statements.s: The primary deficit includes interest payments.
statements.why: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments.

statements.s: Slower growth makes debt harder to stabilise.
statements.why: (r − g) rises.

statements.s: A rising interest rate lowers the debt-stabilising primary surplus.
statements.why: It raises it.

story.title: A tax cut today, a tax bill tomorrow

scenes.text: The government cuts taxes now and borrows to pay for it.
Far-sighted households save the windfall to pay the future taxes — spending is unchanged.

steps.title: The proposition (Barro)
steps.body:
For a given path of government spending, financing by debt or taxes is equivalent: a debt-financed tax cut raises private saving one-for-one, leaving consumption, national saving and interest rates unchanged.

**Assumptions**: forward-looking households, perfect capital markets, lump-sum taxes, intergenerational altruism (bequests), no change in G.

steps.title: Why it may fail
steps.body:
- **Liquidity constraints**: many households cannot borrow, so spend tax cuts.
- **Myopia** and finite horizons.
- **Distortionary taxes**.
- No bequest motive; future taxes may fall on others.
Evidence: partial Ricardian effects at best.

steps.title: Solved: present value
steps.body:
Tax cut ₹1,000 today, repaid with interest at 10% next year (tax ₹1,100).

PV of future tax = 1,100/1.1 = 1,000 ⇒ lifetime wealth unchanged ⇒ Ricardian household saves the full ₹1,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Ricardian equivalence to changes in government spending (it concerns financing, not spending).
- Assuming it holds with liquidity-constrained households.

statements.s: Ricardian equivalence says debt-financed tax cuts do not change consumption.
statements.why: Households save the cut to pay future taxes.

statements.s: Liquidity constraints strengthen Ricardian equivalence.
statements.why: Constrained households spend tax cuts.

statements.s: Ricardian equivalence concerns the timing of taxes, not government spending.
statements.why: G is held constant.

statements.s: Robert Barro revived the idea in modern form.
statements.why: His 1974 paper is the classic statement.

quiz.q: If Ricardian equivalence holds, a debt-financed tax cut leaves national saving:
quiz.why: Private saving rises exactly as public saving falls.
Myopic households do not anticipate future taxes.

scenes.text: Factories run overtime; then orders fall and layoffs begin.
Recovery follows. Why do economies fluctuate?

steps.title: Phases and stylised facts
steps.body:
- Phases: expansion → peak → contraction (recession) → trough → recovery.
- **Procyclical**: consumption, investment, employment, profits. Investment is far more volatile than consumption.
- **Countercyclical**: unemployment.
- Leading indicators: new orders, stock prices, PMI.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
- **Multiplier–accelerator (Samuelson, Hicks)**: interaction of income and induced investment generates cycles.
- **Monetarist**: money supply fluctuations.
- **Real business cycle (Kydland–Prescott)**: technology/productivity shocks with flexible prices; cycles are efficient responses; money neutral.
- **New Keynesian**: demand shocks with sticky prices/wages (menu costs, staggered contracts); cycles involve inefficiency, justify stabilisation.

steps.title: Solved: Samuelson model
steps.body:
Ct = 0.5Y_{t−1}; It = 1.0(C_t − C_{t−1}); G = 100 (constant). Start Y₀ = Y₋₁ = 200; G rises permanently to 110 at t = 1.

- t1: C = 100, I = 0, Y = 210.
- t2: C = 105, I = 5, Y = 220.
- t3: C = 110, I = 5, Y = 225.
- t4: C = 112.5, I = 2.5, Y = 225 → income converges in damped oscillation towards 220 (= 110/0.5).

statements.s: Investment is more volatile than consumption over the cycle.
statements.why: Durable and capital spending swing sharply with expectations.

statements.s: Unemployment is procyclical.

steps.title: Lags
steps.body:
- **Inside lags**: recognition, decision (longer for fiscal policy because of the legislative process).
- **Outside lag**: time for the policy to affect the economy (longer for monetary policy, often 2–6 quarters or more).
- Friedman's critique: long and variable lags can make activist policy destabilising.

steps.title: Automatic stabilisers

- Saying fiscal policy has a longer outside lag than monetary policy — fiscal's main lag is inside.
- Treating automatic stabilisers as discretionary policy.

uni-ba-eco-micro-1.title: Microeconomics I — consumers, producers, competitive markets
uni-ba-eco-micro-1.description: Demand and elasticity, consumer choice, production, costs and perfect competition with worked numericals and unit exams. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA (Hons) Economics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Demand, supply and elasticity
courses.summary: How markets clear: demand and supply functions, shifts versus movements, market equilibrium and comparative statics, price controls, and the four elasticities with their revenue implications.
outcomes: Derive market equilibrium from linear demand and supply functions
Distinguish shifts of a curve from movements along it
Compute arc and point price elasticity and apply the total-revenue test
Interpret income and cross elasticities
Analyse price ceilings, floors and tax incidence

scenes.text: Heavy rains damage the kharif onion crop in Maharashtra. Within weeks mandi prices in Lasalgaon jump.
Households buy fewer onions, traders release stocks, and a new, higher price settles. That is a supply shift and a movement along demand.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Demand function**: Qd = f(P, income M, prices of related goods, tastes, expectations, population).
- **Law of demand**: ceteris paribus, Qd falls as P rises (substitution and income effects).
- **Supply function**: Qs = g(P, input prices, technology, number of sellers, expectations).
- **Movement along** a curve: caused only by the good's own price. **Shift** of a curve: caused by any other determinant.
- **Equilibrium**: Qd = Qs; no excess demand or supply.

steps.title: Solved: comparative statics
steps.body:
Income rises and demand becomes Qd = 130 − 2P (supply unchanged).

1. 130 − 2P = −20 + 4P ⇒ 6P = 150 ⇒ P = 25.
2. Q = 130 − 50 = 80.

Demand shift right ⇒ **both P and Q rise**. A supply shift right would lower P and raise Q.

steps.title: Simultaneous shifts
steps.body: If demand and supply both increase, Q rises for sure but the change in P is ambiguous — it depends on which shift is larger. Always state the ambiguity in exam answers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'a rise in price reduces demand' — it reduces **quantity demanded**.
- Shifting the demand curve when the good's own price changes.
- Forgetting to check that Q* is positive at the solved price.

statements.s: A fall in the price of petrol shifts the demand curve for petrol to the right.
statements.why: An own-price change causes a movement along the demand curve, not a shift.

statements.s: A rise in the price of tea can shift the demand curve for coffee to the right.
statements.why: Tea and coffee are substitutes, so dearer tea raises coffee demand at every price.

statements.s: Better seed technology shifts supply of wheat to the right.
statements.why: Technology lowers cost per unit, so more is offered at each price.

statements.s: If demand and supply both rise, the equilibrium price must rise.
statements.why: Quantity must rise, but price can rise, fall or stay the same depending on the relative shifts.

quiz.q: Qd = 50 − P and Qs = 10 + P. Equilibrium price is:
quiz.why: Setting 50 − P = 10 + P gives 2P = 40, so P = 20 and Q = 30.

quiz.q: A decrease in input costs, other things equal, leads to:
quiz.why: Lower input costs shift supply right, which lowers equilibrium price and raises equilibrium quantity.

quiz.q: Which causes a movement along the demand curve for rice?
options: A change in the price of rice
A change in the price of wheat
quiz.why: Only a change in the good's own price moves along its demand curve; the others shift the curve.

quiz.q: At a price above equilibrium there is:
quiz.why: Above equilibrium quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so there is a surplus that pushes the price down.

scenes.text: A metro raises fares from ₹20 to ₹25 and daily riders fall from 2.0 lakh to 1.8 lakh.
Revenue goes from ₹40 lakh to ₹45 lakh. Demand was inelastic — elasticity predicted it.

steps.title: Measures
steps.body:
- **Price elasticity** Ep = (%ΔQ)/(%ΔP), usually reported as |Ep|.
- **Arc (midpoint)**: Ep = [ΔQ/((Q1+Q2)/2)] ÷ [ΔP/((P1+P2)/2)].
- **Point**: Ep = (dQ/dP)·(P/Q).
- **Geometric (linear demand)**: Ep at a point = lower segment ÷ upper segment of the demand line.
- Categories: perfectly inelastic (0), inelastic (<1), unitary (=1), elastic (>1), perfectly elastic (∞).

steps.title: Solved: arc elasticity of the metro
Solved: point elasticity and revenue
steps.body:
Q = 120 − 3P.

1. At P = 30: Q = 30, Ep = −3 × 30/30 = **−3** (elastic).
2. At P = 10: Q = 90, Ep = −3 × 10/90 = **−0.33** (inelastic).
3. Unit elastic where 3P = Q ⇒ 3P = 120 − 3P ⇒ P = 20, Q = 60. TR = P·Q is maximised there (TR = 1200).
4. Relationship: MR = P(1 − 1/|Ep|), so MR = 0 when |Ep| = 1.

steps.title: Determinants
steps.body: Availability of substitutes, share of the budget, necessity vs luxury, time period (more elastic in the long run), and how broadly the good is defined ("food" is less elastic than "Basmati rice brand X").

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating slope as elasticity: a linear demand curve has constant slope but elasticity varying from ∞ to 0.
- Using different bases for the two percentage changes.
- Concluding a price rise always raises revenue.

bands.text: Perfectly inelastic: quantity does not respond; a price rise raises revenue one-for-one.
Inelastic: raise price to raise total revenue; MR is negative here.
Unitary: total revenue is at its maximum and MR = 0.
Elastic: a price cut raises total revenue; MR is positive.

quiz.why: |Ep| = 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5, so demand is elastic and the price cut raises revenue.

quiz.q: For Q = 120 − 3P, total revenue is maximum at P =
quiz.why: TR is maximum where |Ep| = 1, which for this demand curve occurs at the midpoint P = 20, Q = 60.

quiz.why: Over a longer period buyers find substitutes and change habits, so they respond more to price.

scenes.text: As household incomes rise, spending on coarse grains falls while spending on milk, fruit and eggs rises.
Income elasticity sorts goods into inferior, necessity and luxury — a key input for planning food supply.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Income elasticity** Ey = %ΔQ/%ΔM: Ey < 0 inferior; 0 < Ey < 1 necessity (normal); Ey > 1 luxury.
- **Cross elasticity** Exy = %ΔQx/%ΔPy: > 0 substitutes, < 0 complements, ≈ 0 unrelated.
- **Price elasticity of supply** Es = %ΔQs/%ΔP. A linear supply through the origin has Es = 1; one cutting the price axis has Es > 1; one cutting the quantity axis has Es < 1.

steps.title: Solved: income elasticity
steps.body:
Income rises from ₹40,000 to ₹50,000; monthly milk purchase rises from 30 to 33 litres.

1. %ΔM (midpoint) = 10,000/45,000 = 22.2%.
2. %ΔQ = 3/31.5 = 9.5%.
3. Ey = 9.5/22.2 ≈ **0.43** ⇒ normal necessity.

steps.title: Solved: cross elasticity
steps.body:
Price of petrol rises 20%; demand for two-wheeler purchases falls 4%.

Exy = −4/20 = **−0.2** ⇒ complements (weakly).

steps.title: Engel curves
steps.body: Plotting quantity against income gives the Engel curve. Engel's law: the share of income spent on food falls as income rises — food has Ey < 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every normal good a luxury; luxury needs Ey > 1.
- Ignoring the sign of cross elasticity — the sign is the whole point.

statements.s: A good with income elasticity −0.3 is inferior.
statements.why: Negative income elasticity means demand falls as income rises.

statements.s: Cross elasticity between cars and petrol is positive.
statements.why: They are complements, so cross elasticity is negative.

statements.s: A straight-line supply curve through the origin has unit elasticity at every point.
statements.why: For Q = bP, Es = b·P/Q = 1 everywhere.

statements.s: An income elasticity of 0.8 marks a luxury.
statements.why: Luxuries have Ey above 1; 0.8 is a normal necessity.

quiz.q: Income rises 10%, demand for air travel rises 25%. Ey =
quiz.why: Ey = 25/10 = 2.5, which is above 1, so air travel behaves as a luxury.
A positive cross elasticity means a rise in one price raises demand for the other, the mark of substitutes.

quiz.q: Supply Q = −10 + 2P has elasticity at P = 10 of:
quiz.why: At P = 10, Q = 10, so Es = 2 × 10/10 = 2; a supply line cutting the price axis is elastic.

scenes.text: A city freezes rents below the market level. Tenants cheer, but few new flats are listed.
Waiting lists and side payments appear — the classic shortage under a binding price ceiling.

steps.title: Price ceilings and floors
steps.body:
- **Ceiling** (max price) binds only if set **below** equilibrium ⇒ shortage = Qd − Qs; leads to queues, rationing, black markets.
- **Floor** (min price, e.g. MSP or minimum wage) binds only if set **above** equilibrium ⇒ surplus = Qs − Qd; government may procure the surplus.
- **Consumer surplus** = area under demand above price; **producer surplus** = area above supply below price; controls create **deadweight loss**.

steps.title: Solved: per-unit tax incidence
steps.body:
Same market, tax t = ₹6 per unit on sellers. New supply: Qs = −20 + 4(P − 6).

1. 100 − 2P = −44 + 4P ⇒ 6P = 144 ⇒ buyers pay **P = 24**; sellers keep 18.
2. Q = 52. Buyers bear 4 of 6 (2/3), sellers 2 (1/3).
3. Rule: buyers' share = Es/(Es + |Ed|) — the more inelastic side bears more. Here supply slope 4 vs demand slope 2, so buyers bear 4/(4+2).
4. Tax revenue = 6 × 52 = 312; DWL = ½ × 6 × 8 = 24.

steps.title: Indian context
steps.body: Minimum Support Prices act as floors for procured crops; when MSP is above the market-clearing price, public stocks build up with the Food Corporation of India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a ceiling above equilibrium causes a shortage — it is non-binding.
- Assuming the legal payer of a tax bears its burden; incidence depends on elasticities.

statements.s: A price floor set below equilibrium has no effect.
statements.why: A floor below the market price is non-binding.

statements.s: When demand is perfectly inelastic, buyers bear the entire per-unit tax.
statements.why: Quantity does not fall, so price rises by the full tax.

statements.s: A binding ceiling raises the quantity traded.
statements.why: Quantity traded falls to the quantity supplied at the ceiling price.

statements.s: Deadweight loss from a tax grows with the elasticities of demand and supply.
statements.why: More elastic curves mean a bigger fall in quantity and a larger welfare triangle.

quiz.q: With Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = −20 + 4P, a floor at P = 25 gives a surplus of:
quiz.why: At P = 25, Qs = 80 and Qd = 50, so the surplus is 30 units.

quiz.q: The side of the market with the more inelastic curve:
quiz.why: Incidence falls on the side less able to adjust quantity, i.e. the more inelastic side.

options: lost gains from trades that no longer happen
quiz.why: DWL is the surplus from mutually beneficial trades that the control or tax prevents.

An increase in the price of a complement causes:
questions.why: A dearer complement makes the good less attractive at every price, shifting demand left.

On a linear demand curve, the upper half is:
questions.why: Above the midpoint the lower segment exceeds the upper segment, so |Ep| > 1.

questions.why: Quantity falls about 5% while price rises 10%, so revenue rises about 5% (1.10 × 0.95 = 1.045).

questions.why: An income elasticity above 1 means spending on the good grows faster than income, which defines a luxury.

questions.q: Cross elasticity between printers and ink cartridges is:
questions.why: Printers and ink are complements, so a higher ink price lowers printer demand.

questions.why: A floor above equilibrium raises quantity supplied and lowers quantity demanded, creating a surplus.
