questions.why: Post-tax quantity is 52, so revenue = 6 × 52 = ₹312.

questions.q: If supply is perfectly elastic, a per-unit tax is borne:
questions.why: A horizontal supply curve shifts up by the full tax, so buyers' price rises by the whole tax.

questions.q: MR = P(1 − 1/|Ep|). If |Ep| = 0.8, MR is:
questions.why: 1 − 1/0.8 = −0.25, so MR is negative in the inelastic range.

questions.q: Both demand and supply decrease. Which is certain?
questions.why: Both shifts reduce quantity, while their effects on price work in opposite directions.

questions.q: Elasticity of supply Q = 5 + 3P at P = 5 is:
questions.why: At P = 5, Q = 20, so Es = 3 × 5/20 = 0.75; a supply line cutting the quantity axis is inelastic.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Theory of consumer behaviour
courses.summary: Preferences and utility, indifference curves, the budget constraint, utility maximisation, income and substitution effects (Hicks and Slutsky), derivation of demand, and revealed preference.
outcomes: State the axioms of preference and properties of indifference curves
Solve utility maximisation problems with Cobb–Douglas, perfect substitute and complement preferences
Decompose a price change into substitution and income effects
Classify normal, inferior and Giffen goods
Apply the weak axiom of revealed preference

scenes.text: Riya can rank any two snack bundles. She never contradicts herself, and more is always better.
Joining all bundles she likes equally gives a curve — her indifference curve.

steps.title: Axioms of preference
steps.body:
- **Completeness**: any two bundles can be compared.
- **Transitivity**: A ≽ B and B ≽ C ⇒ A ≽ C.
- **Monotonicity (non-satiation)**: more of a good is preferred.
- **Convexity**: averages are preferred to extremes.

Under these, preferences can be represented by an **ordinal utility function** U(x, y); any increasing transformation represents the same preferences.

steps.title: Indifference curves and MRS
steps.body:
- IC: set of bundles with equal utility. Properties: downward sloping (monotonicity), convex to origin (diminishing MRS), never intersect (transitivity), higher IC = higher utility.
- **MRSxy** = −dy/dx along an IC = MUx/MUy — the amount of y the consumer will give up for one more x.
- Special shapes: perfect substitutes U = ax + by (straight lines, constant MRS = a/b); perfect complements U = min(x/a, y/b) (L-shaped).

steps.title: Solved: MRS of Cobb–Douglas
steps.body:
U = x^0.5 y^0.5.

1. MUx = 0.5 x^−0.5 y^0.5; MUy = 0.5 x^0.5 y^−0.5.
2. MRS = MUx/MUy = **y/x**.
3. At (4, 16): MRS = 4 — she gives 4 units of y for one more x. At (16, 4): MRS = 0.25 — diminishing MRS as x rises ✓.

steps.title: Solved: monotone transformation
steps.body: V = ln x + ln y is a monotone transform of U = xy. MRS from V = (1/x)/(1/y) = y/x, same as from U. Same ICs ⇒ same choices.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing utility numbers across people — ordinal utility allows only ranking.
- Drawing two ICs that cross.
- Writing MRS = MUy/MUx (it is MUx/MUy for x on the horizontal axis).

statements.s: Two indifference curves can intersect if preferences are complete.
statements.why: Crossing ICs would violate transitivity combined with monotonicity.

statements.s: Perfect complements have L-shaped indifference curves.
statements.why: Extra units of one good without the other add no utility.

statements.s: For U = 2x + 3y the MRS is 2/3 everywhere.
statements.why: MUx/MUy = 2/3, constant along straight-line ICs.

statements.s: Doubling every utility number changes the consumer's choices.
statements.why: Any increasing transformation preserves the ranking and the MRS.

quiz.why: MUx = 2xy and MUy = x², so MRS = 2xy/x² = 2y/x.
Convexity means the consumer gives up less y for each extra x as x grows — diminishing MRS.

quiz.q: Left and right shoes are an example of:
quiz.why: Shoes are used in fixed 1:1 proportion, the definition of perfect complements.

options: only the ranking of bundles matters
quiz.why: Ordinal utility only orders bundles; the size of the numbers carries no meaning.

scenes.text: A student has ₹1,200 a month. Books cost ₹200, films ₹100.
Her best bundle is where her highest reachable indifference curve just touches the budget line.

steps.title: Budget line
steps.body:
- Px·x + Py·y = M. Intercepts M/Px and M/Py; slope −Px/Py (market rate of exchange).
- Income rise: parallel outward shift. Fall in Px: line rotates outward around the y-intercept.
- Equal % rise in M, Px, Py: no change (homogeneity of degree zero).

steps.title: Equilibrium conditions
steps.body:
Interior optimum (tangency):
1. **MRSxy = Px/Py**, equivalently MUx/Px = MUy/Py.
2. Px·x + Py·y = M.
3. Second-order: ICs convex at the point.

Lagrangian: L = U(x, y) + λ(M − Px x − Py y); λ = marginal utility of income.

steps.title: Solved: corner and kink solutions
steps.body:
- **Perfect substitutes** U = x + 2y, Px = 10, Py = 15, M = 300: MUx/Px = 0.1 < MUy/Py = 0.133 ⇒ spend all on y: **y = 20, x = 0**.
- **Perfect complements** U = min(x, 2y), Px = 4, Py = 2, M = 100: optimum at x = 2y ⇒ 4(2y) + 2y = 100 ⇒ y = 10, **x = 20**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying MRS = price ratio to perfect substitutes — the answer is a corner.
- Forgetting to exhaust income.
- Mixing axes: slope of budget line is −Px/Py only when x is on the horizontal axis.

activity.label: Share of income a Cobb–Douglas consumer spends on x (a)

bands.text: Small a: x gets a small fixed budget share; with M = 1,200 and Px = 200, x = a × 6.
Middle a: spending on x = a × M regardless of prices; demand for x is unit price-elastic.
Large a: x takes most of the budget; y gets only (1 − a) × M.

quiz.q: U = xy, M = 100, Px = 5, Py = 10. Optimal x is:
At an interior optimum, MUx/Px compared with MUy/Py is:
quiz.why: If the per-rupee marginal utilities differed, shifting spending would raise utility, so they must be equal.

quiz.q: A fall in Px with M and Py fixed makes the budget line:
quiz.why: The y-intercept M/Py is unchanged while the x-intercept M/Px grows, so the line pivots outward.

quiz.q: For perfect complements U = min(x, y), Px = Py = 5, M = 50, the optimum is:
quiz.why: The consumer buys equal amounts: 5x + 5x = 50 gives x = y = 5.

scenes.text: A ration price cut makes wheat cheaper relative to rice, and also makes the family feel richer.
Economists split the total change into a substitution part and an income part.

steps.title: Decomposition
steps.body:
- **Substitution effect (SE)**: change in x due to the change in relative prices, holding real income constant. Always opposite to the price change (non-positive own SE).
- **Income effect (IE)**: change due to the change in purchasing power.
- **Hicks**: real income = original utility (compensating budget line tangent to original IC).
- **Slutsky**: real income = ability to buy the original bundle (compensating line passes through original bundle).
- Total effect = SE + IE.

steps.title: Classifying goods
steps.body:
- Normal: IE reinforces SE ⇒ demand slopes down.
- Inferior: IE opposes SE but is smaller ⇒ demand still slopes down.
- **Giffen**: inferior and IE outweighs SE ⇒ quantity rises when price rises (upward-sloping demand). Every Giffen good is inferior; not every inferior good is Giffen.

steps.title: Solved: Slutsky decomposition
steps.body:
U = xy, M = 120, Py = 1. Px falls from 4 to 2.

1. Original: x = 0.5 × 120/4 = **15**.
2. Final: x = 0.5 × 120/2 = **30**. Total effect = +15.
3. Slutsky income to buy old bundle (x=15, y=60) at new prices: M' = 2(15) + 60 = 90.
4. Compensated x = 0.5 × 90/2 = 22.5 ⇒ **SE = +7.5**, **IE = 30 − 22.5 = +7.5**.

steps.title: Solved: Hicksian SE
steps.body:
Same data. Original utility U = 15 × 60 = 900.

1. At new prices, minimise spending to reach U = 900: x = y/2·… with MRS y/x = 2 ⇒ y = 2x; x·2x = 900 ⇒ x = √450 ≈ 21.21.
2. Hicks **SE ≈ +6.21**, IE ≈ 30 − 21.21 = **+8.79**.
3. Slutsky SE (7.5) differs slightly from Hicks SE (6.21) for a finite price change; they coincide for infinitesimal changes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the substitution effect can be positive for an own-price rise — it never is.
- Calling any inferior good Giffen.
- Drawing the Slutsky line tangent to the old IC (that is Hicks).

statements.s: The own-price substitution effect is always negative (or zero).
statements.why: With real income held constant, a dearer good is never bought in larger quantity.

statements.s: All inferior goods are Giffen goods.
statements.why: Giffen needs the income effect to exceed the substitution effect.

statements.s: The Slutsky compensated budget line passes through the original bundle.
statements.why: Slutsky holds the original bundle affordable.

statements.s: For a normal good, income and substitution effects work in the same direction.
statements.why: A price fall raises real income and normal-good demand rises with income.

quiz.q: In the U = xy example (Px 4 → 2), the total increase in x is:
quiz.why: Demand rises from 15 to 30, a total effect of 15.
Only a negative income effect can outweigh the substitution effect, so the good must be inferior.
Hicks adjusts income so the consumer can just reach the original indifference curve.

lessons.title: Deriving demand, consumer surplus and revealed preference

scenes.text: We cannot see Arjun's utility, but we see what he buys at different prices.
Samuelson showed choices alone can test whether he behaves consistently.

steps.title: From PCC to demand
steps.body:
- **Price consumption curve (PCC)**: locus of optima as Px changes ⇒ plotting x against Px gives the individual demand curve.
- **Income consumption curve (ICC)**: locus of optima as M changes ⇒ gives the Engel curve.
- Market demand = horizontal sum of individual demands.

steps.title: Revealed preference
steps.body:
- If bundle A is chosen when B was affordable, A is **directly revealed preferred** to B.
- **WARP**: if A is revealed preferred to B, then B must never be chosen when A is affordable.
- Consistent choices imply a negative substitution effect — the law of demand for normal goods follows from choices alone.

steps.title: Solved: WARP test
steps.body:
Prices (2, 1): chooses A = (4, 2), spending 10. Prices (1, 2): chooses B = (2, 4), spending 10.

1. Cost of B at first prices = 2(2) + 4 = 8 ≤ 10 ⇒ A revealed preferred to B.
2. Cost of A at second prices = 4 + 2(2) = 8 ≤ 10 ⇒ B revealed preferred to A.
3. Both hold ⇒ **WARP violated**.

steps.title: Solved: consumer surplus
steps.body:
Demand P = 50 − Q, market price ₹20.

1. Q = 30.
2. CS = ½ × 30 × (50 − 20) = **₹450**.
3. If price falls to ₹10: Q = 40, CS = ½ × 40 × 40 = 800 ⇒ gain ₹350.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Summing market demand vertically (that is for public goods).
- Forgetting the affordability check in revealed preference.

statements.s: The income consumption curve is used to derive the Engel curve.
statements.why: It traces optimal quantities as income changes.

statements.s: Market demand for a private good is the vertical sum of individual demands.
statements.why: It is a horizontal sum: add quantities at each price.

statements.s: Revealed preference theory needs a utility function to be observed.
statements.why: It works only from observed choices and prices.

statements.s: A fall in price raises consumer surplus.
statements.why: Existing buyers pay less and new buyers enter.

quiz.why: Tracing optimal x as Px changes yields the individual demand curve.

options: A is chosen over a costlier B
A and B are each revealed preferred to the other
quiz.why: Consistency requires that if A is revealed preferred to B, B is never revealed preferred to A.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Theory of production
courses.summary: Production functions, the short-run law of variable proportions, isoquants and MRTS, returns to scale, Cobb–Douglas properties and the least-cost input combination.
outcomes: Compute TP, AP and MP and identify the three stages of production
Explain isoquant properties and calculate MRTS
Determine returns to scale of a production function
Find the cost-minimising input combination
Interpret elasticity of substitution and Euler's theorem for Cobb–Douglas

lessons.title: Short run: law of variable proportions

scenes.text: A Surat weaving unit has 4 looms. The owner keeps hiring workers.
The first few hires raise output sharply; later hires mostly get in each other's way.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Production function** Q = f(L, K). Short run: at least one input (K) fixed.
- **TP** = total output; **APL** = Q/L; **MPL** = ΔQ/ΔL (or ∂Q/∂L).
- MP > AP ⇒ AP rising; MP < AP ⇒ AP falling; **MP = AP at AP's maximum**.
- **Law of variable proportions**: as more of a variable input is added to fixed inputs, MP eventually diminishes.

steps.title: Three stages
steps.body:
- **Stage I**: from origin to max AP — AP rising; fixed input under-used.
- **Stage II**: from max AP to MP = 0 — AP and MP falling but positive. **Rational producer operates here.**
- **Stage III**: MP < 0, TP falling — irrational.

steps.title: Solved: calculus version
steps.body:
Q = 30L² − L³ (K fixed).

1. MP = 60L − 3L²; AP = 30L − L².
2. Max AP: dAP/dL = 30 − 2L = 0 ⇒ L = 15 (AP = 225; MP = 900 − 675 = 225 ✓ equal).
3. MP = 0 ⇒ L = 20. Stage II: **15 ≤ L ≤ 20**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing diminishing returns (short run, one input varies) with decreasing returns to scale (long run, all inputs scale).
- Claiming TP falls whenever MP falls — TP falls only when MP < 0.

statements.s: When MP exceeds AP, AP is rising.
statements.why: Adding a unit above the average pulls the average up.

statements.s: A rational firm produces where MP of labour is negative.
statements.why: Negative MP means fewer workers would produce more — Stage III is avoided.

statements.s: Diminishing marginal returns is a long-run concept.
statements.why: It arises in the short run with a fixed input.

statements.s: TP is maximum where MP = 0.
statements.why: Beyond that MP is negative and TP declines.

quiz.q: TP rises from 44 to 48 when L goes from 4 to 5. MP of the 5th worker is:
quiz.why: MP = 48 − 44 = 4 units.

quiz.q: For Q = 30L² − L³, AP is maximum at L =
quiz.why: AP = 30L − L² peaks where 30 − 2L = 0, i.e. L = 15.
Stage II runs from maximum AP to the point where MP becomes zero.
AP stops rising exactly when the marginal unit equals the average, so MP cuts AP at AP's peak.

lessons.title: Isoquants, MRTS and returns to scale

scenes.text: A builder can lay a road with many workers and few machines, or few workers and many machines.
Each output level traces a curve of possible mixes — an isoquant.

steps.title: Isoquants
steps.body:
- Isoquant: all (L, K) giving the same Q. Downward sloping, convex (diminishing MRTS), non-intersecting.
- **MRTS(L,K)** = −dK/dL = MPL/MPK.
- **Ridge lines** join points where MPL = 0 or MPK = 0; the economic region lies between them.
- **Elasticity of substitution** σ = %Δ(K/L)/%Δ(MRTS): σ = 1 for Cobb–Douglas, ∞ for perfect substitutes, 0 for fixed proportions (Leontief).

steps.title: Returns to scale
steps.body:
Multiply all inputs by t > 1:
- f(tL, tK) = t·f ⇒ **constant** returns (CRS)
- > t·f ⇒ **increasing** (IRS) — specialisation, indivisibilities
- < t·f ⇒ **decreasing** (DRS) — managerial diseconomies.
For Q = A L^α K^β: α + β = 1 CRS, > 1 IRS, < 1 DRS. Homogeneous of degree α + β.

steps.title: Solved: Cobb–Douglas
steps.body:
Q = 10 L^0.6 K^0.4.

1. MPL = 6 L^−0.4 K^0.4 = 0.6 Q/L; MPK = 0.4 Q/K.
2. MRTS = (0.6/0.4)(K/L) = 1.5 K/L. At L = 10, K = 20: MRTS = 3.
3. α + β = 1 ⇒ CRS. **Euler's theorem**: L·MPL + K·MPK = 0.6Q + 0.4Q = Q — paying each input its MP exhausts output.
4. Output elasticities: 0.6 (labour), 0.4 (capital).

steps.title: Solved: classify RTS
steps.body:
- Q = L^0.5 K^0.8: sum 1.3 ⇒ IRS.
- Q = min(2L, 3K): doubling both doubles Q ⇒ CRS (Leontief).
- Q = L + K + LK: f(2L, 2K) = 2L + 2K + 4LK > 2f ⇒ IRS.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading returns to scale from the exponent of a single input.
- Assuming CRS implies constant MP — MPs still diminish for each input separately.

bands.text: Decreasing returns to scale: doubling inputs less than doubles output; long-run average cost rises.
Constant returns to scale: output doubles exactly; Euler's theorem holds with factor shares α and β.
Increasing returns to scale: doubling inputs more than doubles output; long-run average cost falls.

quiz.q: MRTS for Q = L^0.5 K^0.5 at L = 4, K = 16 is:
quiz.why: MRTS = MPL/MPK = K/L = 16/4 = 4.
The exponents sum to 0.8, below 1, so returns to scale are decreasing.

quiz.q: Elasticity of substitution for Cobb–Douglas is:
quiz.why: For any Cobb–Douglas function σ = 1, a standard result.
With fixed proportions extra units of one input alone add nothing, giving L-shaped isoquants.

story.title: The ₹ budget for a bottling plant

scenes.text: Wages are ₹500 a day and machine rent is ₹1,000 a day. The plant wants 400 crates at least cost.
The answer lies where the isoquant touches the lowest isocost line.

steps.title: Isocost line
steps.body:
- C = wL + rK; slope −w/r.
- **Least-cost condition**: MRTS = w/r ⇔ MPL/w = MPK/r (equal output per rupee).
- Dual problem: maximise Q for a given C gives the same tangency.
- **Expansion path**: locus of tangencies as output rises; a straight ray for homothetic functions such as Cobb–Douglas.

steps.title: Solved: factor price change
steps.body:
Same function, wage rises to ₹1,000 (= r).

1. Now K/L = 1 ⇒ L = K = 400.
2. C = 1000 × 400 + 1000 × 400 = ₹8,00,000.
3. Firm substitutes capital for labour (L falls from 566 to 400) — the factor substitution effect.

steps.title: Exam framing
steps.body: Always write the two equations: (i) tangency MPL/MPK = w/r; (ii) the constraint (target output or budget). Solve simultaneously.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing MRTS = r/w.
- Forgetting that a corner solution occurs with perfect-substitute inputs.

statements.s: At the least-cost point, the marginal product per rupee is equal for all inputs.
statements.why: MPL/w = MPK/r.

statements.s: A rise in the wage, with output fixed, leads the firm to use more labour.
statements.why: It substitutes towards the relatively cheaper capital.

statements.s: For Cobb–Douglas, the expansion path is a straight line through the origin.
statements.why: The function is homothetic, so K/L depends only on w/r.

statements.s: The slope of the isocost line is −r/w with L on the horizontal axis.
statements.why: It is −w/r.

quiz.q: MPL = 20, MPK = 30, w = 10, r = 20. The firm should:
quiz.why: Labour gives 2 units per rupee versus 1.5 for capital, so shifting spending to labour lowers cost.

quiz.q: Q = L^0.5 K^0.5, w = r, Q = 100. Least-cost L is:
quiz.why: With w = r the firm sets K = L, so Q = L = 100.

options: least-cost input mixes as output changes
quiz.why: It joins the tangency points between isoquants and isocost lines as output expands.

lessons.title: Economies of scale and technical progress

scenes.text: An auto plant producing 3 lakh cars a year has far lower cost per car than a workshop making 300.
Specialised robots, bulk buying and cheaper finance all come with size.

steps.title: Sources of economies
steps.body:
- **Internal economies**: technical (indivisible machines, specialisation), managerial, marketing (bulk buying), financial (cheaper credit), risk-bearing.
- **Internal diseconomies**: coordination problems, bureaucracy.
- **External economies**: arise from industry growth — skilled labour pools, supplier networks, infrastructure (industrial clusters like Tiruppur knitwear).

steps.title: Technical progress
steps.body:
- Shifts isoquants toward the origin (same Q with fewer inputs).
- **Hicks classification** at a given K/L: labour-saving (raises MPK relative to MPL), capital-saving (raises MPL relative to MPK), neutral (MRTS unchanged).
- In Q = A L^α K^β, a rise in A is Hicks-neutral.

steps.title: Solved: effect of A
steps.body:
Q = A L^0.5 K^0.5 with L = 25, K = 36.

1. A = 2: Q = 2 × 5 × 6 = 60.
2. A rises 10% to 2.2: Q = 66 (+10%).
3. MRTS = K/L = 1.44 unchanged ⇒ neutral progress.

steps.title: Scale vs proportions
steps.body: Economies of scale relate to the long-run average cost curve; returns to scale relate to the production function. IRS implies economies of scale when input prices are constant, but economies can also come from cheaper input prices at scale (pecuniary economies).

statements.s: A skilled labour pool in an industrial cluster is an external economy.
statements.why: It benefits every firm in the industry, not just one firm's own scale.

statements.s: Hicks-neutral technical progress changes the MRTS at a given K/L.
statements.why: Neutral progress leaves MRTS unchanged.

statements.s: Bulk discounts on raw materials are a marketing/purchasing economy.
statements.why: Large buyers obtain lower input prices.

statements.s: Coordination problems in very large firms are a source of diseconomies of scale.
statements.why: Managerial diseconomies raise long-run average cost.

quiz.why: The same output now needs fewer inputs, so each isoquant moves inward.

quiz.q: Cheaper bank loans for large firms are:
quiz.why: Lower borrowing costs from size are internal financial economies.

quiz.q: In Q = A L^α K^β, a 5% rise in A raises Q by:
quiz.why: Q is proportional to A, so output rises by 5% at given inputs.

questions.why: Stage III is defined by negative marginal product of the variable input.

questions.why: Output per rupee must be equal across inputs.

questions.why: For a linearly homogeneous function L·MPL + K·MPK = Q.

questions.why: An indivisible machine is used more fully at larger output, lowering average cost.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Theory of costs and revenue
courses.summary: Economic versus accounting cost, short-run cost curves and their relationships, long-run average cost as an envelope, and revenue concepts with the profit-maximisation rule.
outcomes: Distinguish explicit, implicit, opportunity and sunk costs
Compute TFC, TVC, TC, AFC, AVC, ATC and MC from data or a cost function
Explain why MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minima
Derive the LAC as an envelope of SACs
Apply MR = MC with the second-order condition

story.title: The engineer who opened a café

scenes.text: Neha quits a ₹9 lakh-a-year job to run a café that shows an accounting profit of ₹6 lakh.
Counting the salary she gave up, her economic profit is −₹3 lakh.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Explicit costs**: actual payments (wages, rent, materials).
- **Implicit costs**: value of owner-supplied resources (own time, own capital, own premises).
- **Opportunity cost**: value of the next best alternative forgone.
- **Accounting profit** = revenue − explicit costs. **Economic profit** = revenue − explicit − implicit costs.
- **Normal profit**: the minimum return to keep the entrepreneur in the business; economic profit = 0.
- **Sunk cost**: already incurred and unrecoverable — irrelevant to forward-looking decisions.

steps.title: Solved: economic profit
steps.body:
Revenue ₹40 lakh; explicit costs ₹34 lakh; owner's forgone salary ₹9 lakh; interest forgone on own ₹10 lakh at 8% = ₹0.8 lakh.

1. Accounting profit = 40 − 34 = **₹6 lakh**.
2. Implicit = 9 + 0.8 = ₹9.8 lakh.
3. Economic profit = 6 − 9.8 = **−₹3.8 lakh** (below normal profit).

steps.title: Private vs social cost
steps.body: Social cost = private cost + external cost (e.g. pollution). Markets with external costs over-produce relative to the social optimum.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including sunk costs in a shutdown decision.
- Treating zero economic profit as a loss — it means normal returns are earned.

statements.s: Rent the owner could have earned from her own shop is an implicit cost.
statements.why: It is the value of an owner-supplied resource.

statements.s: Zero economic profit means the firm is making losses in the accounting sense.
statements.why: Accounting profit equals the implicit costs, so normal profit is earned.

statements.s: A non-refundable licence fee already paid should affect today's output decision.
statements.why: It is sunk and cannot be recovered whatever the firm does.

statements.s: Economic profit is always ≤ accounting profit.
statements.why: Implicit costs are non-negative.

quiz.q: Revenue ₹50, explicit cost ₹30, implicit cost ₹15. Economic profit:
quiz.why: Economic profit = 50 − 30 − 15 = ₹5.
Normal profit is the opportunity cost of entrepreneurship and is counted as a cost in economics.
Spent R&D cannot be recovered and so does not vary with future choices.

scenes.text: Rent and the tandoor's lease are fixed; dal, flour, gas and helpers vary with plates served.
Cost per plate first falls, then rises as the small kitchen gets crowded.

steps.title: Relationships
steps.body:
- TC = TFC + TVC. AFC = TFC/Q (falls continuously, rectangular hyperbola). AVC = TVC/Q. ATC = AFC + AVC.
- MC = ΔTC/ΔQ = ΔTVC/ΔQ (fixed cost does not affect MC).
- U-shaped AVC and MC follow from the law of variable proportions: MC = w/MPL, AVC = w/APL.
- **MC cuts AVC and ATC from below at their minimum points.** Min AVC occurs at a lower Q than min ATC.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking MC depends on fixed cost.
- Drawing MC cutting ATC at ATC's falling part.
- Saying AFC becomes zero — it approaches zero but never reaches it.

statements.s: MC passes through the minimum points of AVC and ATC.
statements.why: Average falls while marginal is below it and rises when marginal is above it.

statements.s: An increase in rent shifts the MC curve upward.
statements.why: Rent is fixed cost; it shifts ATC but not MC or AVC.

statements.s: Minimum AVC occurs at a smaller output than minimum ATC.
statements.why: Falling AFC keeps ATC falling after AVC has started rising.

statements.s: MC = w/MPL, so diminishing MP implies rising MC.
statements.why: Each extra unit needs more labour as MP falls.

quiz.q: TC = 50 + 4Q + Q². MC at Q = 3 is:
For the same function, ATC is minimised at Q =
quiz.why: ATC = 50/Q + 4 + Q is minimised where −50/Q² + 1 = 0, i.e. Q = √50.
AFC × Q = TFC is constant, so AFC traces a rectangular hyperbola.
A marginal unit cheaper than the average pulls the average down.

scenes.text: Before building, a cement maker can choose any plant size. Each size has its own short-run cost curve.
Hugging the lowest of all these curves gives the long-run average cost — the planning curve.

steps.title: LAC as an envelope
steps.body:
- In the long run all inputs vary. **LAC** is the lower envelope of short-run ATC curves; each SAC touches LAC at one point.
- U-shaped LAC reflects economies then diseconomies of scale (not diminishing returns).
- Only at LAC's minimum does the tangent SAC touch at its own minimum (**optimum plant**). To the left, LAC touches SACs on their falling parts; to the right, on their rising parts.
- **LMC** cuts LAC at its minimum; at that point SAC = SMC = LAC = LMC.

steps.title: Shapes in practice
steps.body: Empirical studies often find an **L-shaped LAC**: costs fall then stay flat over a wide range. The output at which LAC first reaches its minimum is the **minimum efficient scale (MES)** — important for market structure.

steps.title: Solved: LAC from a CRS function
steps.body:
Q = L^0.5 K^0.5, w = r = ₹100. Least-cost K = L = Q.

LTC = 100Q + 100Q = 200Q ⇒ LAC = LMC = **₹200**, constant — CRS gives a horizontal LAC.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Explaining the U-shaped LAC by the law of variable proportions.
- Claiming LAC joins the minimum points of all SACs.

statements.s: The LAC curve joins the minimum points of all short-run average cost curves.
statements.why: It is tangent to SACs; only the optimum plant is touched at its minimum.

statements.s: Constant returns to scale with fixed input prices give a horizontal LAC.
statements.why: Doubling output exactly doubles cost.

statements.s: Minimum efficient scale is the lowest output at which LAC is minimised.
statements.why: That is the definition of MES.

statements.s: LMC is above LAC where LAC is falling.
statements.why: LMC is below LAC while LAC falls.

quiz.q: LTC = 1,000Q − 20Q² + 0.2Q³. LAC is minimum at Q =
quiz.why: dLAC/dQ = −20 + 0.4Q = 0 gives Q = 50.

quiz.q: The U-shape of LAC is due to:
quiz.why: In the long run all inputs vary, so only scale effects shape LAC.
At the minimum of LAC the tangent SAC is also at its minimum, so all four coincide.

scenes.text: A Kanchipuram cooperative sells more sarees only by cutting price a little.
It keeps weaving until the extra revenue from one more saree just equals its extra cost.

steps.title: Revenue
steps.body:
- TR = P·Q; AR = TR/Q = P (AR curve = demand curve); MR = dTR/dQ.
- Price-taker: AR = MR = P (horizontal).
- Downward-sloping demand P = a − bQ: MR = a − 2bQ (same intercept, twice the slope).
- MR = P(1 − 1/|e|).

steps.title: Profit-maximisation conditions
steps.body:
π = TR − TC.
1. **First order**: MR = MC.
2. **Second order**: MC cuts MR from below (slope of MC > slope of MR).
3. **Short-run shutdown**: produce only if P ≥ AVC (cover variable cost).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting P = MC for a firm facing downward-sloping demand.
- Ignoring the second-order condition when MC has a falling section (two intersections).

statements.s: For linear demand P = a − bQ, MR has twice the slope of demand.
statements.why: TR = aQ − bQ² gives MR = a − 2bQ.

statements.s: A price-taking firm's MR equals the market price.
statements.why: Each extra unit sells at the same price.

statements.s: Profit is maximised wherever MR = MC, regardless of slopes.
statements.why: MC must cut MR from below; the other intersection is a profit minimum.

statements.s: A firm should shut down in the short run if price is below average total cost.
statements.why: It should keep producing as long as price covers average variable cost.

quiz.why: MR = 60 − 2Q = 20 gives Q = 20.

quiz.q: In the short run a firm shuts down when:
quiz.why: Below AVC, producing loses more than the fixed cost lost by shutting.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is best described as:
questions.why: It is the value of the best option given up.

For TC = 80 + 6Q + 2Q², MC at Q = 4:
ATC for TC = 80 + 6Q + 2Q² is minimised at Q =
questions.why: ATC = 80/Q + 6 + 2Q, minimised where 80/Q² = 2, so Q = √40.

questions.q: A rise in fixed cost affects:
questions.why: Only fixed-cost-based averages change.

questions.q: LAC is tangent to SAC on its falling part when:
questions.why: With economies of scale it pays to under-use a larger plant, so tangency is on the SAC's falling segment.

P = 120 − 3Q, MC = 30. Optimal Q:
questions.why: MR = 120 − 6Q = 30 gives Q = 15.

questions.why: All opportunity costs including normal profit are covered.

questions.why: MC is inversely related to MPL, so peak MPL gives minimum MC.

questions.q: L-shaped LAC suggests:
questions.why: Costs fall up to the minimum efficient scale and then stay flat.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Perfect competition and market welfare
courses.summary: Assumptions of perfect competition, short-run equilibrium and shutdown, the firm and industry supply curves, long-run equilibrium with free entry, constant/increasing/decreasing cost industries, and the efficiency of competitive markets.
outcomes: State the assumptions of perfect competition
Find the short-run profit-maximising output and shutdown point
Derive firm and industry supply curves
Explain long-run zero-profit equilibrium and the number of firms
Analyse allocative and productive efficiency and welfare

scenes.text: Ravi sells tomatoes at the Kolar mandi. Whatever he does, the price is set by thousands of sellers and buyers.
His only decision is how much to grow at that price.

steps.title: Assumptions
steps.body:
- Many buyers and sellers (each a price-taker).
- Homogeneous product.
- Free entry and exit (long run).
- Perfect information; perfect factor mobility.
- No transport costs or government price fixing.

Result: firm's demand curve is horizontal at the market price: P = AR = MR.

steps.title: Short-run cases
steps.body:
Produce where **P = MC** (MC rising):
- P > ATC: supernormal profit.
- P = ATC: normal profit (break-even point = min ATC).
- AVC ≤ P < ATC: loss, but keep producing (covers part of fixed cost).
- P < min AVC: **shut down** (loss = TFC). Min AVC is the **shutdown point**.

steps.title: Solved: three prices
steps.body:
TC = 128 + 2Q² (MC = 4Q, AVC = 2Q, ATC = 128/Q + 2Q). Min ATC at Q = 8 (ATC = 32). Min AVC = 0 at Q → 0.

- **P = 48**: Q = 12, TR = 576, TC = 128 + 288 = 416 ⇒ π = 160.
- **P = 32**: Q = 8, TR = 256, TC = 256 ⇒ π = 0 (break-even).
- **P = 16**: Q = 4, TR = 64, TC = 160 ⇒ loss 96 < TFC 128 ⇒ keep producing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shutting down whenever there is a loss.
- Using the falling part of MC as supply.

bands.text: Below ₹32 (min ATC): the firm makes a loss but still produces Q = P/4 because price exceeds AVC.
At ₹32: break-even — Q = 8 and only normal profit.
Above ₹32: supernormal profit; in the long run new firms enter and the price falls.

quiz.q: A perfectly competitive firm's MR curve is:
quiz.why: Each unit sells at the given market price, so MR = P.

quiz.q: For TC = 128 + 2Q² at P = 40, output is:
quiz.why: P = MC gives 40 = 4Q, so Q = 10.

quiz.q: The shutdown point is the minimum of:
quiz.why: Below min AVC the firm cannot even cover variable cost and should stop producing.

quiz.q: If AVC < P < ATC, the firm:
options: produces at a loss smaller than TFC
quiz.why: Revenue covers variable cost and part of fixed cost, so producing loses less than shutting down.

lessons.title: Supply curves of the firm and industry

story.title: From one farm to the mandi

scenes.text: Each farm's supply is its MC curve above the shutdown point.
Add the quantities of all farms at each price and you get the market supply.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
- **Short-run firm supply** = MC curve above min AVC (zero below).
- **Short-run industry supply** = horizontal sum of firm supplies (number of firms fixed).
- Producer surplus (SR) = TR − TVC = area above supply, below price.

steps.title: Solved: industry supply
steps.body:
100 identical firms, each with MC = 4Q (min AVC = 0).

1. Firm supply: q = P/4.
2. Industry: Q = 100 × P/4 = **25P**.
3. Market demand Qd = 1,500 − 25P ⇒ 25P = 1,500 − 25P ⇒ **P = 30**, Q = 750 (7.5 each).

steps.title: Solved: producer surplus
steps.body:
From the previous market, P = 30, Q = 750 along Q = 25P.

steps.title: Free entry and exit
steps.body:
- Profits ⇒ entry ⇒ supply shifts right ⇒ price falls. Losses ⇒ exit ⇒ price rises.
- Long-run equilibrium: **P = MR = SMC = SAC = LMC = min LAC**; economic profit = 0.
- Each firm produces at its minimum efficient scale.

steps.title: Long-run industry supply
steps.body:
- **Constant-cost industry**: input prices unchanged as industry grows ⇒ horizontal LR supply at min LAC.
- **Increasing-cost**: industry expansion raises input prices (external diseconomies) ⇒ upward-sloping LR supply.
- **Decreasing-cost**: external economies lower costs ⇒ downward-sloping LR supply.

steps.title: Solved: number of firms
steps.body:
Each firm: LTC = q³ − 10q² + 40q. Market demand Qd = 2,400 − 50P.

1. LAC = q² − 10q + 40; min at 2q − 10 = 0 ⇒ **q = 5**, LAC = 25 − 50 + 40 = **15**.
2. LR price P = 15 ⇒ Qd = 2,400 − 750 = 1,650.
3. Number of firms = 1,650/5 = **330**.

steps.body:

LR price stays ₹15; Q = 3,000 − 750 = 2,250 ⇒ firms = 450 (120 enter). Each still produces 5.

steps.title: Efficiency results
steps.body:
- **Allocative efficiency**: P = MC — the value of the last unit to buyers equals its cost.
- **Productive efficiency**: output at min LAC (long run).
- Competitive equilibrium **maximises total surplus** (CS + PS) when there are no externalities, public goods or information problems.
- Any deviation (tax, quota, ceiling) creates deadweight loss.

1. Demand price at 500: P = (1,500 − 500)/25 = 40; supply price: 500/25 = 20.
2. DWL = ½ × (40 − 20) × (750 − 500) = **₹2,500**.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: Efficiency says nothing about equity: a competitive outcome can be efficient yet highly unequal. Market failures (externalities, public goods, asymmetric information) are studied in Microeconomics II.

story.title: The only cable operator in town

scenes.text: A small town has one cable TV operator. She can raise the monthly fee — but some homes will cancel.
She picks the fee where one more subscriber adds as much revenue as cost.

steps.title: Sources and equilibrium
steps.body:
- **Barriers to entry**: control of key inputs, patents/licences, economies of scale (natural monopoly), network effects, legal restrictions.
- Monopolist faces the market demand curve; MR < P for Q > 0.
- **Equilibrium**: MR = MC with MC cutting MR from below; price read from demand.
- Monopolist always operates on the **elastic** part of demand (MR > 0 requires |e| > 1 when MC > 0).
- **No supply curve**: the same MC can be consistent with different prices depending on demand elasticity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting P = MC for a monopolist.
- Saying a monopolist charges 'the highest possible price' — it maximises profit, not price.
- Claiming monopolies always earn profit; losses are possible if demand is low.

statements.s: A profit-maximising monopolist with positive MC never produces on the inelastic part of demand.
statements.why: Inelastic demand means MR < 0, which cannot equal a positive MC.

statements.s: A monopolist has a well-defined supply curve like a competitive firm.
statements.why: Price depends on demand elasticity, so there is no one-to-one price–quantity supply relation.

statements.s: Monopoly output is lower than competitive output with the same costs.
statements.why: MR lies below demand, so MR = MC occurs at a smaller Q.

statements.s: The Lerner index of a perfectly competitive firm is 1.
statements.why: P = MC, so the index is 0.

quiz.why: When LAC falls over the whole range of market demand, one firm can supply most cheaply.

steps.title: Conditions and rule
steps.body:
- Conditions: market power, ability to separate buyers, no resale (arbitrage), different elasticities.
- **Rule**: MR1 = MR2 = MC. Price is higher in the **less elastic** market.
- From MR = P(1 − 1/|e|): P1/P2 = (1 − 1/|e2|)/(1 − 1/|e1|).

Profit = (50 − 20) × 60 = **₹1,800** < ₹2,000. Discrimination raises profit by ₹200; total output (60) is the same here because demands are linear.

lessons.title: First- and second-degree discrimination, two-part tariffs

scenes.text: In a bazaar, a seller tries to guess each customer's maximum willingness to pay.
Supermarkets instead offer 'buy 3, pay for 2' — letting buyers sort themselves.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **First-degree (perfect)**: each unit sold at the buyer's reservation price. MR = demand curve; output = competitive level; **no DWL**, but CS = 0 (all surplus to the seller).
- **Second-degree**: price varies with quantity or version (block pricing, bulk discounts); buyers self-select.
- **Third-degree**: different prices to identifiable groups.
- **Two-part tariff**: entry fee + per-unit charge (club membership, mobile plans). With identical consumers, set per-unit price = MC and entry fee = CS at that price.

steps.title: Solved: perfect discrimination
steps.body:
P = 120 − 2Q, MC = 20.

1. Sell until P = MC ⇒ Q = 50.
2. Profit (before FC) = area between demand and MC = ½ × 50 × (120 − 20) = **₹2,500**.
3. Compare single-price monopoly variable profit: (70 − 20) × 25 = ₹1,250.

steps.title: Solved: two-part tariff
steps.body:
Each consumer: P = 10 − q; MC = 2.

1. Per-unit price = 2 ⇒ q = 8.
2. Entry fee = CS = ½ × 8 × (10 − 2) = **₹32**.
3. Profit per consumer = 32 (per-unit price just covers MC).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying perfect discrimination is inefficient — it reaches the efficient output.
- Confusing bulk discounts (2nd degree) with student discounts (3rd degree).

statements.why: Output expands to where P = MC.

statements.why: The seller captures it all.

statements.why: Price depends on quantity bought.

statements.why: This maximises surplus, which the fee then captures.

steps.title: Regulating natural monopoly
steps.body:
- **Marginal-cost pricing** (P = MC): efficient but, since MC < AC when AC is falling, causes losses ⇒ needs subsidy.
- **Average-cost pricing** (P = AC): no subsidy, small DWL.
- **Price cap (RPI − X)** and rate-of-return regulation.
- Competition policy in India: Competition Act, 2002 enforced by the Competition Commission of India (abuse of dominance, anti-competitive agreements, mergers).

scenes.text: Hyderabad has hundreds of biryani outlets. Each recipe is a bit different, so each shop has a few loyal customers.
When one shop gets famous and profitable, new shops open nearby.

steps.title: Features and equilibrium
steps.body:
- Many firms, **differentiated products**, free entry, some selling costs (advertising).
- Each firm faces a downward-sloping but fairly elastic demand.
- **Short run**: MR = MC; profit or loss possible.
- **Long run**: entry shifts each firm's demand left until it is **tangent to LAC** ⇒ P = AC, zero economic profit, but P > MC.

steps.title: Excess capacity
steps.body: At the tangency, LAC is still falling ⇒ output is below min-LAC output. The gap is **excess capacity**; consumers 'pay' for variety. There is also allocative inefficiency (P > MC).

steps.title: Solved: short run
steps.body:
A café faces P = 40 − Q, TC = 50 + 10Q.

1. MR = 40 − 2Q = 10 ⇒ Q = 15, P = 25.
2. π = 25 × 15 − (50 + 150) = 375 − 200 = **₹175** > 0 ⇒ new cafés will enter in the long run until profit is zero.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming long-run output is at min LAC (that is perfect competition).
- Saying profit is zero because P = MC — it is zero because P = AC.

statements.s: In long-run monopolistic competition, the demand curve is tangent to LAC.
statements.why: Entry continues until economic profit is zero.

statements.s: Monopolistically competitive firms produce at minimum LAC in the long run.
statements.why: The tangency is on the falling part of LAC, leaving excess capacity.

statements.s: Product differentiation gives each firm some price-setting power.
statements.why: Loyal buyers do not all switch for a small price rise.

statements.s: In long-run equilibrium P = MC.
statements.why: P = AC but P > MC because demand slopes down.

quiz.q: Excess capacity means the firm produces:
quiz.why: At the tangency LAC is still falling, so output is less than the cost-minimising scale.

quiz.q: Long-run profit under monopolistic competition is:
quiz.why: Free entry removes economic profit.

quiz.q: Which market fits monopolistic competition best?
quiz.why: Restaurants are many, differentiated and easy to open.

scenes.text: Two firms dominate cement in a region. Each must decide capacity, guessing what the other will produce.
Strategic interdependence is the heart of oligopoly.

steps.title: Cournot (quantity) model
steps.body:
- Firms choose quantities simultaneously, each taking the rival's output as given.
- With P = a − b(q1 + q2) and MC = c: reaction function q1 = (a − c − b q2)/(2b).
- Symmetric Nash equilibrium: **q = (a − c)/(3b)** each; total 2(a − c)/(3b).
- With n firms: total = n(a − c)/[(n + 1)b] → competitive output as n → ∞.

steps.title: Solved: Stackelberg
steps.body:
Same market, firm 1 leads (moves first, knowing firm 2's reaction q2 = (90 − q1)/2).

1. Leader's demand: P = 120 − q1 − (90 − q1)/2 = 75 − q1/2.
2. MR = 75 − q1 = 30 ⇒ **q1 = 45**; q2 = 22.5; Q = 67.5; **P = 52.5**.
3. Profits: leader 22.5 × 45 = 1,012.5; follower 22.5 × 22.5 = 506.25. First-mover advantage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the rival's output as fixed when solving Stackelberg for the leader.
- Forgetting that Cournot total output lies between monopoly and competition.

Small n: Q = 90n/(n + 1); for n = 2, Q = 60 and P = 60; for n = 3, Q = 67.5 and P = 52.5.
Large n: total output approaches 90 and price approaches MC = 30 — the competitive outcome.

lessons.title: Bertrand and the kinked demand curve

scenes.text: Two airlines on the same route keep undercutting each other's fares.
In other markets, firms leave prices unchanged for years even when costs move.

steps.title: Bertrand (price) model
steps.body:
- Identical products, firms set prices simultaneously, constant MC, no capacity limits.
- Undercutting continues until **P = MC** — the **Bertrand paradox**: two firms give the competitive outcome.
- Resolutions: capacity constraints (Edgeworth), product differentiation, repeated interaction.

steps.title: Sweezy kinked demand
steps.body:
- Rivals **match price cuts** but **ignore price rises** ⇒ demand is elastic above the current price and inelastic below — a kink.
- MR has a **vertical gap** at the kink output; MC can move within the gap without changing price or output ⇒ **price rigidity**.
- Limitation: explains why price stays put, not how it was set.

steps.title: Solved: MR gap
steps.body:
Above kink: P = 60 − 0.5Q; below kink: P = 80 − 1.5Q (the two meet at Q = 20, P = 50).

1. MR above = 60 − Q ⇒ at Q = 20: **40**.
2. MR below = 80 − 3Q ⇒ at Q = 20: **20**.
3. Gap 20 to 40: any MC between ₹20 and ₹40 at Q = 20 leaves P = 50.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing the kink with rivals matching price rises.
- Saying the Bertrand paradox holds with differentiated products.

statements.s: With identical products and constant MC, Bertrand duopoly gives P = MC.
statements.why: Any price above MC would be undercut.

statements.s: In the kinked demand model, rivals match price increases.
statements.why: They match cuts and ignore increases.

statements.s: The kinked demand model explains how the initial price is determined.
statements.why: It only explains rigidity around an existing price.

statements.s: Product differentiation weakens the Bertrand paradox.
statements.why: Each firm keeps some buyers even at a higher price.

scenes.text: Oil exporters agree to cut output to raise prices.

steps.title: Cartels
steps.body:
- Joint profit maximisation: act as a multi-plant monopolist (MR = combined MC; allocate so MC equal across members).
- **Instability**: each member's MR at the cartel price exceeds its MC ⇒ incentive to cheat.
- Cheating is less likely with few members, easy monitoring, repeated interaction and credible punishment.
- Cartels are illegal under India's Competition Act, 2002 (anti-competitive agreements).

steps.title: Solved: cheating gain
steps.body:
P = 120 − Q, MC = 30, two firms sharing monopoly output 45 (22.5 each), P = 75.

1. Each firm's cartel profit = 45 × 22.5 = 1,012.5.
2. Firm 1 cheats, best response to q2 = 22.5: q1 = (90 − 22.5)/2 = 33.75.
3. P = 120 − 56.25 = 63.75; firm 1 profit = 33.75 × 33.75 = **1,139.06** > 1,012.5 ⇒ incentive to cheat.

steps.title: Price leadership
steps.body:
- **Dominant-firm model**: a large firm sets price; small fringe firms act as price-takers. Leader's residual demand = market demand − fringe supply; leader sets MR = MC on residual demand.
- **Barometric leadership**: a firm whose price changes reflect market conditions is followed.

scenes.text: Two suspects are questioned separately. Each can confess or stay silent.
Whatever the other does, confessing looks better — so both confess and both do worse.

steps.title: Elements
steps.body:
- **Players, strategies, payoffs**; normal form = payoff matrix (row player's payoff first).
- **Strictly dominant strategy**: better than every other strategy whatever rivals do.
- **Dominant-strategy equilibrium**: every player plays a dominant strategy.
- **Iterated elimination** of strictly dominated strategies can solve some games.

steps.title: Solved: prisoners' dilemma
steps.body:
Payoffs (years in jail, negative): 
- Both silent: (−1, −1); A confesses, B silent: (0, −10); A silent, B confesses: (−10, 0); both confess: (−5, −5).

1. If B silent: A prefers confess (0 > −1). If B confesses: A prefers confess (−5 > −10).
2. Confess is dominant for both ⇒ equilibrium **(confess, confess)** with (−5, −5).
3. Yet (silent, silent) gives both a better result ⇒ equilibrium is **not Pareto-optimal**.

steps.title: Economic examples
steps.body: Advertising wars between two firms, arms races, overfishing of a common lake, and cartel cheating all share the prisoners' dilemma structure: individual incentives undermine joint gains.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the column player's payoff as the first number.
- Assuming every game has a dominant strategy.

steps.title: Nash equilibrium
steps.body:
- A strategy profile where **no player can gain by changing strategy unilaterally**; each strategy is a best response to the others.
- Find pure NE by underlining best responses in the matrix; a cell with both underlined is a NE.
- A game can have zero, one or several pure NE (e.g. **battle of the sexes** has two).
- **Nash's theorem**: every finite game has at least one NE, possibly in mixed strategies.

steps.title: Mixed strategies
steps.body: A player randomises to make the **opponent indifferent** between their strategies. Solve: choose p so the opponent's expected payoffs from each pure strategy are equal.

steps.title: Solved: mixed NE
steps.body:
Zero-sum game, row payoffs (column gets the negative): UL = 3, UR = 0, DL = 0, DR = 1.

1. Row plays U with prob p. Column's payoff from L = −3p; from R = −(1 − p). Equal ⇒ 3p = 1 − p ⇒ **p = 0.25**.
2. Column plays L with prob q. Row's payoff from U = 3q; from D = 1 − q. Equal ⇒ **q = 0.25**.
3. Value of the game to row = 3 × 0.25 = **0.75**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing a player's mixing probability to make *that player* indifferent — it is chosen to make the *opponent* indifferent.
- Assuming NE must be efficient.

statements.s: Battle of the sexes has two pure-strategy Nash equilibria.
statements.why: Both coordinating outcomes are mutual best responses.

statements.s: Matching pennies has a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.
statements.why: It has only a mixed equilibrium with each side playing 50:50.

statements.s: At a Nash equilibrium, no player can gain by deviating alone.
statements.why: Each strategy is a best response to the others.

statements.s: A dominant-strategy equilibrium is also a Nash equilibrium.
statements.why: Dominant strategies are best responses to everything, including each other.

quiz.why: Row is indifferent when 3q = 1 − q, giving q = 0.25.

scenes.text: A supermarket chain threatens a price war if a rival opens next door.
Once the rival has opened, would the war really pay? If not, the threat is empty.

steps.title: Extensive form
steps.body:
- Game tree: decision nodes, branches, payoffs at terminal nodes.
- **Backward induction**: solve the last mover's choice first, then move up the tree.
- **Subgame-perfect equilibrium (SPE)**: a NE in every subgame — rules out **non-credible threats**.
- **Commitment** (e.g. sunk capacity) can make a threat credible.

steps.title: Solved: entry deterrence
steps.body:
Entrant: Enter or Stay out (stay out ⇒ (0, 10) for entrant, incumbent). If Enter, incumbent: Fight ⇒ (−2, 2) or Accommodate ⇒ (3, 5).

1. Last stage: incumbent compares 2 (fight) vs 5 (accommodate) ⇒ **accommodate**.
2. Entrant anticipates 3 > 0 ⇒ **enters**.
3. SPE: (Enter, Accommodate). The NE (Stay out, Fight) relies on a non-credible threat.

steps.title: Solved: commitment
steps.body: Suppose the incumbent first sinks ₹4 in extra capacity that pays only in a fight: fight now gives 2 + 4 = 6 > accommodate 5 − 0 = 5. Fighting becomes credible, the entrant expects −2 and **stays out**; incumbent earns 10 − 4 = 6 > 5. Commitment pays.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Solving a game tree from the top down.
- Accepting every Nash equilibrium of a sequential game — only subgame-perfect ones survive.

statements.s: Backward induction starts from the final decision node.
statements.why: Earlier movers anticipate later best responses.

statements.s: A threat that the threatener would not want to carry out is non-credible.
statements.why: Subgame perfection rejects it.

statements.s: Every Nash equilibrium of a sequential game is subgame perfect.
statements.why: Some NE rely on threats off the equilibrium path.

statements.s: Sunk investment can make a threat credible.
statements.why: It changes the incumbent's payoffs from fighting.

quiz.why: The incumbent prefers accommodating once entry happens, so the entrant enters.

Neither starts a price war — tomorrow matters.

steps.title: Finite vs infinite repetition
steps.body:
- **Finitely repeated** PD with a known last round: backward induction ⇒ defect every round.
- **Infinitely repeated** (or uncertain end): cooperation can be sustained by **trigger strategies** if players are patient.
- **Grim trigger**: cooperate until the rival defects, then defect forever.
- **Tit-for-tat**: copy the rival's previous move.

steps.title: Solved: discount-factor condition
steps.body:
Per-round payoffs: cooperate 6, cheat once 9, punishment 3 forever. Discount factor δ.

1. Cooperate: 6/(1 − δ).
2. Cheat: 9 + 3δ/(1 − δ).
3. Cooperate if 6 ≥ 9(1 − δ) + 3δ ⇒ 6 ≥ 9 − 6δ ⇒ **δ ≥ 0.5**.

steps.title: Folk theorem (idea)
steps.body: With sufficiently patient players, many outcomes — including full cooperation — can be sustained as equilibria of an infinitely repeated game.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming cooperation in a finitely repeated PD with known end.
- Forgetting the discount factor when comparing payoff streams.

bands.text: Impatient: the one-time gain from cheating (3) outweighs the future loss — cooperation breaks down.
δ = 0.5: exactly indifferent between cooperating and cheating.
Patient: future losses from punishment outweigh the gain — grim trigger sustains cooperation.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Factor markets and distribution
courses.summary: Marginal productivity theory, derived demand for labour, labour supply and the backward-bending curve, monopsony and minimum wages, economic rent and quasi-rent, and theories of interest and profit.
outcomes: Derive the firm's labour demand from MRP or VMP
Explain the backward-bending labour supply curve
Solve monopsony wage and employment
Distinguish economic rent, transfer earnings and quasi-rent
Summarise classical, loanable funds and liquidity preference theories of interest and risk/innovation theories of profit

scenes.text: An Assam tea estate pays pluckers ₹250 a day. Each extra plucker adds less tea than the last.
The estate hires until the value of the last plucker's tea equals her wage.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- Factor demand is **derived demand** — it depends on demand for the output.
- **VMP** = P × MPL (competitive output market). **MRP** = MR × MPL (general).
- Hiring rule (competitive labour market): **MRP = w**. The downward-sloping part of MRP below ARP's maximum is the firm's labour demand.
- Elasticity of labour demand is higher when output demand is elastic, substitutes for labour are easy, labour's cost share is large, and in the long run.

steps.title: Solved: monopoly in the output market
steps.body:
Q = 10L and product demand P = 100 − Q/10, so P = 100 − L.

1. TR = P × Q = (100 − L)(10L) = 1,000L − 10L².
2. MRP = dTR/dL = **1,000 − 20L**.
3. With w = ₹400: 1,000 − 20L = 400 ⇒ **L = 30**.
4. VMP at L = 30 = P × MP = 70 × 10 = 700 > MRP (400): output-market power reduces hiring.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using VMP when the firm has output-market power (use MRP).
- Forgetting that labour demand shifts when output price changes.

statements.s: Demand for labour is a derived demand.
statements.why: Firms want workers for the output they produce.

statements.s: A competitive firm hires labour until VMP = w.
statements.why: The last worker's contribution to revenue equals her wage.

statements.s: A rise in the price of the output shifts labour demand to the left.
statements.why: Higher P raises VMP at each L, shifting demand right.

statements.s: MRP is greater than VMP when the firm is a monopolist in the output market.
statements.why: MR < P, so MRP < VMP.

quiz.q: P = ₹20, MP of the 5th worker = 15, wage ₹250. The 5th worker should be:
quiz.why: VMP = 20 × 15 = ₹300 exceeds the ₹250 wage, so hiring her adds ₹50 to profit.

quiz.q: Labour demand is more elastic when:
quiz.why: Easy substitution lets firms cut labour sharply when wages rise.

story.title: The only factory in the town

scenes.text: A sugar mill is the only big employer in its taluka. To hire more, it must raise wages for everyone.
So it hires fewer workers at a lower wage than a competitive market would.

steps.title: Labour supply
steps.body:
- Individual chooses between income and leisure; a wage rise has a substitution effect (work more) and an income effect (leisure is normal ⇒ work less).
- At high wages the income effect may dominate ⇒ **backward-bending supply curve**.
- Market supply is normally upward sloping.

steps.title: Monopsony
steps.body:
- Single buyer of labour faces upward-sloping supply w(L).
- **Marginal expenditure** ME = d(wL)/dL > w.
- Hire where **MRP = ME**; pay the wage from the supply curve ⇒ L and w below competitive levels.
- A minimum wage between the monopsony and competitive wage can **raise both wage and employment**.

steps.title: Solved: monopsony
steps.body:
Supply w = 10 + L, MRP = 100 − 2L.

1. Total wage bill = (10 + L)L ⇒ ME = 10 + 2L.
2. MRP = ME: 100 − 2L = 10 + 2L ⇒ **L = 22.5**, w = **32.5**.
3. Competitive: 100 − 2L = 10 + L ⇒ L = 30, w = 40.
4. Minimum wage ₹40 ⇒ ME = 40 up to L = 30 ⇒ hire 30 at ₹40 — both rise.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paying the monopsony wage equal to MRP — the wage comes from the supply curve, below MRP.
- Claiming minimum wages always reduce employment.

activity.label: Minimum wage (₹) in the monopsony example

bands.text: Below ₹32.5: non-binding — the mill pays ₹32.5 and hires 22.5.
Between ₹32.5 and ₹40: both the wage and employment rise (employment = w − 10).
Above ₹40: employment falls along MRP (L = (100 − w)/2), so unemployment appears.

quiz.q: For supply w = 20 + 2L, marginal expenditure is:
quiz.why: Wage bill = 20L + 2L², so ME = 20 + 4L.

quiz.q: A backward-bending supply curve arises when:
options: income effect dominates at high wages
quiz.why: At high wages people buy more leisure with their higher income, working fewer hours.

quiz.q: With the monopsony example, a minimum wage of ₹36 leads to employment of:
quiz.why: At ₹36 the supply curve gives L = 36 − 10 = 26, and MRP at 26 (48) exceeds 36, so 26 are hired.

scenes.text: A star batsman would play for a modest fee if cricket were his only option.
Everything above that fee is economic rent — payment for scarcity.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Ricardian rent**: surplus from land due to differences in fertility/location; no-rent (marginal) land earns zero.
- **Modern (economic) rent**: earnings above **transfer earnings** (the minimum needed to keep a factor in its current use).
- Perfectly inelastic supply ⇒ entire earnings are rent; perfectly elastic ⇒ all transfer earnings.
- **Quasi-rent** (Marshall): short-run surplus over variable cost to factors fixed in the short run (machines) = TR − TVC.

steps.title: Solved: rent vs transfer earnings
steps.body:
An engineer earns ₹18 lakh; her best alternative is ₹12 lakh.

Transfer earnings = **₹12 lakh**; economic rent = **₹6 lakh**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 'rent' to mean only house rent.
- Treating quasi-rent as long-run — it disappears as supply adjusts.

statements.s: If factor supply is perfectly inelastic, all its earnings are economic rent.
statements.why: No payment is needed to keep it in use.

statements.s: Marginal land earns positive Ricardian rent.
statements.why: By definition, no-rent land earns zero.

statements.s: Quasi-rent is TR minus TVC in the short run.
statements.why: It is the return to factors fixed in the short run.

statements.s: Transfer earnings are the minimum payment needed to keep a factor in its present use.
statements.why: That is the definition.

quiz.q: A doctor earns ₹30 lakh; best alternative ₹20 lakh. Economic rent:
quiz.why: Rent = earnings − transfer earnings = 30 − 20 = ₹10 lakh.
More fertile land yields a surplus over the marginal land.
Quasi-rent = 80 − 50 = 30.

scenes.text: Savers want a reward for waiting; borrowers will pay for funds that earn returns.
Entrepreneurs who bear uncertainty and innovate claim the residual — profit.

steps.title: Theories of interest
steps.body:
- **Classical**: interest is set where saving (reward for abstinence/waiting) equals investment.
- **Loanable funds** (Robertson, Ohlin): supply = saving + dishoarding + new bank credit; demand = investment + hoarding.
- **Keynes' liquidity preference**: interest is the reward for parting with liquidity; set by money demand (transactions, precautionary, speculative) and money supply.
- Nominal vs real: real ≈ nominal − expected inflation (Fisher).

steps.title: Theories of profit
steps.body:
- **Knight**: profit is the reward for bearing **uncertainty** (non-insurable), not risk (insurable).
- **Schumpeter**: profit arises from **innovation** — new products, processes, markets — and is competed away by imitation.
- **Hawley**: reward for risk-taking.
- **Clark**: profit arises in a dynamic economy from changes.

steps.title: Solved: Fisher equation
steps.body:
Nominal interest on a fixed deposit 7%; expected inflation 5%.

Real rate ≈ 7 − 5 = **2%**. Exact: (1.07/1.05) − 1 = **1.90%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing Knight's risk (insurable) with uncertainty (not insurable).
- Treating Keynes' theory as a theory of saving — it is a monetary theory of interest.

statements.s: Knight linked profit to uninsurable uncertainty.
statements.why: Insurable risks become costs; uncertainty earns profit.

statements.s: Schumpeter's innovation profits persist forever.
statements.why: Imitation competes them away until the next innovation.

statements.s: In Keynes' theory, interest is the reward for parting with liquidity.
statements.why: It is determined by money demand and supply.

statements.s: Loanable funds theory includes bank credit in the supply of funds.
statements.why: Supply = saving + dishoarding + new bank credit.

quiz.why: Real ≈ nominal − expected inflation = 3%.

quiz.why: Schumpeter saw innovating entrepreneurs as the source of profit and economic development.

quiz.q: The speculative demand for money is part of:
quiz.why: Keynes added the speculative motive linked to expected bond prices.

questions.why: Value of marginal product is output price times marginal product.

questions.why: VMPs are 480, 360, 240 and 120, so only the first two workers add at least ₹300 each.

questions.why: The income effect dominates and workers take more leisure.

questions.why: It is the surplus over the minimum required to keep the factor in use.

questions.q: Quasi-rent applies to factors that are:
questions.why: Marshall used it for short-run returns to machines and other temporarily fixed factors.

Profit as reward for uncertainty bearing is due to:
questions.why: Frank Knight distinguished uninsurable uncertainty from insurable risk.

questions.why: Hiring one more worker raises the wage for all, so marginal expenditure exceeds the wage.

courses.title: Unit 5 · General equilibrium, welfare and market failure
courses.summary: Exchange and production in the Edgeworth box, Pareto efficiency, the two fundamental welfare theorems, social welfare functions, and the main market failures — externalities, public goods and asymmetric information — with policy responses.
outcomes: Explain Pareto efficiency in exchange, production and product mix
State the first and second welfare theorems
Solve externality problems and the Pigouvian tax
Find the efficient quantity of a public good
Explain adverse selection, moral hazard and the Coase theorem

scenes.text: Asha has many biscuits and little juice; Bilal has the opposite.
They trade until no further swap can make one happier without making the other sadder.

steps.title: Efficiency conditions
steps.body:
- **Pareto efficient**: no reallocation can make someone better off without making someone worse off.
- **Exchange**: MRS^A_xy = MRS^B_xy — tangency of ICs in the Edgeworth box; the locus is the **contract curve**.
- **Production**: MRTS^X_LK = MRTS^Y_LK — gives the production possibility frontier.
- **Product mix**: MRT_xy (slope of PPF) = MRS_xy.
- Under perfect competition all three hold because everyone faces the same prices: MRS = Px/Py, MRTS = w/r, MRT = MCx/MCy = Px/Py.

steps.title: Solved: is this allocation efficient?
steps.body:
A has U = xy at (2, 8); B has U = xy at (6, 4).

1. MRS^A = y/x = 4; MRS^B = 4/6 = 0.67.
2. Not equal ⇒ **not Pareto efficient**.
3. A values x more (4 > 0.67), so A should get more x from B in exchange for y — both gain.

steps.title: Welfare theorems
steps.body:
- **First**: every competitive equilibrium (with no externalities, complete markets) is Pareto efficient.
- **Second**: any Pareto-efficient allocation can be reached as a competitive equilibrium after suitable lump-sum redistribution of endowments (with convex preferences and technology).
- Efficiency ≠ equity; choosing among efficient points needs a **social welfare function** (utilitarian W = ΣUi; Rawlsian W = min Ui).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Pareto efficiency implies fairness.
- Applying the first welfare theorem when externalities are present.

statements.s: On the contract curve, the two consumers' MRS are equal.
statements.why: It is the locus of tangencies of their indifference curves.

statements.s: A Pareto-efficient allocation must be equitable.
statements.why: Giving everything to one person can be Pareto efficient.

statements.s: The second welfare theorem uses lump-sum transfers to reach a chosen efficient point.
statements.why: Redistribute endowments, then let markets work.

statements.s: The Rawlsian welfare function maximises the sum of utilities.
statements.why: It maximises the utility of the worst-off person.

quiz.why: If MRS differed, a trade would benefit both consumers.

quiz.q: The first welfare theorem says competitive equilibrium is:
quiz.why: Under its assumptions, no one can be made better off without harming another.

quiz.q: Product-mix efficiency requires MRT to equal:
quiz.why: The rate at which the economy can transform goods must match the rate consumers are willing to swap them.

story.title: The dyeing unit and the river

scenes.text: A textile dyeing unit releases effluent into a river used by downstream farmers.
Its private costs ignore the farmers' losses, so it produces too much.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Negative externality**: MSC = MPC + MEC > MPC ⇒ market over-produces.
- **Positive externality** (education, vaccination): MSB > MPB ⇒ under-production.
- **Pigouvian tax** = MEC at the efficient output; **Pigouvian subsidy** for positive externalities.
- Other remedies: regulation/standards, tradable permits (cap-and-trade), assigning property rights.

steps.title: Solved: Pigouvian tax
steps.body:
Demand P = 100 − Q, MPC = 20 + Q, MEC = 10 per unit.

1. Market: 100 − Q = 20 + Q ⇒ **Q = 40, P = 60**.
2. Social: 100 − Q = 30 + Q ⇒ **Q* = 35, P = 65**.
3. DWL = ½ × 10 × (40 − 35) = **25**.
4. A tax of ₹10 per unit moves the market to Q* = 35.

steps.title: Coase theorem
steps.body: If property rights are well defined and **transaction costs are low**, private bargaining reaches the efficient outcome whoever holds the rights; the assignment only affects distribution. It fails with many parties or high bargaining costs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting the Pigou tax equal to the price.
- Claiming Coase works with millions of affected people.

statements.s: With a negative externality, market output exceeds the efficient output.
statements.why: Firms ignore external costs.

statements.s: Vaccination creates a positive externality.
statements.why: Others gain from reduced disease spread.

statements.s: The Coase theorem needs low transaction costs.
statements.why: Bargaining must be cheap enough to happen.

statements.s: A Pigouvian tax should equal the firm's average cost.
statements.why: It should equal marginal external cost at the efficient output.

quiz.q: In the example, the efficient quantity is:
quiz.why: Setting demand equal to MSC = 30 + Q gives Q = 35.

options: capping total emissions and letting firms trade
quiz.why: The cap fixes the total while trading lets low-cost abaters cut most.
Buyers ignore benefits to others, so private demand is too low.

scenes.text: Once a streetlight is up, everyone on the lane benefits, and no one can be stopped from seeing.
Each household hopes someone else will pay — the free-rider problem.

steps.title: Characteristics
steps.body:
- **Non-rival**: one person's use does not reduce another's.
- **Non-excludable**: cannot prevent non-payers from benefiting.
- Pure public goods: national defence, lighthouse, street lighting. **Club goods**: excludable, non-rival (cable TV). **Common resources**: rival, non-excludable (fish stocks).
- **Samuelson condition**: provide where **ΣMB_i = MC** — vertical summation of individual demands.

steps.title: Solved: efficient provision
steps.body:
Two residents: MB1 = 50 − Q, MB2 = 30 − Q. MC = 40.

1. ΣMB = 80 − 2Q (for Q ≤ 30).
2. 80 − 2Q = 40 ⇒ **Q* = 20**.
3. At Q = 20, MB1 = 30, MB2 = 10 — Lindahl prices 30 and 10 sum to MC.

steps.title: Solved: free riding
steps.body: Acting alone, resident 1 buys where MB1 = MC: 50 − Q = 40 ⇒ Q = 10; resident 2 buys none (MB2 < 40 at all Q). Private provision = 10 < 20 ⇒ under-provision.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Summing public-good demands horizontally.
- Calling everything provided by government a public good (e.g. rail tickets are excludable).

statements.s: Public goods are both non-rival and non-excludable.
statements.why: These two features define a pure public good.

statements.s: Fish in the open sea are a pure public good.
statements.why: They are rival, so they are a common resource.

statements.s: Efficient public-good provision sums marginal benefits vertically.
statements.why: All users enjoy the same unit.

statements.s: Free riding leads to over-provision of public goods by markets.
statements.why: It leads to under-provision.

quiz.q: MB1 = 40 − Q, MB2 = 20 − Q, MC = 30. Efficient Q:
quiz.why: ΣMB = 60 − 2Q = 30 gives Q = 15, where both MBs are positive.

quiz.q: A toll road with little traffic is closest to a:
quiz.why: It is excludable through tolls but non-rival until congested.

quiz.q: Tragedy of the commons applies to goods that are:
quiz.why: Open access plus rivalry leads to overuse.

scenes.text: Sellers know whether their car is a gem or a lemon; buyers do not.
Buyers offer an average price, good cars leave, and the market shrinks.

steps.title: Problems
steps.body:
- **Adverse selection** (hidden type, before the deal): Akerlof's lemons; health insurance attracts high-risk buyers.
- **Moral hazard** (hidden action, after the deal): insured drivers become careless; bailouts encourage risk-taking.
- **Principal–agent problem**: managers (agents) may not maximise shareholders' (principals') value.

steps.title: Solved: lemons unravelling
steps.body:
Half the cars are good (worth ₹4 lakh to buyers, sellers accept ₹3.5 lakh); half are lemons (worth ₹2 lakh, sellers accept ₹1.5 lakh).

1. Buyers can't tell ⇒ pay expected value = 0.5 × 4 + 0.5 × 2 = ₹3 lakh.
2. Good-car owners need ₹3.5 lakh ⇒ withdraw.
3. Buyers learn only lemons remain ⇒ price falls to ₹2 lakh ⇒ **only lemons are traded**.

steps.title: Remedies
steps.body:
- **Signalling** (Spence): warranties, education degrees, brand reputation.
- **Screening**: insurers' deductibles and medical tests.
- Mandatory insurance pools, certification, disclosure rules.
- For moral hazard: co-payments, deductibles, performance-linked pay, monitoring.

- Mixing up adverse selection (hidden information before) with moral hazard (hidden action after).
- Thinking signalling must be productive — it works if it is costlier for low types.

uni-ba-eco-public-finance.title: Public Finance — government, taxes, spending, debt
uni-ba-eco-public-finance.description: Role of government, public goods and externalities, principles and incidence of taxation, public expenditure and debt, fiscal federalism and the Indian tax system. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA (Hons) Economics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Role of government and public goods
courses.summary: Musgrave's three branches, market failure as a rationale for intervention, public goods and the Samuelson and Lindahl solutions, merit goods, and public choice critiques of government failure.
outcomes: Explain Musgrave's allocation, distribution and stabilisation functions
Identify market failures that justify intervention
Solve for efficient public-good provision and Lindahl prices
Distinguish merit goods and public goods
Explain government failure and the median voter theorem

scenes.text: The government builds roads markets would under-provide — allocation.
It taxes the rich more and funds pensions — distribution. And it fights recessions — stabilisation.

steps.title: Functions
steps.body:
- **Allocation**: provide public goods, correct externalities and other market failures.
- **Distribution**: adjust the distribution of income and wealth (progressive taxes, transfers).
- **Stabilisation**: maintain high employment, price stability, external balance (fiscal policy, automatic stabilisers).
- Musgrave (1959) treated them as separate 'branches' for analysis.

steps.title: Rationale: market failure
steps.body: Public goods, externalities, natural monopoly, asymmetric information, incomplete markets, unemployment/inflation, and equity concerns.

steps.title: Examples in India
steps.body: Allocation: national highways, defence. Distribution: progressive income tax, NFSA, MGNREGA. Stabilisation: counter-cyclical spending in 2020–21.

statements.s: Musgrave's three functions are allocation, distribution and stabilisation.
statements.why: That is his classification.

statements.s: Progressive taxation relates mainly to the stabilisation function.
statements.why: It is mainly distribution, though it also stabilises automatically.

statements.s: Correcting externalities falls under allocation.
statements.why: It improves resource allocation.

statements.s: Natural monopoly is a type of market failure.
statements.why: Single-firm supply leads to underproduction or high prices.

quiz.why: It aims at employment and price stability.

quiz.q: Musgrave's 'Theory of Public Finance' was published in:
quiz.why: Richard Musgrave, 1959.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a market failure?
quiz.why: Perfect competition yields efficiency under standard assumptions.

scenes.text: Two families value a cleaner pond differently.
Lindahl suggested each pays a share equal to their marginal benefit.

steps.title: Conditions
steps.body:
- **Samuelson condition**: ΣMRS_i = MRT (ΣMB = MC) — vertical summation.
- **Lindahl equilibrium**: each person pays a personalised tax share ti with Σti = 1, such that at those prices everyone demands the same quantity; ti·MC = MBi.
- Problem: people may **under-report** preferences (free-rider) — mechanism design (Clarke–Groves tax) addresses truthful revelation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Summing horizontally.
- Forgetting that Lindahl shares must sum to one.

statements.s: Samuelson's condition sums MRS across individuals.
statements.why: Everyone consumes the same unit.

statements.s: Lindahl prices are the same for all individuals.
statements.why: They are personalised by marginal benefit.

statements.s: Free-riding leads people to under-state their valuation.
statements.why: They hope others pay.

statements.s: Lindahl tax shares sum to one.
statements.why: Together they cover marginal cost.

quiz.why: They make honest reporting a dominant strategy.

scenes.text: PM POSHAN provides hot meals in government schools.
Society values children's nutrition and attendance more than parents alone might.

steps.title: Merit and demerit goods
steps.body:
- **Merit goods** (Musgrave): society judges consumption should exceed what individuals choose (education, vaccination, nutrition) — may reflect information gaps or paternalism.
- **Demerit goods**: tobacco, alcohol — discouraged via taxes and regulation.
- Merit goods are often rival and excludable — not public goods.

steps.title: Solved: Pigouvian subsidy
steps.body:
Vaccination: private MB = 100 − Q, MC = 40, external benefit 20 per dose.

- Market: 100 − Q = 40 ⇒ Q = 60.
- Social: 120 − Q = 40 ⇒ **Q* = 80**.
- A subsidy of ₹20 per dose achieves Q* (cost to budget = 20 × 80 = ₹1,600).

steps.title: Instruments
steps.body: Taxes/subsidies (price), regulation/standards (quantity), tradable permits, direct provision, information campaigns, nudges.

statements.s: Education is a pure public good.
statements.why: It is rival and excludable; it is a merit good.

statements.s: Tobacco taxes target a demerit good.
statements.why: They discourage harmful consumption.

statements.s: A Pigouvian subsidy equals the marginal external benefit at the efficient output.
statements.why: It aligns private and social benefits.

statements.s: Merit goods were defined by Musgrave.
statements.why: He introduced the concept.

quiz.why: 90 − Q = 30 gives Q = 60.
Equal to the marginal external benefit.
Society seeks to discourage its consumption.

scenes.text: Politicians want votes; bureaucrats want bigger budgets; lobbies want favours.
Public choice theory applies economics to these actors.

steps.title: Ideas
steps.body:
- **Median voter theorem**: with single-peaked preferences over one issue, majority voting picks the median voter's preferred outcome.
- **Arrow's impossibility theorem**: no voting rule satisfies all of a set of reasonable conditions for three or more options.
- **Condorcet paradox**: majority preferences can cycle.
- **Government failure**: rent-seeking, logrolling, bureaucratic budget maximisation (Niskanen), short-termism, capture.

steps.title: Solved: median voter
steps.body:
Five voters' preferred spending on a park (₹ lakh): 10, 20, 35, 50, 80.

Median = **35** ⇒ majority voting selects ₹35 lakh (any proposal beats alternatives further from 35). Mean = 39 differs.

steps.title: Solved: Condorcet cycle
steps.body:
Voter 1: A > B > C; Voter 2: B > C > A; Voter 3: C > A > B.

A beats B (1, 3), B beats C (1, 2), C beats A (2, 3) ⇒ **cycle**, no Condorcet winner.

statements.s: The median voter theorem needs single-peaked preferences.
statements.why: Otherwise cycles may occur.

statements.s: Arrow's theorem shows a perfect voting rule exists.
statements.why: It shows none satisfies all conditions.

statements.s: Rent-seeking is spending resources to obtain transfers rather than create value.
statements.why: That is its definition.

statements.s: Niskanen modelled bureaucrats as budget maximisers.
statements.why: His 1971 model.

quiz.why: The fourth of seven values is 40.

quiz.why: Pairwise majorities can cycle.
Legislators exchange votes on different bills.

questions.why: Redistribution through taxes and transfers.

questions.why: Vertical sum of marginal benefits equals marginal cost.

Merit goods are:

questions.why: Musgrave's definition.

Median voter outcome with 12, 18, 30, 45, 70:

questions.why: Social choice from individual rankings.
