courses.title: Unit 2 · Principles, incidence and efficiency of taxation
courses.summary: Canons of taxation, benefit and ability-to-pay principles, progressive, proportional and regressive taxes, tax incidence and shifting, excess burden, the Ramsey rule and the Laffer curve.
outcomes: State Adam Smith's canons and the ability-to-pay principle
Classify taxes by average and marginal rates
Compute tax incidence and excess burden
Apply the Ramsey inverse-elasticity rule
Explain the Laffer curve

scenes.text: Adam Smith listed four qualities in 1776: equality, certainty, convenience, economy.
Modern debates add efficiency, simplicity and flexibility.

steps.title: Canons
steps.body:
- **Smith's canons**: equality (in proportion to ability), certainty, convenience (of payment), economy (low collection cost).
- Later additions: productivity, elasticity/buoyancy, flexibility, simplicity, diversity.
- **Benefit principle**: pay according to benefits received (tolls, user charges).
- **Ability-to-pay**: **horizontal equity** (equals treated equally) and **vertical equity** (more able pay more); sacrifice theories — equal absolute, equal proportional, equal marginal (least aggregate) sacrifice.

steps.title: Progressivity
steps.body:
- **Progressive**: average tax rate rises with income.
- **Proportional**: constant average rate.
- **Regressive**: average rate falls with income (many indirect taxes on necessities are regressive relative to income).
- **Tax buoyancy** = %Δ tax revenue / %Δ GDP (includes effect of rate changes); **elasticity** excludes discretionary changes.

steps.title: Solved: classify
steps.body:
Income 1 lakh pays ₹5,000; 10 lakh pays ₹80,000.

Average rates: 5% and 8% ⇒ **progressive**.

Buoyancy: revenue +12% when nominal GDP +10% ⇒ buoyancy = **1.2**.

statements.s: A tax is progressive if its average rate rises with income.
statements.why: That is the definition.

statements.s: Highway tolls follow the ability-to-pay principle.
statements.why: They follow the benefit principle.

statements.s: Horizontal equity means people with equal ability pay equal tax.
statements.why: Equals treated equally.

statements.s: Economy as a canon means low collection costs.
statements.why: Smith's fourth canon.

quiz.q: Income ₹4 lakh pays ₹20,000; ₹8 lakh pays ₹32,000. The tax is:
quiz.why: Average rates fall from 5% to 4%.
Taxing highest incomes first minimises total sacrifice.

story.title: Who really pays the fuel tax?

scenes.text: Fuel taxes are collected from oil companies.
But taxi drivers and commuters bear much of the burden through higher pump prices.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Impact**: who is legally liable. **Incidence**: who finally bears the burden. **Shifting**: forward (to buyers) or backward (to input suppliers).
- Partial equilibrium: buyers' share = Es/(Es + |Ed|); sellers' share = |Ed|/(Es + |Ed|).
- Statutory incidence does not matter for economic incidence (in competitive markets).
- General equilibrium: Harberger model — a tax on capital in one sector may be borne by all capital.

steps.title: Solved: incidence
steps.body:
Qd = 100 − P, Qs = P. Tax t = 10 on sellers.

1. Supply becomes Qs = P − 10 ⇒ 100 − P = P − 10 ⇒ Pb = 55, Ps = 45, Q = 45.
2. Pre-tax P = 50 ⇒ buyers bear **5**, sellers **5** (equal slopes).
3. Revenue = 450.

steps.title: Solved: elasticity shares
steps.body:
Es = 2, |Ed| = 0.5.

Buyers' share = 2/2.5 = **80%**; sellers bear 20% — inelastic demanders bear most.

statements.s: Economic incidence depends on elasticities, not on who writes the cheque.
statements.why: Statutory incidence is irrelevant in competitive markets.

statements.s: If demand is perfectly elastic, buyers bear the whole tax.
statements.why: Sellers bear it; price to buyers cannot rise.

statements.s: Backward shifting passes the tax to input suppliers.
statements.why: Through lower input prices.

statements.s: Impact and incidence always coincide.
statements.why: Taxes can be shifted.

quiz.q: Qd = 120 − 2P, Qs = 2P, tax 10 on sellers. Buyer price:
Legal liability for a tax is called:
quiz.why: Impact is where the tax is first levied.

scenes.text: Eighteenth-century England taxed windows; people bricked them up.
The tax raised little but made people worse off — excess burden.

steps.title: Excess burden
steps.body:
- Loss in welfare beyond revenue collected = deadweight loss ≈ ½ × t × ΔQ.
- Rises with the **square** of the tax rate and with elasticities.
- **Lump-sum taxes** have no substitution effect ⇒ no excess burden (but are inequitable/impractical).

steps.title: Solved: DWL
steps.body:
Qd = 100 − P, Qs = P.

- t = 10: Q falls 50 → 45 ⇒ DWL = ½ × 10 × 5 = **25**.
- t = 20: Q = 40 ⇒ DWL = ½ × 20 × 10 = **100** — doubling the tax quadruples DWL.

steps.title: Ramsey rule and Laffer curve
steps.body:
- **Ramsey (inverse elasticity) rule**: to raise revenue with minimum excess burden, tax rates should be inversely proportional to demand elasticities (t_i ∝ 1/|e_i|) — conflicts with equity (necessities are inelastic).
- **Laffer curve**: revenue is zero at 0% and 100% rates and peaks in between; above the peak, cutting rates raises revenue. Where the peak lies is an empirical question.

steps.title: Solved: Ramsey ratio
steps.body:
|e_x| = 0.5, |e_y| = 2.

t_x/t_y = 2/0.5 = **4** — the inelastic good should bear a tax rate four times higher (ignoring equity).

statements.s: Excess burden rises roughly with the square of the tax rate.
statements.why: Both the wedge and the quantity loss grow with t.

statements.s: Lump-sum taxes create no excess burden.
statements.why: They do not change relative prices.

statements.s: The Ramsey rule says tax elastic goods more heavily.
statements.why: Tax inelastic goods more heavily.

statements.s: The Laffer curve implies tax cuts always raise revenue.
statements.why: Only above the revenue-maximising rate.

quiz.q: Qd = 100 − P, Qs = P, t = 6. DWL:
quiz.why: Q falls by 3; DWL = ½ × 6 × 3 = 9.
Inverse ratio of elasticities: 3/1.

quiz.q: Revenue at a 100% income tax rate on the Laffer curve is:
quiz.why: No one would earn taxable income.

scenes.text: Income tax is deducted from Priya's salary.
GST is hidden in every bill she pays at the store.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
- **Direct taxes** (income, corporate, wealth): impact and incidence on the same person; can be progressive; less inflationary; but evasion and disincentive concerns.
- **Indirect taxes** (GST, customs, excise): shifted to consumers; wide coverage; convenient; tend to be regressive relative to income.
- Indirect vs direct in welfare: Hicks–Joseph analysis showed an income tax imposes less welfare loss than an excise raising the same revenue (single-consumer, partial analysis), because it avoids distorting relative prices.

steps.title: Solved: regressivity of a uniform GST
steps.body:
18% GST on consumption. Household A earns ₹2 lakh and consumes all; B earns ₹20 lakh and consumes ₹10 lakh.

- A's GST = 36,000 ⇒ 18% of income.
- B's GST = 1,80,000 ⇒ **9% of income** — regressive relative to income.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying indirect taxes are always regressive — differentiated rates (e.g. exempting essentials) reduce regressivity.
- Confusing incidence relative to income with relative to consumption.

statements.s: Direct taxes are usually more progressive than indirect taxes.
statements.why: Rates can rise with income.

statements.s: A uniform consumption tax is regressive relative to income.
statements.why: Richer households save more.

statements.s: Indirect taxes cannot be shifted.
statements.why: They are typically shifted to consumers.

statements.s: Hicks and Joseph compared income and excise taxes raising equal revenue.
statements.why: Income tax had lower welfare cost in their analysis.

quiz.why: Its burden rests on the company and its owners.

quiz.q: An advantage of indirect taxes is:
quiz.why: They are collected at the point of sale from many buyers.

questions.q: Smith's canons include:
questions.why: The four classic canons.

questions.q: Revenue +15%, GDP +10%. Buoyancy:
Vertical equity means:
questions.why: Different abilities, different taxes.

questions.q: Es = 3, |Ed| = 1. Sellers' share:
Qd = 200 − P, Qs = P, t = 20. Buyer price:
DWL in that case:
Tax revenue in that case:
Ramsey rule recommends higher taxes on goods with:
questions.why: They cause less distortion.

questions.q: Lump-sum taxes avoid:
questions.why: Relative prices are unchanged.

questions.q: Income 10 lakh, consumption 6 lakh, 15% consumption tax. Tax as % of income:
A tax with average rate falling as income rises is:
questions.why: Lower-income people pay a higher share.

questions.why: DWL is proportional to t².

courses.title: Unit 3 · Public expenditure and public debt
courses.summary: Theories of growth of public expenditure (Wagner, Peacock–Wiseman), classification of spending, social cost–benefit analysis, subsidies, and the burden and management of public debt.
outcomes: Explain Wagner's law and the displacement effect
Classify expenditure as revenue/capital and developmental/non-developmental
Perform a simple social cost–benefit analysis
Evaluate subsidies and their targeting
Discuss the burden of public debt and the Domar condition

scenes.text: As countries industrialise, governments take on more roles — regulation, welfare, infrastructure.
Wars and crises push spending up, and it rarely falls back fully.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
- **Wagner's law**: public expenditure grows faster than national income as economies industrialise (income elasticity of public spending > 1).
- **Peacock–Wiseman**: spending rises in steps during social upheavals (wars, crises) — **displacement effect**, **inspection effect** (new needs revealed), **concentration effect** (central government's share rises).
- Baumol's cost disease: productivity lags in services raise relative cost of public services.

steps.title: Solved: testing Wagner
steps.body:
GDP grows 8%; public expenditure grows 10%.

Elasticity = 10/8 = **1.25** > 1 ⇒ consistent with Wagner's law; share of spending in GDP rises.

steps.title: Classification (India)
steps.body:
- **Revenue expenditure**: does not create assets (salaries, interest, subsidies).
- **Capital expenditure**: creates assets or reduces liabilities (roads, loans to states, repayment of debt).
- Older classification: plan/non-plan (dropped from 2017-18); developmental/non-developmental.

statements.s: Wagner's law predicts the share of public spending in GDP rises with development.
statements.why: Income elasticity above one.

statements.s: Peacock–Wiseman emphasised gradual, smooth growth.
statements.why: They emphasised step increases during crises.

statements.s: Interest payments are revenue expenditure.
statements.why: They create no assets.

statements.s: Plan/non-plan classification was dropped from 2017-18.
statements.why: Replaced by revenue/capital focus.

quiz.why: 5/6 ≈ 0.83, inconsistent with Wagner.
It creates a durable asset.

quiz.q: The displacement effect is due to:
quiz.why: Their study of UK spending 1890–1955.

story.title: Should the state build a bridge?

scenes.text: A bridge costs ₹100 crore today and saves travellers time and fuel for years.
Discounting benefits tells us whether society gains.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
- List costs and benefits including externalities; value at **shadow prices** where market prices mislead (e.g. unemployed labour, foreign exchange).
- Discount at a **social discount rate**.
- Decision rules: **NPV > 0**; benefit–cost ratio (BCR) > 1; internal rate of return > social discount rate.
- Approaches: Little–Mirrlees (world prices as numéraire), UNIDO guidelines.

steps.title: Solved: bridge
steps.body:
Cost 100 now; benefits 30 per year for 5 years; r = 8%.

1. Annuity factor = (1 − 1.08⁻⁵)/0.08 = (1 − 0.6806)/0.08 = 3.993.
2. PV of benefits = 30 × 3.993 = **119.8**.
3. NPV = **19.8** > 0; BCR = 1.198 ⇒ build.

steps.title: Solved: shadow wage
steps.body:
Project hires 1,000 workers at ₹400/day from a pool of unemployed whose opportunity cost is ₹150/day.

Shadow labour cost = 1,000 × 150 = **₹1.5 lakh/day** instead of ₹4 lakh — making labour-intensive projects more attractive socially.

statements.s: A project is worthwhile if NPV at the social discount rate is positive.
statements.why: Benefits exceed costs in present value.

statements.s: Shadow wages for unemployed labour may be below market wages.
statements.why: The opportunity cost is low.

statements.s: A higher social discount rate favours long-lived projects.
statements.why: It reduces the weight of distant benefits.

statements.s: Little–Mirrlees uses world prices as numéraire.
statements.why: That is the method's hallmark.

quiz.q: Cost 50; benefit 60 in one year; r = 10%. NPV:

options: market prices don't reflect social opportunity costs
quiz.why: They correct distortions.

scenes.text: Urea is heavily subsidised in India, so farmers use a lot of it.
Over-use of nitrogen relative to other nutrients harms soil balance.

steps.title: Economics of subsidies
steps.body:
- Rationale: merit goods, positive externalities, equity, price stabilisation.
- Costs: fiscal burden, deadweight loss, distortion of input mix, leakages and poor targeting.
- Major Indian subsidies: food (NFSA), fertiliser, petroleum (LPG).
- Reforms: **Direct Benefit Transfer**, targeting via databases, nutrient-based subsidy for P and K fertilisers.

steps.title: Solved: subsidy cost and DWL
steps.body:
Qd = 100 − P, Qs = P. Subsidy ₹10 per unit to producers.

1. New supply Qs = P + 10 ⇒ 100 − P = P + 10 ⇒ P = 45 (buyers), sellers receive 55, Q = 55.
2. Fiscal cost = 10 × 55 = **₹550**.
3. DWL = ½ × 10 × (55 − 50) = **₹25**.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

statements.s: Subsidies can create deadweight loss by encouraging over-consumption.
statements.why: Units are produced whose cost exceeds value.

statements.s: DBT aims to reduce leakages in subsidy delivery.
statements.why: Benefits go directly to bank accounts.

statements.s: Urea is covered by the nutrient-based subsidy scheme.
statements.why: NBS covers P and K fertilisers; urea has a separate regime.

statements.s: Subsidies always improve efficiency.
statements.why: Only when correcting market failures.

quiz.q: Qd = 120 − P, Qs = P, subsidy 20. Quantity:
A justification for subsidising vaccines is:
quiz.why: Vaccination protects others too.

story.title: Do we owe it to ourselves?

scenes.text: Most of India's government debt is held by domestic banks and institutions.
Does debt shift burden to future generations? Economists disagree.

steps.title: Views
steps.body:
- **Classical**: debt is a burden — diverts private saving to unproductive use.
- **Lerner ('we owe it to ourselves')**: internal debt is a transfer among citizens, not a national burden; **external debt** is a real burden (resources go abroad).
- **Buchanan**: burden falls on future taxpayers who pay without having chosen.
- **Modigliani**: debt crowds out capital, leaving future generations a smaller capital stock.
- **Ricardian equivalence** (Barro): timing of taxes does not matter.

steps.title: Domar condition
steps.body: Debt-to-GDP ratio stabilises if nominal growth g exceeds the nominal interest rate r (with primary deficits not too large). Long-run ratio with constant deficit d (share of GDP) and growth g: b* = d/g.

steps.title: Solved: Domar ratio
steps.body:
Fiscal deficit 5% of GDP every year; nominal GDP growth 10%.

Long-run debt ratio b* = 0.05/0.10 = **50% of GDP**. If growth slows to 8%: b* = 62.5%.

statements.s: Lerner argued internal debt is not a burden on the nation as a whole.
statements.why: Interest is a transfer among citizens.

statements.s: External debt involves a real resource transfer abroad.
statements.why: Interest and principal leave the country.

statements.s: Modigliani argued debt can reduce the capital stock left to future generations.
statements.why: Through crowding out.

statements.s: With a constant deficit ratio, higher growth raises the long-run debt ratio.
statements.why: b* = d/g falls.

quiz.q: Deficit 4% of GDP, growth 8%. Long-run debt ratio:
'We owe it to ourselves' is associated with:
quiz.why: Lerner's functional finance view.

questions.why: Spending grows faster than income.

Which is capital expenditure?
questions.why: Loans create financial assets.

BCR with PV benefits 90, PV costs 100:
A higher social discount rate makes long-term projects:
questions.why: Distant benefits are discounted more.

questions.q: Qd = 100 − P, Qs = P, producer subsidy 20. Quantity:
DWL of that subsidy:
Peacock–Wiseman's concentration effect refers to:
questions.why: Crises concentrate functions at the centre.

questions.q: Debt burden on future generations through crowding out is Modigliani's view of:
questions.why: Less private capital is accumulated.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Fiscal federalism
courses.summary: Assignment of functions and taxes across levels of government, Oates' decentralisation theorem, Tiebout sorting, vertical and horizontal imbalances, the economics of grants, and India's federal fiscal architecture including local bodies.
outcomes: Explain the decentralisation theorem and Tiebout model
Distinguish vertical and horizontal fiscal imbalance

steps.title: Theory
steps.body:
- **Musgrave**: stabilisation and distribution mainly central; allocation of local public goods can be decentralised.
- **Oates' decentralisation theorem**: if there are no spillovers and no cost advantage of central provision, local provision matched to local preferences is at least as efficient as uniform central provision.
- **Tiebout (1956)**: mobile citizens 'vote with their feet', sorting into localities offering preferred tax–service bundles — a quasi-market for local public goods.
- Taxes on mobile bases (capital, corporate income) better central; immobile bases (property) suit local governments.

steps.title: Solved: uniform vs local provision
steps.body: Region A wants 10 units of a local good, region B wants 30. Central uniform provision: 20 in both. Welfare loss per region = ½ × (gap)² × slope (slope 1): ½ × 10² = 50 each ⇒ total **100**. Decentralised provision: loss **0** (no spillovers).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring spillovers — they argue for central or coordinated provision.
- Assuming Tiebout works with immobile populations.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:

- **Horizontal imbalance**: differences in fiscal capacity and needs among states.
- Remedies: tax sharing, grants, equalisation formulas.
- In India, states account for the larger share of general government expenditure but a smaller share of revenue raised.

steps.title: Solved: vertical gap

States' own revenue ₹30 lakh crore; states' expenditure ₹55 lakh crore.

scenes.text: A lump-sum grant lets a district spend as it likes.
A matching grant pays half of each rupee spent on schools — making schools 'cheaper' for the district.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Unconditional (lump-sum)**: income effect only.
- **Conditional non-matching (block)**: must be spent on a category; acts like lump-sum if the recipient already spends more than the grant.
- **Matching (open-ended)**: lowers the price of the aided good ⇒ income and **substitution effects** ⇒ larger increase in aided spending per rupee of grant.
- **Flypaper effect**: grant money 'sticks where it hits' — raises local public spending more than an equal rise in residents' income would.

steps.title: Solved: matching grant
steps.body:
A district spends on education E and other goods; budget ₹100 crore. Without grants it spends 30 on E. A 50% matching grant halves the price of E.

If the district's preferences are Cobb–Douglas with 30% share on E:
- Without grant: E = 0.3 × 100/1 = 30.
- With grant (price 0.5): E = 0.3 × 100/0.5 = **60** — grant cost to the Centre = 30.
- A lump-sum grant of 30 instead: E = 0.3 × 130 = **39** — matching grant stimulates E more.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming conditional grants always raise spending on the aided item by the full grant.
- Forgetting the substitution effect of matching grants.

steps.title: Rules used here (assumptions)
steps.body:
FY 2025-26 / **AY 2026-27**, new regime (section 115BAC, default), resident individual, as announced in Budget 2025-26:
- Slabs: 0–4 lakh nil; 4–8 lakh 5%; 8–12 lakh 10%; 12–16 lakh 15%; 16–20 lakh 20%; 20–24 lakh 25%; above 24 lakh 30%.

steps.title: Features
steps.body:
- Destination-based, dual GST (CGST + SGST; IGST inter-state).
- Input tax credit removes cascading.
- Original structure (2017): 0, 5, 12, 18, 28% plus compensation cess.
- 2025 rationalisation: mainly **5% and 18%**, with a special higher rate on select luxury/demerit items; compensation cess being phased out.
- Composition scheme for small taxpayers; GSTN IT backbone; e-invoicing and e-way bills.
- Excluded: alcohol for human consumption; petroleum products currently outside GST levy.

steps.body:
Supplier sells inputs ₹400 (+72 GST); manufacturer sells ₹1,000 (+180); retailer sells ₹1,300 (+234).

Net payments: supplier 72; manufacturer 180 − 72 = 108; retailer 234 − 180 = 54. Total = **234** = 18% of final value ✓.

steps.body:

courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Demand and its elasticities, cardinal utility, indifference-curve analysis with the budget line, income and substitution effects, and consumer surplus.
outcomes: Learners can compute point and arc elasticities and apply the revenue test
Learners can find consumer equilibrium with utility and indifference curves
